World.title: Nigerian economy: The micro sits on the macro, By ‘Tope Fasua
World.content:
Luckily the worst is over. The years 2023 and 2024 were for reform adjustments. While 2025 was the year that inflation went down and stayed down. From 2026 and going forward, these are the years we will start to count the sectors that are soaring and the human beings that are touched positively. But all over the world, it is now about hard work, good sense, adaptation, tech and so on. Nobody should sit back to be served on a platter, especially if you are young, able, educated and eligible.

A lot has aligned for the Nigerian economy. It is certainly not the doom and gloom that some people paint. And those of us who keenly study every movement in the economy must never be cowed to point out what’s working. We stand at a threshold, an epoch of greatness. But we must manage our enthusiasm. Life is not a bed of roses anywhere in the world. It will never be in Nigeria – or anywhere – for everyone. We must therefore test our statements, our expectations, for reasonability. For now, a lot is aligning on the macro space, waiting for the micro to layer on. In fact, the micro is already working for some segments of the economy. It’s also important to know that no nation stands in isolation; we work within a global ecosystem. There cannot be job losses and fears from AI in other countries while we merely complain about graduates not finding employment here, rather than think hard and reposition, for instance. That said, here are some 20-ish indices currently ‘giving’ on the macro side, as Gen Zees will say:

Falling inflation at 14.63 per cent. Targeting single digit by 2027. Falling interest rate levels. Targeting single digit. The Central Bank has already signalled this with a 300 basis points (3 per cent) interest rate reset. GDP growing at 4.43 per cent. Prospects to hit 5 per cent or more by end of year. Growing naira GDP figures. From ₦250 trillion five years ago to ₦531 trillion today. It is important to make this distinction because whereas measuring dollar GDP is important for global comparisons, we spend Naira in Nigeria and purchasing power parity economics teaches us that comparing dollar for dollar from US to Nigeria is erroneous and dishonest. A dollar here does the work of ten in the US. Even at that, there is a major recovery in our Dollar GDP from $253 trillion in 2024 to $377 billion today. ₦130 trillion or $100 bn added to Nigerian stock market and 94 per cent of players are local, meaning that Nigerians are prioritising Nigeria and bringing back money into the country from abroad. $100 bn of inflow is remarkable. And a burgeoning stock market means healthy companies across all sectors. The stock market is a barometer for the whole economy. Nigeria recapitalised banks with 80 per cent local money for ₦4.75 trillion Recapitalised insurance companies with local money with up to ₦1.5 trillion Nigeria has had three years straight of growing balance of payment surpluses. That is $12 billion for the first half of 2026. It was $6 billion for the whole of 2024 Nigeria has had 13 straight quarters of trade surpluses since Bola Tinubu ascended. We have been selling more than we buy as a country. This is significant. Stable to strengthening Nnaira – with adequate reserves, market makers believe the naira is now UNDERVALUED and will gain to at least 1200 to the $ by end of year or into next year. Even the IMF calls the naira at ₦1.127 to the US dollar. Foreign reserves at 18 years high of $56 trillion with prospects to beat the 2007 high of $62 billion, thus setting new records and showing great economic stability. Robust capital inflow of $6 billion in the first half of 2026 alone. Zero states owing salaries unlike 27 under Buhari, 20 under Jonathan and 10 under Obasanjo. Pensioners’ liabilities getting cleared at federal and state levels. Low debt to GDP ratio of 38 per cent, signalling an under-borrowed nation by peer comparison. Highly liquid states with growing Investments in local infrastructure e.g. local roads and bridges, agriculture and water, among other ventures. Rẹ-industrialisation now happening with Nigerian companies standing in the breach. FMCGs, car assemblies, lithium factories, solar panel factories, even a chip maker in the semiconductor arena, apart from Fintechs and banks now taking their businesses abroad. In the oil and gas space, about 55 per cent of Nigeria’s crude production is now handled by local players – Seplat, Rennaisance, MRS, and the rest. Explosion of e-Commerce and payment systems repositioning many Nigerians into better business liquidity. Our fintechs have taken their businesses to Europe, for instance. More investments by states and the federal government in agriculture for food security. Plus, private sector participation in mechanised farming. Niger. Jigawa. Kano are some of the states in this space. There seems to be an explosion of real estate and construction sectors. Many have complained that rents and house prices have leapfrogged. That may mean a new upper and middle class is being created from the ashes of the old system.

Many more developments exist that I may not have captured. These form the MACROECONOMIC FOUNDATIONS upon which microeconomic or the people’s bellies and pockets are meant to thrive. I have preached that building a solid foundation (macroeconomy) for the country was very crucial. Focusing on immediate needs of the people is important, but without a foundation from which we could spring, it will be a waste of time and resources, and a courtship with economic collapse. If you want to build a skyscraper, a solid base is important. The government cannot keep throwing bricks in the hoping that they will stick together. There must be method, deliberateness, seriousness and focus. Even Mr. President’s worst opponents agree that something has shifted for good in the macro space. They cannot wriggle away from that. The international community acknowledges too.

And already, even in the micro space – people’s kitchens, people’s pockets, company balance sheets, some momentum is already being achieved. Some sectors are moving ahead of the pack and redefining their destinies.

Below are the segments already benefiting from this great repositioning:

Civil servants across the country who now get paid regularly. They number in MILLIONS…they and their dependants are doing better today Students benefiting from NELFUND, and their parents who would have been under tremendous pressure to come up with school fees. These parents have been saved the trouble of coming up with close to ₦400 billion in school fees. Some 1.6 million students are benefiting from NELFUND and getting ₦20,000 monthly stipends means ₦32 billion relieving their troubles. This money goes to landlords, mamaputs, markets around the students. Universities and polytechnics now getting their fees regularly and fulfilling their contractual obligations with contractors and teachers and non-teaching staff. Hence no major strikes and delays for students. Exporters of commodities and FCMGs …including Nigerian car companies. They benefit from a weaker Naira but are making brisk business. Workers, regulators and contractors of oil and gas companies. They make more money when crude prices are high. They number at least a million and have many dependants (each oil company worker has an average of 10 dependants – workers and family. Banks, telecoms, fintech companies, their staff and dependents. These companies declare trillion in yearly profits. Our fintechs are very aggressive and are setting global records. Manufacturing companies, their staff, value chain suppliers, and their dependants. A few years ago, these companies made losses. Many couldn’t find dollars to bring in their inputs of machinery, spares etc. Today, they no longer suffer. Google and see that the FMCG conglomerates are back in black. Companies who understand tech leverage especially those who have online presence. Many Nigerians are making cool money from the new global and Nigerian Economy from the comfort of their homes eg online deliveries. I have realised that many companies that complain are/were unable to develop and online presence and expand their markets or are steeped in some obsolescence. Media workers …broadcasters.. on-air personalities, companies, and their dependants. In the new info age, these guys are minting it. Sometimes from spreading sensational news about Nigeria. That gets the clicks. Yes State government contractors, their staff and dependants. States now pay contractors quickly because they are very liquid. Many contractors now choose to work at state level. And by many reports (World Bank, NBS etc), there is an explosion of infrastructure building at state level. Transporters using CNG and making super profits. Those in the outsourcing space including young Nigerians who work remotely for foreign companies. Tech gurus. Real estate sector where they sell properties in the billions and somehow find clients. Plus, there’s a real real estate boom in most Nigerian cities. Entertainers, Event planners, Caterers. I know a local caterer who bought the land where she sells recently for about ₦300m. I was shocked. She told me herself. I know another that just completed her building worth over a billion naira.

So, I believe millions of Nigerians are already being touched. The civil service at state and local government level alone consist of between three to four million people, who have multiple dependents. Getting their arrears paid and getting their salaries promptly is something – at least the food poverty problem is mostly solved for them. The other sectors and activities we have analysed above too matter. And for each job or activity that is revived, there are many people who are touched in the loop. As u rounded this up, I was sent one of those viral WhatsApp posts by one of the President’s ardent opposers. It went like ‘Some educated Nigerians believe that hunger is reforms, poverty is reforms’ etc. There you go. I replied to the man – a former bank MD – immediately, wondering how some Nigerians expect reforms to bring no adjustments. Some Nigerians want change. But it has to be someone else changing.

Luckily the worst is over. The years 2023 and 2024 were for reform adjustments. While 2025 was the year that inflation went down and stayed down. From 2026 and going forward, these are the years we will start to count the sectors that are soaring and the human beings that are touched positively. But all over the world, it is now about hard work, good sense, adaptation, tech and so on. Nobody should sit back to be served on a platter, especially if you are young, able, educated and eligible. Step up! Stake your claim in the productive space. Stay positive and things will change for the better. More of the benefits are coming. And you can look at the policies I listed above line by line and see whatever I didn’t capture. Each policy opens a new vista of possibilities.

‘Tope Fasua is the special adviser to the President on Economic Matters.

World.title: Africa’s downstream petroleum sector at defining point of transformation – NMDPRA’s ex-CEO
World.content:
The former Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA), Farouk Ahmed, has called for effective and efficient regulation of Nigeria’s downstream petroleum sector amid ongoing reforms and changing global market dynamics.

Mr Ahmed, who resigned last year after corruption and abuse-of-office allegations levelled against him by Aliko Dangote, President and Chief Executive of the Dangote Group, made the call while delivering a goodwill message at the celebration of 20 years of OTL Africa Downstream Energy Week in Lagos.

“My four decades of experience have reinforced one enduring lesson: that is, effective regulation cannot operate in isolation from the industry it serves. Good regulation rests on sound policy, credible data, professional competence, meaningful stakeholder consultation, transparency and a clear-eyed understanding of market realities,” he said.

The appearance marks the first time Mr Ahmed has spoken publicly at an industry event since leaving the regulatory agency. He was also presented with an award of special recognition for his role in the growth and success of OTL Africa Energy Week at the gala.

Mr Dangote had accused the former NMDPRA chief of economic sabotage, alleging that the regulator’s policies undermined domestic refining in Nigeria.

He specifically accused the NMDPRA leadership of colluding with international traders and petroleum importers to frustrate local refining by continuing to issue import licences for petroleum products.

Mr Dangote also questioned Mr Ahmed’s sources of wealth, alleging that four of his children attended secondary schools in Switzerland at a combined cost of several million dollars. He argued that the expenditure raised questions about possible conflicts of interest and the integrity of regulatory oversight in the downstream petroleum sector.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Dangote further alleged that Mr Ahmed spent more than $5 million on his children’s secondary education in Switzerland. He identified the children and their schools as Faisal Farouk of Montreux School; Farouk Jr. of Aiglon College; Ashraf Farouk of Institut Le Rosey; and Farhana Farouk of La Garenne International School. According to Mr Dangote, each child spent six years at their respective institutions.

In December last year, Mr Dangote petitioned the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC) through his lawyer, accusing Mr Ahmed of corruption, abuse of office and economic sabotage. Mr Ahmed has denied any wrongdoing.

The petition followed a public dispute between both men over petroleum importation policies implemented under Mr Ahmed’s leadership at the NMDPRA.

Mr Dangote maintained that the policies undermined Nigeria’s domestic refining capacity, particularly the operations of his multi-billion-dollar refinery.

However, Mr Ahmed had argued that petroleum supply in Nigeria should not be monopolised and that import permits should remain accessible to other market players to promote competition.

Against the backdrop of the allegations and controversy, Mr Ahmed eventually resigned from the NMDPRA.

Regulation and industry transformation

In his remarks at the OTL Africa event, Mr Ahmed argued that responsible operators must recognise that regulation, when properly designed, consistently applied, and fairly enforced, provides the certainty, confidence, and stability required for investment, competition, and sustainable growth.

“This is why platforms such as OTL are important. They help bridge the gap between regulatory objectives and commercial realities. They encourage constructive dialogue, promote mutual understanding, and create opportunities for stakeholders to move beyond competing interests towards common solutions,” he said.

He said he attended the occasion with the perspective of a professional who has devoted more than four decades to petroleum regulation and industry development, including his experience as the NMDPRA’s pioneer Chief Executive.

From that perspective, Mr Ahmed said institutions and platforms that endure for two decades do so because they address genuine needs, deliver sustained value and remain responsive to changing demands.

“OTL Africa has demonstrated these qualities. Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, twenty years is more than a milestone; it is a testament to vision, resilience, consistency, and the power of partnership,” he said.

Over the years, he noted, OTL has provided a platform for regulators, operators, investors, policymakers and other stakeholders to exchange ideas, examine emerging challenges, share experiences and collectively seek solutions to issues confronting the industry.

He said the importance of such a platform could not be overstated, given the strategic role of the petroleum and energy industries in economic development.

According to him, the downstream sector affects virtually every aspect of economic life, from transportation and manufacturing to power generation, agriculture, trade and household welfare. Its efficiency, stability and sustainability, he added, have direct implications for national development and people’s quality of life.

Africa’s downstream industry at a turning point

Mr Ahmed said Africa’s downstream petroleum industry was at a defining point of transformation, requiring coordinated and decisive action from governments and industry stakeholders.

He identified energy security, infrastructure deficits, financing constraints, product quality, supply-chain efficiency, market integration, environmental sustainability and the changing global energy landscape as some of the critical issues confronting the industry.

While describing these challenges as significant, he said they also presented considerable opportunities for Africa.

The continent, he argued, has the potential to develop a more integrated, competitive, efficient and resilient downstream energy market.

Realising this potential, he said, would require stronger regional cooperation, investment in storage and distribution infrastructure, modern refining capacity, appropriate technology, transparent market practices and regulatory frameworks that encourage investment while protecting consumers and the public interest.

He also emphasised the need to invest in human capital, noting that the industry’s future would depend not only on infrastructure and capital but also on the competence, integrity and innovative capacity of the professionals who operate and regulate it.

Mr Ahmed urged OTL to evolve beyond a conference and exhibition platform into a stronger catalyst for practical industry solutions, strategic partnerships, investment opportunities and measurable outcomes.

He said discussions at the event should translate into action, partnerships should develop into projects, and ideas generated should contribute to tangible improvements across Africa’s energy value chain.

Institutional continuity and future of the industry

The former regulator also emphasised the importance of institutional continuity, calling for the preservation and transfer of industry knowledge and experience to younger professionals.

He said the experience accumulated over decades must be deliberately shared to prepare the next generation of regulators, entrepreneurs, engineers and energy leaders to address emerging challenges with fresh strategic thinking.

As OTL marked its 20th anniversary, Mr Ahmed urged industry stakeholders to look beyond celebrating past achievements and renew their commitment to the sector’s future.

He called on regulators to strengthen their commitment to fairness, transparency and predictable policies; operators to pursue efficiency, innovation and responsible business practices; investors to provide the capital and long-term commitment required for sustainable development; and policymakers to improve the business environment.

“Above all, let us recognise that Africa’s energy future cannot be built by regulators alone, by operators alone, or by investors alone. It must be built through partnership, trust, and a shared determination to succeed,” he said.

He expressed the hope that OTL’s next 20 years would deliver stronger partnerships, greater investment, smarter regulation, more efficient markets and broader, more reliable energy access for Africans.

“Let us not merely gather to discuss Africa’s energy future; let us unite—with purpose, discipline and urgency—to build it,” he said.

World.title: Badejo’s Timor-Leste award and the power of unseen diplomacy, By Anuoluwapo Deborah Babawale
World.content:
…this honour spotlights Nigerian excellence on the global diplomatic stage. While Nigeria frequently dominates international headlines for its own domestic security and governance struggles, Nigerians like Professor Badejo have spent decades designing peace and governance architectures across Somalia, Liberia, Darfur, and Guinea-Bissau. This award is undeniable proof that Nigeria possesses the intellectual and diplomatic capital to solve complex governance crises, raising the question of how much more we could achieve if we fully harnessed that same institutional expertise at home.

The survival of a nation extends far beyond the medals and applauses garnered at high-level ceremonies. Instead, it takes people sitting in windowless rooms while negotiating with hostile military juntas. Many time they get no applause for their efforts, but if they make one clerical error, a peace treaty can collapse entirely.

Recently, President José Ramos-Horta of Timor-Leste conferred the prestigious Medal of the Order of Timor-Leste on Nigerian scholar-diplomat and founder of Yintab Strategy Consults, Professor Babafemi A. Badejo. Yet, amidst the diplomatic fanfare, the moment that struck me most was Badejo’s acceptance speech. Rather than claiming sole credit for what he has achieved, he dedicated the medal to “every quiet peace support operation official and mediator, every civil society worker, and every ordinary citizen who does the unglamorous work of holding a country together while nobody is watching or applauding.”

High-profile presidential summits and United Nations (UN) speeches are just 10 per cent of the iceberg visible above the water. The “unglamorous work” that Mr Badejo highlighted is the 90 per cent beneath the surface, holding everything up.

This is the true baseline of peace. It is the quiet resilience of the market woman who ensures that food keeps moving despite a coup, the teachers who open classrooms amidst political unrest, and the ordinary citizens who line up in the scorching sun or pouring rain, risking everything to vote democracy back into existence.

The significance of this award also extends far across the continental stage. Here we have an Asian president and Nobel Peace Prize laureate from Timor-Leste, a small nation that survived its own conflict, honouring a Nigerian professor for helping to fix governance in a West African Lusophone nation. This is South-South cooperation in its purest form…

Alongside these is an invisible army of peacebuilders: grassroots mediators de-escalating community tensions before a shot is fired, local early warning monitors tracking threat indicators in fragile rural zones, and technical advisors staying up past midnight turning political grievances into workable constitutional frameworks. Together, they hold nations together while global superpowers look the other way.

This philosophy of quiet, foundational institution-building defined the mission that earned Badejo his honour in Timor-Leste. From January 2013 to June 2014, following a disruptive military coup in Guinea-Bissau, Professor Badejo served as chief of staff to Mr Ramos-Horta, then special representative of UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon. Together, they rebuilt the fractured working relationship between the United Nations and ECOWAS, and helped restore constitutional order through transparent elections in 2014, a process to which Timor-Leste contributed over US$8 million.

Working alongside a Timorese technical team, they designed the Governance Efficacy Amelioration Programme (GEAP), a blueprint recognised by UN Security Council Resolution 2157. While the 2014 election was the visible milestone that everyone celebrated, the underground technical work of building institutional reforms like GEAP, so the government could actually function, was the unseen labour that prevented an immediate relapse into crisis. Rather than chasing quick fixes, Badejo’s career has consistently connected peace, human rights, humanitarianism, and development, seen across his foundational role in the 2000 Djibouti Initiative for Somalia, the African Union Humanitarian Agency (AUHA) framework, and his Situational Quadruple Nexus (SQN) model.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The significance of this award also extends far across the continental stage. Here we have an Asian president and Nobel Peace Prize laureate from Timor-Leste, a small nation that survived its own conflict, honouring a Nigerian professor for helping to fix governance in a West African Lusophone nation. This is South-South cooperation in its purest form: Global South nations stepping up to solve each other’s crises without waiting for Western powers.

The image of Professor Badejo holding up that medal for the “unseen peacebuilders” sends a powerful message: quiet labour for peace matters, even when no cameras are rolling. Africa will only secure lasting stability when we stop obsessing over ceremonial summits and start valuing and investing in the quiet, unglamorous work of institution-building, civil society, and everyday citizens working hand in hand to build our nations.

With West Africa currently grappling with a resurgence of unconstitutional changes of government, militia violence, and shrinking civic space, this recognition is a timely wake-up call for African leaders. Instead of waiting for a foreign “messiah” to rescue our institutions, we must look inward and pool our own capabilities. As Badejo rightly noted, “small” Timor-Leste committed $8 million and technical expertise to help stabilise Guinea-Bissau. When developing nations merge their financial resources, technical intellect, and grassroots resilience, the transformation we desire becomes possible.

Closer home, this honour spotlights Nigerian excellence on the global diplomatic stage. While Nigeria frequently dominates international headlines for its own domestic security and governance struggles, Nigerians like Professor Badejo have spent decades designing peace and governance architectures across Somalia, Liberia, Darfur, and Guinea-Bissau. This award is undeniable proof that Nigeria possesses the intellectual and diplomatic capital to solve complex governance crises, raising the question of how much more we could achieve if we fully harnessed that same institutional expertise at home.

The image of Professor Badejo holding up that medal for the “unseen peacebuilders” sends a powerful message: quiet labour for peace matters, even when no cameras are rolling. Africa will only secure lasting stability when we stop obsessing over ceremonial summits and start valuing and investing in the quiet, unglamorous work of institution-building, civil society, and everyday citizens working hand in hand to build our nations.

Anuoluwapo Deborah Babawale is a political scientist and governance researcher specialising in security architectures and conflict early warning mechanisms.

World.title: Oye laments rising hardship, poverty despite higher revenue for FG, States
World.content:
…Calls for Measurable Results for Govt Spending, Says Revenue Gains Must Translate into Better Lives for Nigerians

The Chairman of the Alliance for Economic Research and Ethics, Dele Kelvin Oye, has called on the Federal and state governments to ensure that increased public revenues translate into better living conditions for Nigerians, noting that Nigeria’s fiscal positions have improved but yet to produce a level of citizen satisfaction that reflects the gains.

Oye said governments must move beyond revenue generation and focus on delivering measurable improvements in public services, infrastructure and economic opportunities.

He made the call while commenting on the revised 2026 State Performance Index (pSPI) by Phillips Consulting, which showed that despite improved fiscal conditions across parts of the federation, citizens’ experience of government performance remained only marginally positive.

The report recorded a national composite citizen satisfaction score of 3.01 out of five, barely above the neutral midpoint of 3.00.

Oye said the findings underscored the need for governments to demonstrate how increased revenues were improving the lives of citizens, rather than relying on budget figures and financial performance indicators.

He noted that higher revenues should create room for governments to repair roads, improve water systems, equip health facilities, support businesses and strengthen education, adding that revenue was only a resource for development, not development itself.

According to the report, finding employment recorded the lowest citizen rating at 2.31, placing it in the critical category. Clean water scored 2.67, government support for businesses 2.71, security 2.84, while law-enforcement conduct recorded 2.85.

Oye said the figures reflected the everyday challenges confronting Nigerians and highlighted the gap between fiscal performance and the quality of public services.

He cautioned that higher revenue could fail to produce meaningful development where funds were poorly allocated, released late, lost through weak procurement or spent on projects that were never completed or maintained.

He said government budgets should therefore be assessed not only by the amount allocated or spent, but by the results achieved and the number of citizens who benefited.

Oye called for the inclusion of measurable service-delivery outcomes in the assessment of government performance, including whether projects were completed on time and within budget, whether public facilities were functional and whether citizens experienced improvements after delivery.

He also urged governments to publish transparent information on public spending, procurement, project completion and service outcomes to enable citizens to monitor how public funds were being used.

The Alliance for Ethics chairman proposed that every state, the Federal Capital Territory and local government publish a 90-day public delivery plan focused on no more than three of its weakest service areas.

He said the plans should contain clear targets, timelines, funding arrangements and publicly accessible monitoring systems, with governments required to explain missed milestones and publish corrective measures.

Oye stressed that the proposed 90-day plans should serve as the first phase of a longer-term delivery programme, rather than promises to resolve complex challenges such as unemployment, insecurity or water access within three months.

He said the objective was to ensure that citizens could track public funds from allocation to project completion and determine whether the resulting services were improving their lives.

Oye further called for stronger coordination among the Federal, state and local governments, noting that challenges such as employment, public safety, water, sanitation and primary healthcare required cooperation across the different tiers of government.

He said the Federal Government should provide a stable national economic environment and transparent funding arrangements, while state and local governments must ensure that resources within their control were efficiently managed and directed towards the needs of citizens.

Oye maintained that stronger fiscal conditions offered governments an opportunity to improve public welfare, but insisted that the opportunity must be matched by transparency, accountability and effective use of public resources.

He said the ultimate test of government performance was not the size of its revenue or budget, but the quality of life that public spending made possible for Nigerians.

According to him, “Nigeria is at a crucial point in its public-finance journey. State governments have recently received and reported higher nominal revenues. That should create room to repair roads, improve water systems, equip health facilities, support enterprise and strengthen education. But revenue is not development; it is only the resource from which development may be built.

“The revised 2026 pcl. State Performance Index (pSPI) puts this challenge in clear view. It records stronger fiscal conditions across parts of the federation, aided by larger Federation Account distributions, higher VAT receipts, exchange-rate effects and other national macroeconomic adjustments. Yet the report’s 2026 citizen survey records a national composite score of only 3.01 out of 5, just above its neutral midpoint of 3.00.

“The conclusion should be sober. The figure does not prove that public services have not improved at all. It does show that stronger fiscal conditions have not yet translated into a level of citizen experience that commands broad confidence. Under the report’s own scale, satisfaction only marginally outweighs dissatisfaction.”

He added, “Alliance for Ethics will treat the pSPI as a starting point for accountability, not a final judgment on any state. We will ask whether governments publish delivery compacts, make data usable, manage fiscal risks, complete projects, maintain public assets and respond to the services citizens rate most weakly.

“Citizens, journalists, civil society and businesses should keep asking five questions: What exactly changed? Where is the independent evidence? Who benefited and who was left out? What did it cost, including future debt? Can the public inspect the result without an appointment, a press pass or special access?

“Nigeria does not lack revenue headlines, plans or project announcements. What it needs is a more rigorous public ethic: money must be allocated well, released on time, spent transparently, converted into functioning services and measured by the change it produces in people’s lives.

“The pSPI’s score of 3.01 is not a reason for despair. It is a reason for discipline. Higher nominal receipts create an opportunity; only effective utilisation and measurable outcomes create development. A government should be judged not only by the size of its budget, but by the quality of life its budget makes possible.”

World.title: 2027: Political permutations favour Tinubu – Deputy Senate President
World.content:
Deputy Senate President, Barau Jibrin.

By Henry Umoru

ABUJA- THE Deputy President of the Senate, Senator Barau Jibrin, APC, Kano North has expressed optimism that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu will emerge victorious in the January 16, 2027, presidential election, citing assessments by political analysts and the prevailing political situation in the country.

Senator Barau spoke at the weekend during the inauguration of campaign committees for Dawakin Tofa, Tofa and Rimin Gado Local Government Areas of Kano State, where he charged party members to work collectively towards securing victory for all candidates of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in the forthcoming general elections.

In a statement signed on Sunday by his Special Adviser, Media and Publicity, Ismail Mudashir, the Deputy President of the Senate said the foundation laid by President Tinubu during his first term would, by the grace of Allah, yield the desired results in his second term.

Barau Jibrin who expressed appreciation to party leaders, elected representatives, local government chairmen, Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf and other stakeholders for their support and commitment to the APC, assured them that the unity and cooperation currently enjoyed by the party would be sustained.

“Based on the assessments of political analysts and the current state of Nigerian politics, all indications suggest that, by Allah’s grace, Bola Ahmed Tinubu will win the presidential election,” he said.

He noted that Kano, being one of the largest states in the country and second only to Lagos in terms of the latest registered voters, deserved greater attention and opportunities from the Federal Government.

According to him, the Governor’s decision to lead the people from the New Nigeria People’s Party (NNPP) to the APC was a strategic move that have enhanced Kano’s political relevance and improved its access to developmental opportunities.

The Deputy President of the Senate expressed confidence that the political unity achieved in Kano would translate into tangible benefits for the people, particularly with the alignment of councillors, local government chairmen, state legislators, members of the National Assembly and the Governor under the APC.

He added that the coming elections would usher in a new phase of political and developmental activities, with elected representatives expected to contribute meaningfully to the development of their respective constituencies.

Senator Barau explained that the campaign committees were carefully constituted to accommodate party leaders, members of the party’s executive committees, former and serving legislators, councillors, local government chairmen, new party members and respected elders.

He urged members of the committees to take their responsibilities seriously and mobilise effectively for the APC ahead of the elections.

“What is required of you is to play your part actively in securing victory. Mobilise, campaign and ensure that all APC candidates emerge victoriously from top to bottom. May Allah grant us success and enable us to achieve our goals,” he said.

ENDS

World.title: 2027: ‘We’ll not allow rigging’ — Dino Melaye warns INEC
World.content:
Former Kogi West senator, Dino Melaye, has accused the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) of taking steps to rig the 2027 general elections, warning that any attempt to manipulate the polls would be resisted.

Melaye made the allegation in a post on his X handle on Sunday, claiming that recent activities by the electoral body suggest what he described as “anticipatory rigging”.

“The activities of INEC in recent times point at anticipatory rigging. Which will be resisted,” Melaye wrote.

The former lawmaker also called on INEC to redeem its image ahead of the 2027 elections, insisting that Nigerians would not tolerate electoral manipulation.

“INEC must be born again this time because we will not allow rigging. Rig and say your final prayer,” he added.

Melaye, a chieftain of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), has remained a vocal critic of the electoral commission since the 2023 general elections.

His comments come amid controversy over the discovery of AI-generated photographs in INEC’s preliminary voters’ register, as well as complaints by political parties over the omission of some candidates from the commission’s final list.

World.title: 2027: ADC-PCC challenges Tinubu to defend failure to deliver electricity
World.content:
By Luminous Jannamike

ABUJA – The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has challenged President Bola Tinubu to account for his failure to deliver on his 2023 electricity pledge, insisting that he should not seek re-election without fulfilling the promise.

The council said Nigerians had not forgotten Tinubu’s categorical declaration during the 2023 presidential campaign that they should not vote for him for a second term if he failed to deliver electricity, dismissing attempts by the APC to reinterpret his words as an afterthought.

In a statement by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, the ADC-PCC was reacting to comments by Dele Alake, spokesperson of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, defending the President’s electricity record.

“Don’t vote for me for second term if I fail to deliver electricity,” the President had told Nigerians during the 2023 campaign.

The opposition campaign council argued that more than three years after the pledge, Nigerians were still grappling with persistent power outages, repeated national grid collapses and inadequate electricity supply.

It accused the Tinubu administration of increasing the financial burden on consumers through higher electricity bills, discriminatory tariff classifications and continued estimated billing, despite the much-publicised Presidential Metering Initiative.

The council also said businesses, including hotels and other hospitality facilities, had resorted to rationing electricity by switching off power for guests during daytime hours to reduce operating costs.

Dismissing the administration’s reliance on the Electricity Act and bond programmes to defend its record, the ADC-PCC insisted that policy documents and financial instruments could not substitute for actual electricity supply.

“An Act is not electricity. A bond prospectus does not power homes and factories. Nigerians cannot eat statutes. What Nigerians need is electricity that works, not another round of explanations and publicity,” the council said.

It further accused the administration of imposing higher tariffs without ensuring reliable supply, leaving households, manufacturers and small businesses to contend with rising operating costs.

The ADC-PCC also questioned the implementation of the Presidential Metering Initiative, alleging that electricity distribution companies continued to impose estimated bills on consumers.

“The President’s own condition for seeking a second term was straightforward: deliver electricity or do not ask Nigerians for another mandate,” the council maintained.

It urged the APC to address the President’s 2023 commitment directly, rather than attempt to dilute his words, warning that the administration’s electricity record would be a major issue as Nigerians prepare to decide whether to renew Tinubu’s mandate in the January 16, 2027 election.
