Meanwhile, Rogan — still the most popular podcaster in the U.S. — has publicly criticized Trump twice: over the White House hosting a UFC fight this summer and the war in Iran.

Comedian and podcaster Theo Von, in glasses, arrives prior to the second inauguration of President Donald Trump at the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 20, 2025. Since then, Von has been more critical of the president. (Al Drago-Pool/Getty Images)

CBC reached out to Rogan, Von, Schulz and Carlson for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.

Right-leaning podcasters mentioning Trump less

In an effort to quantify conservative podcasters' disenchantment with Trump, The Wall Street Journal studied how often podcasters such as Rogan and Ben Shapiro have referred to him since the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election. According to the Journal’s reporting, mentions of Trump have dropped 70 per cent.

" There were two main plunges: one was right after the election, after which it steadily dropped, and then it dipped again after the Iran war started," Wall Street Journal reporter Neil Mehta told CBC News.

Wall Street Journal reporter Neil Mehta has studied how right-leaning podcasters have covered Donald Trump since he was elected president a second time. (CBC)

"Podcasters and content creators are the predominant source of news for young people. But they also prioritize being seen as real and authentic — that’s the sell," Mehta said.

For Sasaki, a number of pivotal moments demonstrate the podcasters' shift away from Trump.

In early October, Theo Von, who hosts This Past Weekend, interviewed New York's left-leaning Mayor Zohran Mamdani. They discussed socialism, affordability and inequality.

"This to me showed what we already could see … that the conversation was really changing," said Sasaki. "In the lead-up to the 2024 election, [Von] had Trump on, who appeared very relatable. And then Mamdani went on the show and appeared even more relatable."

Sasaki also pointed to CBS News exit polling data that showed roughly 60,000 Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 also voted for Mamdani in 2025.

"What Trump and that campaign was able to do in 2024 was go to the spaces where young men were, speak to them in their vernacular with cultural references that they relate to, and say, ‘I know that you’re struggling, I see your struggles and we’re going to do something about it,’" Sasaki said.

But "assuming this demographic of young men is all in on MAGA and can’t swing [away] would be an error in judgment."

Trump out of step with young men: expert

Aparicio said that by potentially not voting in this year's midterms, "I want to emphasize the point that young men should not be taken for granted by the Republicans."

Podcaster Joe Rogan has publicly criticized Donald Trump twice this year, including calling the war in Iran a 'giant quagmire' and not what his MAGA followers voted for. (The Joe Rogan Show/YouTube)

Ultimately, Sasaki believes Trump may be missing what young men in 2026 really care about.

"This demographic is more worried than ever about the economy. They feel very little job security, many can’t imagine ever buying a home and are even living below the poverty line," he said.

Aparicio says Trump began looking untrustworthy shortly after he won in 2024.

"The first real sign was him campaigning that he would release the Epstein files and then began gaslighting his followers [when he took office] and saying they don't exist," he said.

He also believes the economy has gotten worse and that the U.S. involvement in the war in Iran and its endorsement of Israel's actions in Gaza are making things harder for Americans.

"Hopefully if I work hard, I will be able to afford a home and raise a family," Aparicio said.

"The way things are going, I really don’t feel sure about that."

World.title: Carney calls December byelections for 6 ridings in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called byelections for a total of six ridings located in Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan — races that will give the Liberals a chance to strengthen their thin majority in the House of Commons.

The byelections will be held on Dec. 7, according to a news release sent out Sunday morning.

Half of the races will be in Quebec, in the ridings of Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie and Laurier-Sainte-Marie — seats previously held by Bloc Québécois, NDP and Liberal MPs, respectively.

In Ontario, the ridings to be contested are Scarborough North and Brantford-Brant South.

Former Liberal MP Shaun Chen, who had held Scarborough North since 2015, stepped down last August citing health issues . He later ran for Toronto City Council and won .

In September, Conservative Larry Brock resigned as MP for Brantford-Brant South. Prior to his resignation , Brock said he had accepted a position at the Brantford Crown Attorney's office.

WATCH | Liberals sweep B.C., Ontario, Quebec byelections in August: Liberals flip Quebec riding in byelection sweep, CBC News projects | Duration closed caption 2:24 In the first federal byelections since the Canada-U.S. trade war resumed, CBC News projects the Liberals will win all three seats in Quebec, Ontario, and B.C. The Quebec riding of Chicoutimi–Le Fjord will be largely impacted by tariffs.

The Saskatchewan riding is Yorkton-Melville. Conservative Cathay Wagantall had held the seat since 2015 before officially stepping down at the end of August.

As it stands, the Liberals have a thin majority in the House of Commons with 173 seats. Losing all six races will not affect their ability to govern, but wins will allow the party to bolster its ranks.

Another riding will soon be vacant: Parry Sound–Muskoka , which has been represented by Conservative MP Scott Aitchison since 2019. In September, Aitchison said he would officially step down at the end of the fall sitting.

Who's running in Quebec

In the lead-up to the byelection call, parties have been steadily announcing their candidates.

For the Quebec races, the Liberals are running former Quebec MNA Chantal Soucy in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, human rights advocate Jean-Sébastien Vallée in Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie and former Desjardins CEO Guy Cormier in Laurier-Sainte-Marie.

Former Montreal Alouettes player Luc Brodeur-Jourdain will run under the Conservative banner in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton. The party has not yet announced candidates in the other two contests.

Elections Canada signs in the Beaches-East York riding in Toronto on Aug. 31. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

The NDP will run Mathieu Boisvert in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot, former Parti Québécois leadership candidate and labour advocate Pierre Céré in Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie, and epidemiologist Nimâ Machouf in Laurier-Sainte-Marie.

The Bloc Québécois has confirmed former director general of the International Dairy Federation, Caroline Émond, will run under its banner in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton. No other candidates have been announced yet.

In a statement to CBC News on Friday, the Green Party confirmed Martin Grenier will run in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton, while nominations remain open in Rosemont-La Petite-Patrie and Laurier-Sainte-Marie.

Candidates in Ontario and Saskatchewan

In Scarborough North, the Liberals are running former Toronto District School Board trustee James Li and the Greens are running Vicki Jewt. The Conservatives and NDP have not yet announced their candidates.

For Brantford-Brant South, the Liberals will run Joy O'Donnell, president of the Chamber of Commerce Brantford-Brant. The Conservatives will run Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis.

The NDP has not yet announced its candidate, and the Green Party says nominations are open in that riding as well.

Larry Brock stepped down as MP for the Ontario riding Brantford–Brant South, formerly Brantford–Brant South–Six Nations, in September. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

The Conservatives may face a challenge in Brantford-Brant South after the party chose to bypass a local nomination contest and appoint Davis as its candidate. The party said at the time it wanted to ensure a candidate was ready to hit the ground running.

After the appointment of Davis as candidate, pastor and longtime Conservative Dave Carroll announced he would run as an independent candidate in the riding. That could draw votes away from Davis, who is already expected to face an uphill battle against the Liberals.

In Yorkton-Melville, the Liberals are running Aaron Kienle, the Conservatives are running Nelson Pohl and the Greens will run Valerie Brooks. The NDP has not confirmed its candidate yet.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Cost-of-living protests spread across Europe with unrest in France and Germany
World.content:
Cost-of-living protests spread across Europe with unrest in France and Germany

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 15:52 UTC Full article

The protests began a month ago at a high school on the outskirts of Paris over the state of schools and widened to the cost of living

Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of France and Germany on Saturday to protest against the cost of living and deteriorating public services, in mostly peaceful demonstrations that ended in clashes between police and masked groups in several cities. In France, where the third day of protests in a month took place, 565 people were arrested.

According to France’s interior ministry, some 320,000 people took part in about 150 demonstrations across the country, down from an estimated 410,000 the previous weekend. In Paris, 70,000 marched along boulevards on the outskirts to avoid the city centre, some in Halloween costumes. The protests, called by students, trade unions and former members of the “yellow vest” movement, passed off calmly until the end, when masked groups hurled paving stones at police in Paris, who responded with teargas and baton charges. There were also incidents in Marseille, Lyon and Toulouse, where water cannon were used. Four police officers and a gendarme were injured in the capital. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who had deployed 70,000 officers, denounced an “extraordinary” level of violence and described a petrol bomb attack on a riot officer as “attempted murder”.

The protests began a month ago at a high school on the outskirts of Paris over the state of schools and widened to the cost of living. The first major day, on October 17, ended with the looting of hundreds of shops in several cities. Students announced new blockades of high schools and universities on Tuesday and Thursday, ahead of a trade union demonstration called for November 5.

In Germany, thousands of young people demonstrated in dozens of cities at the call of the group “Gen Z regelt!” (“Gen Z has got this”) “for education, health, the climate and an affordable life”. After largely peaceful marches, police used water cannon in Cologne against protesters throwing fireworks; in Frankfurt at least two shops were looted, according to a Reuters witness, and in Hamburg burning barricades were set up, according to the newspaper Bild.

There were also clashes in Tirana, the capital of Albania, at a new protest demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Police were on alert in Barcelona, over calls from an anonymous TikTok network, and in Italy, after recent clashes in Milan, Turin and Bologna.

World.title: Argentine intellectuals reject the Falklands “national cause” amid escalating tensions with London
World.content:
Argentine intellectuals reject the Falklands “national cause” amid escalating tensions with London

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 14:48 UTC Full article

The dissenting voices come at a time of maximum tension

Nearly a hundred Argentine intellectuals, jurists, historians and politicians have signed a declaration rejecting the transformation of the Falklands dispute into a “national cause” that “admits no dissent”, and criticising Javier Milei’s government for acting with “flagrant opportunism” amid escalating tensions with the United Kingdom over the Sea Lion oil project.

The declaration, entitled “Malvinas and dissent” and published in early October in the newspaper Perfil, is signed by, among others, jurist Roberto Gargarella, constitutional lawyer Daniel Sabsay, former justice minister Ricardo Gil Lavedra, former minister Graciela Fernández Meijide, economist Pablo Gerchunoff, writer Santiago Kovadloff and historians Luis Alberto Romero, Hilda Sabato and Federico Lorenz.

The signatories do not deny the dispute. They accept “the existence of this international disagreement”, with its “diplomatic and legal” dimensions, and acknowledge differing views among themselves, for example on whether the islanders should take part in any negotiations. But they warn that the issue “long ago ceased to be essentially a dispute and became a supposed national cause” that “admits no relevant dissent” and brands anyone who strays from it a “bad Argentine”. “The national cause is, in short, an abuse of state, political, social and cultural authority,” they argue. They particularly criticise Article 111 of the sovereignty defence bill, which in their view established “a vague criminal offence and the criminalisation of dissent”; the government acknowledged in mid-October that it would have to be removed. “On Malvinas, this is all we ask: that unanimity stop speaking in our name,” they conclude.

One of the signatories, Alejandro Cowes, who describes himself as a lawyer, went further in a text posted on Saturday in English and Spanish in a public Facebook group about the islands. Cowes accuses the government of using the “sacred national cause” as “a tool for internal state coercion and domestic political consumption” and revives Argentine political scientist Carlos Escudé’s thesis of the “malignant lie”: the idea that a tough policy will raise Britain’s costs, when to do so Argentina would have to multiply its own against a power with far greater resources. He criticises the sanctions on companies linked to hydrocarbon exploitation and the purchase of F-16 fighters, and concludes that the islands are British and that their inhabitants have “the inalienable right to self-determination”, a position not reflected in the collective declaration.

The dissenting voices come at a time of maximum tension. The sovereignty defence bill secured committee approval on October 27, after sanctions were narrowed in response to US objections, and the ruling party plans to debate it in the Chamber of Deputies on November 12. Two days earlier, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will hold the hearing in Hamburg on Argentina’s request to halt Sea Lion. Milei has reiterated that “the Malvinas are Argentine”, while ruling out “military solutions”.

The claim to sovereignty over the islands is enshrined in a transitional provision of Argentina’s Constitution and enjoys broad public support, as the declaration itself acknowledges.

World.title: Democrats seek to retake Congress in Tuesday’s US midterm elections
World.content:
Democrats seek to retake Congress in Tuesday’s US midterm elections

1st Sunday, November 2026 - 14:48 UTC Full article

Trump has headlined 28 rallies during the campaign, all in Republican-leaning states, urging supporters to vote “as if I were on the ballot”

The United States holds midterm elections on Tuesday in which the Democratic Party hopes to regain control of Congress, with the polls in its favour. At stake are all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats, in a vote shaping up as a test of Donald Trump’s second presidency.

Democrats lead Republicans by 51% to 42.6% on the generic ballot, according to a polling average from surveys collected by The New York Times. Polls suggest Republicans will lose the House and do not rule out their losing the Senate as well, a possibility considered remote before the summer. The Cook Political Report has moved races towards the Democrats in recent weeks, with close Senate contests in states such as Texas, Michigan, Kansas and Iowa.

Trump has headlined 28 rallies during the campaign, all in Republican-leaning states, urging supporters to vote “as if I were on the ballot”. Early voting has passed 51 million ballots, pointing to high turnout. Elon Musk has spent at least US$267 million supporting Republican candidates, according to The New York Times.

Polls list the cost of living, the war with Iran and immigration policy among voters’ main concerns, against a backdrop of low presidential approval ratings. Congress has an approval rating of 14%, one of the lowest recorded ahead of a midterm election. A Democratic majority in either chamber would allow the opposition to block White House initiatives and open investigations into the first half of the term.

Besides Congress, Americans will elect thousands of state and local officials and vote on hundreds of ballot measures, including a proposal to tax billionaires in California and a Montana initiative to curb the influence of undisclosed money in campaigns.

World.title: From Montevideo to Luján: Leo XIV’s tour of Uruguay and Argentina
World.content:
From Montevideo to Luján: Leo XIV’s tour of Uruguay and Argentina

31st Saturday, October 2026 - 01:14 UTC Full article

“It fills me with joy to return to the continent where I have lived so many moments of my life,” wrote the pontiff, who was born in Chicago and spent almost two decades as a missionary in Peru

Pope Leo XIV will begin a tour of South America in Montevideo on November 6 that will take him to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, with open-air Masses, meetings with Presidents Yamandú Orsi and Javier Milei, and events with young people, workers and prisoners. His stop in Argentina, from November 8 to 11, will be the first papal visit to the country since John Paul II’s in April 1987.

“It fills me with joy to return to the continent where I have lived so many moments of my life,” wrote the pontiff, who was born in Chicago and spent almost two decades as a missionary in Peru. “May this journey be an opportunity to open our hearts to one another, strengthen our communion as brothers and sisters, and renew our commitment to proclaim the Gospel with joy.” Leo XIV, 71, is recovering from lung cancer surgery on October 13; last week he cancelled a helicopter trip to Assisi as a medical precaution, but the Vatican has announced no changes to the tour.

Uruguay, November 6-8

The Pope will leave Rome on Friday 6 and land at Carrasco airport about eight and a half hours later. That afternoon, Montevideo’s Plaza Independencia will host the official welcome ceremony; he will meet Orsi and celebrate vespers at 7.05 p.m. in the Metropolitan Cathedral.

On Saturday 7 he will fly to Paysandú, on the border with Argentina, to celebrate Mass at 10 a.m. in Parque París Londres. Back in the capital, he will visit the parish of Our Lady of Guadalupe in the Casavalle neighbourhood, meet the education community at the Catholic University of Uruguay and lead a prayer vigil at 7 p.m. at the Centenario Stadium.

On Sunday 8 he will celebrate Mass at 10.30 a.m. in the city of Florida, in front of the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, Uruguay’s patron saint, on her feast day, a coincidence that was decisive in starting the tour there. At 3.10 p.m. he will leave for Buenos Aires.

Argentina, November 8-11

The Pope will land at Aeroparque Jorge Newbery on Sunday 8 at 4.30 p.m. After paying tribute at the monument to General San Martín, he will meet Milei at the Casa Rosada and, at 6.30 p.m., address authorities, civil society and the diplomatic corps at the Palacio Libertad.

On Monday 9 he will visit the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole and celebrate Mass at 11.30 a.m. at the Monument of the Spaniards in Palermo. In the afternoon he will meet trade unionists, business leaders and social movements at the Catholic University of Argentina, work being one of the themes of his pontificate, and leaders of other faiths at the Palacio San Martín, before celebrating vespers with the bishops at the Metropolitan Cathedral.

On Tuesday 10 he will travel to Córdoba, where he will celebrate Mass at 10 a.m. at the Military Aviation School and meet clergy at the cathedral. Back in Buenos Aires, he will lead a youth vigil at 8.15 p.m. at the Monument of the Spaniards.

On Wednesday 11 he will visit the Devoto prison complex and celebrate Mass at 10 a.m. at the Basilica of Our Lady of Luján, the country’s main shrine. The farewell is scheduled for 1.30 p.m. at Ezeiza, from where he will fly to Lima.

Argentina’s government declared the visit of national interest and set three public holidays: Monday 9 nationwide, Tuesday 10 in the city of Buenos Aires and Córdoba province, and Wednesday 11 in Buenos Aires province. Francis, the first Argentine pope, never returned to his country during his pontificate.

World.title: Specialised prosecutors appeal Milei’s dismissal in the $LIBRA case and seek to reopen it
World.content:
Specialised prosecutors appeal Milei’s dismissal in the $LIBRA case and seek to reopen it

30th Friday, October 2026 - 18:21 UTC Full article

According to the prosecutors, the investigation is not exhausted

Argentina’s Office of Administrative Investigations, a specialised prosecution service for crimes committed by public officials, has appealed the dismissal of charges against President Javier Milei, his sister and presidential chief of staff Karina Milei, and nine other defendants in the case over the $LIBRA cryptocurrency, and asked for the investigation to be reopened, arguing that key evidence is still missing.

The office, headed by prosecutor Sergio Rodríguez, joined the case and took over the criminal prosecution, which had been dropped by prosecutor Eduardo Taiano when he requested the dismissals later granted by federal judge Marcelo Martínez De Giorgi. Besides seeking to reopen the case, it filed a subsidiary appeal so that, if the request is rejected, the Federal Appeals Court can review the decision.

According to the prosecutors, the investigation is not exhausted. Pending steps include tracing the funds, recovering and analysing communications, investigating possible commercial agreements and examining the money movements linked to the case. They also question that the evidence was assessed piece by piece rather than as a whole, and argue that technical difficulties or incomplete responses cannot justify closing the case. They also propose examining whether the president’s conduct could amount to the crime of conflicts of interest in the exercise of public office.

The filing responds to a request from two organisations acting in the case as friends of the court, the Centre for the Investigation and Prevention of Economic Crime and the Institute of Comparative Studies in Criminal and Social Sciences, which had criticised Taiano’s handling of the case, including his refusal to summon Milei for questioning. The decision now rests with Federal Court No. 8, temporarily headed by Judge Daniel Rafecas while Martínez De Giorgi is on leave. The investors who lost money, removed from their role as plaintiffs, have also appealed and are awaiting a ruling from the Federal Court of Criminal Cassation.

In February 2025, Milei shared the $LIBRA cryptocurrency on X; its value soared and collapsed within hours, causing losses for thousands of investors. The president deleted the post, denied promoting the project and has rejected any wrongdoing.

World.title: Hackers steal US$6.3 billion in crypto from Binance in the sector’s biggest-ever heist
World.content:
Hackers steal US$6.3 billion in crypto from Binance in the sector’s biggest-ever heist

30th Friday, October 2026 - 18:18 UTC Full article

The Secret Service, the federal agency responsible for financial crimes, said it was “working around the clock” with the private sector “to identify, freeze, trace, and recover” the funds

Hackers stole about US$6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, the world’s largest digital asset exchange, in the biggest theft in the sector’s history, which the US Secret Service is investigating with other agencies. Blockchain analytics firms point to a hacking group linked to North Korea, though there has been no official attribution.

Most of the theft took place in about 20 minutes from 20:05 GMT on Thursday, from the wallets Binance uses to process transactions, according to TRM Labs. Its chief policy officer, Ari Redbord, told the BBC that such speed “is the product of long preparation”: the attackers had funded an operator wallet 36 hours earlier and prepared in advance the signatures to authorise the transfers. According to TRM, they compromised the platform’s “signing infrastructure”.

Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng said the attack “was not carried out by one person”. The initial investigation pointed to an engineer’s laptop, but “additional points of breach” were later uncovered. The attackers exploited an Ethereum network mechanism known as EIP-7702 to gain control of a wallet without passing through normal approval controls, and used a “self-destruct mechanism” to erase their traces, according to Teng, who said customer losses would be covered by the company’s protection fund, a US$1 billion bitcoin reserve, and its own resources. Binance says it has begun recovering some funds. Withdrawals remain suspended and the company expects to resume them within about 40 hours; it will publish a full proof-of-reserves report on Monday.

The Secret Service, the federal agency responsible for financial crimes, said it was “working around the clock” with the private sector “to identify, freeze, trace, and recover” the funds, in coordination with the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia. The FBI said it was “aware of the incident”.

About half of the stolen assets were stablecoins that their issuers — Tether, Circle, Ripple and World Liberty Financial, the Trump family’s crypto venture — have frozen. TRM estimates that about US$2.4 billion in bitcoin and ether is beyond reach, as no company can block them.

TRM Labs and Chainalysis said they had “high confidence” that the culprit is TraderTraitor, also known as Lazarus, a North Korea-linked group the FBI blamed for the theft of about US$1.5 billion from the Bybit exchange in 2025, until now the sector’s largest. Chainalysis detected Binance funds commingling with those from another recent attack attributed to North Korean actors. Pyongyang routinely denies involvement in such thefts. Bitcoin fell about 4% after news of the attack.

World.title: Leo XIV becomes the first pope to vote in a US election
World.content:
Leo XIV becomes the first pope to vote in a US election

30th Friday, October 2026 - 17:17 UTC Full article

The Chicago-born pope voted “as a citizen” and as he has done “whenever he has had the opportunity”, according to a statement from the Holy See press office

Pope Leo XIV has voted by mail in the US midterm elections to be held on November 3, making him the first pontiff to take part in an election in that country, the Vatican said on Friday.

The Chicago-born pope voted “as a citizen” and as he has done “whenever he has had the opportunity”, according to a statement from the Holy See press office. “In keeping with this well-established practice of civic participation, he sent his ballot by mail to Chicago,” the statement said, without indicating whom he voted for.

Robert Francis Prevost, as he was known before his election as pope in May 2025, spent almost two decades in Peru as a missionary and later as a bishop, and holds US and Peruvian citizenship. “The Holy Father also confirmed that during his years of residence in Peru he exercised his right to vote whenever he met the requirements to do so,” the Vatican said.

Leo XIV, 71, is recovering from lung cancer surgery on October 13. He is due to begin a tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on November 6, running until November 17.

World.title: Venezuela names Oliver Blanco, a former opposition aide, as foreign minister
World.content:
Venezuela names Oliver Blanco, a former opposition aide, as foreign minister

30th Friday, October 2026 - 17:00 UTC Full article

A graduate in International Studies, Blanco was an aide to Henry Ramos Allup, a leader of the opposition Democratic Action party, when he presided over the National Assembly elected in 2015

Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez has appointed Oliver Blanco, a 35-year-old diplomat who began his political career alongside a veteran opposition leader, as foreign minister in a reshuffle of her government’s international team. Blanco replaces Félix Plasencia, whom Rodríguez has tasked with moving to the United Kingdom to recover Venezuelan gold held at the Bank of England.

“I will defend our sovereignty and the national interest, always working to achieve concrete benefits for the people,” Blanco said on taking office, adding that the moment requires “building from our differences” a country where “everyone has a place”. Rodríguez said she hoped “this strengthened team will keep advancing the changes and Venezuela’s geopolitical recovery, in areas of cooperation and friendship with all countries”.

A graduate in International Studies, Blanco was an aide to Henry Ramos Allup, a leader of the opposition Democratic Action party, when he presided over the National Assembly elected in 2015, the first controlled by the opposition. After stepping back from party politics, he joined Rodríguez’s government following the US military operation in January that removed Nicolás Maduro from power: he was appointed deputy minister for Europe and North America on February 23 and, in July, first deputy foreign minister. Since then he has been involved in restoring relations with countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Chile and Israel.

Plasencia, an associate of Rodríguez since the 1990s, becomes head of International Affairs at the Presidency with a specific task. “He must settle in the United Kingdom until we recover the gold that belongs to Venezuelans,” Rodríguez said. The gold, some 31 tonnes of bars from the Central Bank of Venezuela’s reserves worth about US$4 billion, has been frozen at the Bank of England since 2019, when London recognised Juan Guaidó as interim president. Its recovery is one of the government’s main demands in its negotiations with the opposition led by Dinorah Figuera.

Rodríguez also appointed Marynna Saatdjian as deputy minister for North America and Europe, Saúl Ameliach as deputy minister for International Trade and Yuri Pimentel, a former communications minister under Hugo Chávez, as first deputy foreign minister. The changes come a day after the acting president promised elections under a “renewed” electoral authority, without setting a date.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Baja man protests three-week CFE outage by hosting open bar in lobby
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

LA PAZ, Baja California Sur — Demonstrating remarkable civic resourcefulness in the face of infrastructure challenges, a local resident whose electricity was cut off for three weeks converted the customer service lobby of the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) into a temporary open-bar hospitality suite on Tuesday afternoon.

Equipped with a five-speed countertop blender, a sack of limes, coarse salt and bottles of tequila and damiana, the La Paz resident plugged directly into a primary outlet behind the ticket-dispensing kiosk, offering freshly blended margaritas to fellow customers waiting in line for billing dispute resolutions.

“If the federal grid cannot deliver electricity to my freezer, I must bring my ice to the grid,” said the resident, who noted that three weeks of unanswered service tickets and unkept reconnection promises had left his home appliances thoroughly non-functional. “The administrative process takes three hours anyway. It is simply good manners to offer refreshments while we wait for ticket number 47 to be called.”

CFE staff reportedly observed the operation with a mixture of bureaucratic neutrality and procedural deliberation, noting that while utility regulations prohibit unauthorized commercial vending in public facilities, current policy contains no explicit clause regarding the non-commercial distribution of frozen cocktails in waiting areas.

The impromptu tasting station quickly stabilized lobby morale, with several citizens in line offering to supply additional ice and fresh citrus in exchange for priority access to the blender’s frozen treats. One CFE employee estimated that the protest successfully reduced perceived wait times across the branch by about 40%, despite no change in actual ticket processing speed.

Utility representatives later confirmed that while the man’s power status remains under review, official policy guidelines are currently being evaluated to determine whether guest appliance usage in administrative lobbies constitutes a billable service tier.



The not-quite-so-powerless resident, meanwhile, promised to bring the rest of his kitchen appliances the following day if his service still hadn’t been reinstated.

World.title: In Tepoztlán, the dead get one more week to celebrate
World.content:
If you’ve ever seen Disney’s “Coco,” you’ll remember Miguel Rivera had to complete his journey from the Land of the Dead to the world of the living before the afterlife closed for another year. In Mexican culture, that’s usually one day after the veil between the two planes is lifted.

But in Tepoztlán, a Pueblo Mágico with mountains resembling the world of “Avatar,” the farewell to the dead doesn’t end on Nov. 2.

The dead linger for another week — and while they do, the celebration continues.

What is ‘La Octava’?

The term “La Octava” comes from Roman liturgy. It describes an eight-day cycle in which “the believer is turned from one bound to this world into one bound to heaven.”

The Catholic Church continues to celebrate octaves, such as the Octave of Christmas (Dec. 25 to Jan. 1) and the Octave of Easter, from Easter Sunday to Divine Mercy Sunday.

In Tepoztlán, people also commonly observe an octave after a death.

“When somebody dies, we hold a rosary for eight days, until, on the last day, we officially send the dead to the underworld,” says 78-year-old Thomas Muzquiz, a Tepozteco.

Thomas connects this Catholic practice with the celebration of Day of the Dead.

“When Catholicism was introduced to Mexico, it merged with Indigenous tradition,” he explains.

Day of the Dead beautifully fuses pre-Hispanic beliefs with Catholic observance. Food offerings, copal and flower trails coexist alongside processions of saints’ images and crosses.

But when we look behind the copal smoke and past the vivid decorations, we can see that Day of the Dead in Tepoztlán and its octave is more than just a remembrance of those who have passed.

It is about continuing to work on relationships and caring for one another, welcoming the deceased with love and respect: to hang out together, eat their favorite food and have a shot or two of their favorite mezcal, while mariachis set the tone for the night.

La Octava de Tepoztlán and pondering the meaning of death

In Tepoztlán, the first calling of the dead begins at midnight on Oct. 18. Churches across Tepoztlán ring their bells to remind residents that the dead are just around the corner. On Nov. 1 and 2, families welcome their deceased loved ones with offerings and flowers.

“We put cempasúchil out because it is believed to be the only flower the dead can see and smell,” adds Anabel Muzquiz, Thomas’ daughter and a professional tour guide.

But the welcome does not end on Nov. 2. Tepoztlán accommodates its deceased for another week.

On Nov. 8 and 9, one can still experience the spirit of Day of the Dead in Tepoztlán, when residents reunite for La Octava and finally send their deceased home. Nov. 8 is dedicated to children, while Nov. 9 marks the farewell to adults.

On Nov. 9, people gather at the cemetery to clean and decorate the graves of their dead kin. A procession of saints’ images from different barrios in Tepoztlán travels to the main cemetery in the town center for Mass and remembrance.

“There’s rice pudding, fruit or green mole, mezcal and coffee — whatever they liked,” says Elena, Thomas’ wife, describing the altars renewed on Nov. 9. “The children make little skulls out of chilacayotes and ask for sweets. There are mariachis, and there’s food.”

Walking the streets of Tepoztlán, visiting the different churches in the barrios or strolling around the cemeteries on Nov. 9 is a beautiful opportunity to experience the spirit of Day of the Dead apart from the big festivities and locura of the main event.

It invites people to reflect on their extraordinary relationship with the deceased and gives them another week to ponder the meaning of death, while copal smoke and cardboard skeletons fill the surroundings with humor and a sense of playfulness.

What makes Day of the Dead so peculiar in Morelos?

Other parts of Morelos, like Tepoztlán, are known for their elaborate rituals around Day of the Dead. The Indigenous community of Coatetelco, for example, has a tradition of hanging floating altars decorated with corn.

Its observances also begin in September, when the milpa yields its first corn harvest.

In her paper, “La fiesta: recreación de la cultura y la tradición,” anthropologist Dr. María Cristina Saldaña Fernández describes the Mesoamerican worldview underlying traditions of honoring the dead, in which duality — observed in day and night, cold and heat, life and death — played a fundamental role.

She also mentions how pre-Hispanic observances honoring the dead were connected to the agricultural calendar and coincided with the harvest.

This worldview understood life and death as a continuous process, like the germination, growth, death and return of crops, which can still be observed in Coatetelco and their corn-filled altars.



‘It’s becoming diluted, becoming more like Halloween’

However, although the cycle of life and death prevails, Day of the Dead celebrations, whether in Morelos or elsewhere, are subject to change.

“I remember how people used to light bonfires on every street corner to gather around,” says Thomas, remembering Day of the Dead in Santiago Tepetlapa some 70 years ago. “Back then, the chilacayote was the best. Now you see more mass-produced plastic pumpkins and costumes. It’s becoming diluted, becoming more like Halloween. It’s a different version now. Each generation changes things in response to its surroundings.”

According to Saldaña’s paper, politics, literature, media and cinema have also shaped the celebration, adding new elements while discarding others.

But even as La Octava changes, visitors can still respectfully join the festivities and bid farewell to the dead for another year — all while sipping their favorite mezcal, joining old friends and family, and building new relationships with the living and the deceased.

Katy Alivraz is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: From the archive: How Mexico’s Day of the Dead helps us remember the people we’ve lost
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in October 2019 — shows us how remembering lost loved ones can be a colorful celebration of life, love and the memories that keep them with us.

Day of the Dead is by far my favorite holiday in Mexico. My first experience with it was in 2002, when I was here as a university student.

The director of my study abroad program here in Xalapa piled a few of us into his pickup truck and we drove to Naolinco, a picturesque mountain town known for its leather products.

I was immediately enchanted. Altars were all over the place — in people’s homes, in public spaces, in restaurants and stores. As we walked along the street, people invited us into their homes for tamales, bread and homemade wine.

There were carolers at the cemetery. Carolers! With guitars! The brightly colored petals and exquisite smell of cempasúchil, “marigolds,” were everywhere.

Since then, Day of the Dead has caught on north of the border as well. Even before the popular movie “Coco” came out, the southern Texas city I return home to was starting to embrace its Mexican heritage in more expansive ways than it ever had before, with altars, decorated skulls and papel picado, “colorful tissue paper with designs,” suddenly appearing alongside Halloween decorations.

Who knew that the dead could bring us together?

Each year in my home we set up our altar with the same enthusiasm with which we decorate the Christmas tree. As the years pass and more people we know and love die, we’ve had to switch to a bigger table, as our collection of dead has grown.

My grandmother is there, as is my mother. Traditionally, the flower petals are to be sprinkled from the altar to the front door so that the dead can find their way back home from the other side to enjoy the offerings laid out for them.

My grandmother, in life, would not have appreciated her place on the altar. Like many Protestants of a certain age, she was suspicious of the “magical” elements mixed in with modern Catholicism.

Day of the Dead is, of course, a mixture of Catholic and Indigenous tradition, one that the Spaniards were only partially successful at co-opting. At least they got to move the dates to the ones they wanted. (I like to think that my grandmother, now on the other side, would be totally cool with it.)

Death is a universal reality, and all cultures have different ways of dealing with it. When I was growing up in central Texas, death was taboo, something no one wanted to talk about; it was sad at best and terrifying at worst.

Halloween was a time not to think about the dead we knew, but to have fun dressing up and getting candy (and subsequent cavities). When I learned later of the history of Halloween from pagan tradition to Catholicism’s version, All Saints’ Day, I felt decidedly more creeped out.

Why should we spend any time at all thinking about death? How uncomfortable!

How to confront death

My attitude since has evolved considerably. Now that I’m an adult, death has moved closer and closer to me in the form of the passing of actual people I’ve known and loved, and in the reality and certainty of my own mortality as the years go by.

I’m hopefully still a long way from it, but none of us really knows, do we? For something that’s such a firm fact of life, we sure do avoid thinking about it a lot.

Mexicans don’t (as much), and I think there’s something to be learned from that. We can accept that we’re going to die. We can paint skulls on our faces to remind all of us that life is for the living — that we won’t be around forever, so we’d better get to it!

What does Day of the Dead do for us? It keeps the memories of our loved ones alive. It keeps this culture alive and reminds us of the people we came from. Feel guilty about not thinking enough of your loved ones that have already passed on? Don’t: remembering to do that is built into an annual holiday here.

I am not religious myself. I don’t pretend to know what happens after death, though as an agnostic I fully expect that we simply cease to exist in the way a flame from a candle goes out. As Richard Dawkins has said, we know that consciousness is wrapped up in the brain, and we know that the brain rots, so I have no illusions.

To me, this news is not too disappointing, as I’m fairly certain that, as a dead person, I would not have the consciousness to care. Disappointing would be getting to that point of not existing and not having done anything worthwhile.

That said, I do believe that there is a way to keep our dead alive, and Day of the Dead helps us to do that. Because while they might not still be around, they live on in us, and this holiday helps us remember that in an active way. The ways they shaped us, influenced us, taught us and loved us live on.

Death is sad. We don’t usually wish for it, but learning to accept it and not fear it (at least not too much) is a worthy exercise. Celebrate, remember and love your dead. Sit and chat with them a while.

Share some hot chocolate, some tamales, some pan de muerto, play their favorite music, decorate your face the way their faces look now.

Welcome them back, at least for a couple of days, and celebrate your own beating heart.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.
