World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Farewell to Cárdenas, a resignation at the INE and a record-breaking Catrina
World.content:
Listen to this article

The headlines of the week in Mexico began with news of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s reelection in Brazil, which left President Claudia Sheinbaum “very happy” and, in her words, was “a breath of fresh air” for Latin America and the Caribbean.

But at home, Mexico’s governing political movement Morena suffered another setback as the resignation of National Electoral Institute (INE) president Guadalupe Taddei raised fresh doubts about the integrity of figures tied to the government, even as Sheinbaum insisted Morena is not to blame. Meanwhile, the opposition National Action Party (PAN) announced six presumptive gubernatorial candidates for the 2027 elections.

This week also brought the death of Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, a towering figure of Mexico’s democratic transition. And as the country heads into Day of the Dead (and Formula 1 Grand Prix) weekend, Sheinbaum called on new generations to preserve the holiday’s traditions.

Didn’t have time to catch Mexico’s top stories of the week of Oct. 26? Here’s what you missed.

Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas dies at 92

Cárdenas, a three-time presidential candidate and the son of President Lázaro Cárdenas, died in Mexico City on Wednesday. A member of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) for more than 30 years, he left the party in 1987 and ran in 1988 as the candidate of a left-wing coalition. He is widely believed to have won that election, but Carlos Salinas de Gortari was declared the winner. Cárdenas went on to co-found the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), contested the 1994 and 2000 elections, and served as Mexico City’s first elected mayor from 1997 to 1999.

Sheinbaum called him “a man of steadfast principles,” and Thursday’s mañanera centered on a tribute to him. Asked what he leaves the Mexican left, she answered: “Honesty and democracy.” A public tribute with his coffin present was set for Friday at the Palacio de Bellas Artes. His son Lázaro Cárdenas Batel is Sheinbaum’s chief of staff.

INE president resigns; Sheinbaum weighs in

Guadalupe Taddei announced her resignation as INE president on Sunday after media outlets, including Reforma, reported that companies tied to businessman José Alfredo Hernández Casillas, with whom she reportedly has a close personal relationship, won lucrative INE contracts. She is the first head of the INE or its predecessor, the IFE, to resign since 1990. The Federal Auditor’s Office has opened an investigation, and Taddei said: “Each allegation must be examined with evidence.”

On Monday, Sheinbaum called the resignation “good” and said an audit was needed. On Tuesday, she pushed back on journalist Carlos Loret de Mola’s claim that “Taddei is Morena,” noting that the Chamber of Deputies, not the president, chose Taddei, who was picked by lottery in 2023. By Thursday, Sheinbaum went further, saying she believes Taddei “betrayed the trust of the people of Mexico.” She also said her government will propose turning the state-run printer Talleres Gráficos de México into a state-owned company to supply most electoral materials. The INE’s focus remains the June 6, 2027, elections.

IMSS workers promised 8% raise

After weeks of protests, Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) director Zoé Robledo presented a plan of 12 actions in 120 days. It includes an 8% salary increase, permanent positions for almost 11,000 temporary workers, 2,500 new specialist doctors, more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys, and a push to guarantee medicines and clear the surgical backlog. Whether it satisfies workers, and ends shortages that have outlasted earlier government efforts, remains to be seen.

Dog poisonings rattle Condesa

Poison hidden in sausage left in and around Mexico City’s centrally located Parque España killed at least three dogs Tuesday, prompting an animal cruelty investigation. The toll later reached four. Attorney General Bertha Alcalde Luján said tests found methomyl, a highly toxic insecticide, in capsules placed inside the meat, and authorities recovered 14 suspect pieces.

On Friday, police arrested a 58-year-old man, identified as Salvador “N,” a block from the park after he resembled a person in images circulating on social media. He was detained for resisting arrest, and prosecutors cautioned that they had not yet established whether he was responsible. Residents are avoiding the park, and Cuauhtémoc borough Mayor Alessandra Rojo de la Vega urged pet owners not to let animals eat anything off the ground.

Guadalajara water plan and allegations of torture

On Wednesday, Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus announced a “historic agreement” with the federal government to invest 25 billion pesos (US $1.33 billion) in Guadalajara’s water infrastructure. The plan centers on two new aqueducts, from Lake Chapala and from the Calderón Reservoir, due by the end of 2028. The federal government will contribute 14.5 billion pesos and Jalisco 10.2 billion, and Lemus promised no new debt, privatization or rate increases. The announcement followed large protests demanding clean tap water.

The Oct. 11 protest in particular remains contentious. Two women, among around 10 people who have filed complaints with the Federal Attorney General’s Office, allege they were tortured by Jalisco state police. At least 39 people were arrested and dozens hurt. Lemus has conceded “serious mistakes” were made, Security Minister Juan Pablo Hernández denied ordering force and Sheinbaum has repeatedly denounced the alleged torture.

Citizen scientists make their mark

In Michoacán, residents who spotted unusual marks in a streambed led researchers to at least 50 dinosaur footprints near Apatzingán. The National Institute of Anthropology and History believes the Late Cretaceous tracks were left by three types of dinosaurs and says further study is needed to pin down species.

In Tabasco, residents of Barra de Santa Ana are working to restore coastal dunes. A 30-member community brigade trained by Eni Mexico and UNESCO will replant vegetation and install sand catchers. Erosion has hit 85% of the 30-kilometer coastline between Boca de Santa Ana and Boca de Panteones, and up to 3.5 meters of shoreline are lost each year.

Sheinbaum moves to keep Mexico’s masterpieces at home

Following the Gelman Collection controversy, Sheinbaum plans to strengthen the Monuments Law to prohibit the permanent export of privately owned works declared artistic or historical monuments. A preliminary draft was published Oct. 15. The change would reconcile the law with 10 presidential decrees protecting works by artists including Diego Rivera, Frida Kahlo and David Alfaro Siqueiros. The timing matters, as the Supreme Court is set to hear a challenge to the 1984 Kahlo decree.

Day of the Dead highlights

Mexico City’s cempasúchil production hit a record 10 million plants, up 53.8% from last year, grown mainly on Xochimilco’s chinampas.

The capital unveiled the world’s tallest Catrina in the Zócalo. At 33.4 meters, the papier-mâché figure tops Puerto Vallarta’s 2023 record holder and is the city’s fifth Guinness record this year. The offering is on display through Nov. 3.

At Friday’s mañanera, held amid marigolds and Catrina figures, Sheinbaum described the Mexican view of “death as part of life” and said the holiday has “recovered” from Halloween’s influence, partly thanks to films like “Coco.”

Economy: Exports surge, growth slows and India talks begin

Mexico’s economy grew 0.9% in the third quarter from the previous quarter, down from 1.4% but above the 0.7% economists expected. Year over year, growth of 3.2% was the largest in 12 quarters, helped by a weak third quarter in 2025.

Exports, meanwhile, reached US $77.79 billion in September, up 37.9% and the third-highest monthly total on record. Over the first nine months, exports rose 30.4% to $627.19 billion, driven by computer and electronic equipment sold to the United States amid an AI data center boom. Mexico posted a $9.25 billion trade surplus, but its oil deficit of $25.68 billion already exceeds the 2025 total.

On the trade front, Mexico and India signed terms of reference on Monday for negotiations on a preferential trade agreement. Merchandise trade between the two totaled $8.74 billion in 2024, and a Mexican business mission to India is under discussion for early 2027.

Charlyn Corral makes history at the Ballon d’Or

Pachuca forward Charlyn Corral, 35, won the Gerd Müller trophy for Best Striker of the Year at Monday’s Ballon d’Or ceremony, becoming the first Mexican woman to earn the distinction. She scored 49 goals in 49 matches for club and country and shared the honor with Harry Kane.

In her acceptance speech, she also asked the audience to recognize compatriot Scarlett Camberos, who was among the 30 nominees for the main award.

Looking ahead

Whether Jalisco’s 25 billion-peso water plan will be enough to keep Guadalajara’s streets calm is an open question. The two aqueducts are not due until the end of 2028, work “could” start next year, and the Oct. 11 allegations of police abuse remain under investigation, so residents may be left with promises rather than clean tap water for some time. On trade, Sheinbaum agreed with Donald Trump that a deal with the United States is “very close”, and on Wednesday she said talks were advancing as both sides weigh whether an interim agreement is possible before U.S. midterm elections next Tuesday, Reuters reported. Mexico is still seeking a “significant reduction” in U.S. tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, while Washington is pressing concerns over automotive content and Chinese investment.

Even a pre-election deal would leave questions for the next Congress, according to an opinion piece in The Hill by Duncan Wood and Ivan Zapien. They argue that a change in control of Congress would not end U.S. pressure on Mexico over trade, migration and security, but a Democratic House could summon officials, scrutinize the USMCA talks and push for tougher labor and environmental enforcement, while Republicans keep pressing on energy and China. Either way, they write, Mexico should expect to answer to more of Washington, more often, after the U.S. declined in July to extend the USMCA for another 16 years.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Why I’m grateful my son is getting the Halloween-Día de Muertos experience I never had
World.content:
The funny thing about growing up in California with Mexican immigrant parents is that you are perpetually intimate with, and distant from, your Mexican roots. Every holiday season, therefore, becomes a delightfully unique interpretation of both cultures mashed together.

Tamales wrapped in banana leaves and filled with turkey for Thanksgiving? Opening gifts at midnight for Noche Buena, and then again on Christmas morning? Getting your face smashed into a birthday cake?

These are all welcome in my life as a Mexican-American who must constantly toggle between my two identities on both soils.

Sometimes, though, one cultural norm or ideology can overtake the other, leaving one half egregiously overlooked, if not completely erased. For me, that has always been the case with Día de Muertos.

Halloween was the festive U.S. tradition my household embraced in its most suburbanized form: dressing up as Ninja Turtles, trick-or-treating with pumpkin-shaped buckets, and devouring pounds of Jolly Ranchers, fun-sized Snickers and M&Ms for weeks after.

I’ve never been the king of spooky season, but I’ve also never avoided it. As I grew older and met my wife, our family Halloween tradition became dressing up in custom-made outfits that reflected our personalities or the region we lived: two high school teachers dressed as our favorite punctuation marks; two Boston post-grads dressed as the local subway trains. (Spoiler: this year we are dressing up as Chedraui employees.)

And yet, despite traveling to Mexico regularly throughout my life, and having immigrant parents who spoke Spanish and were connected to their roots in Veracruz in different ways, I don’t have any real Día de Muertos memories from my childhood.

Finding the tradition

It wasn’t until the 2010s that I recall the concept entering mainstream culture in California and elsewhere beyond Mexico. For my wife and me — both as a couple, but also in our respective Mexican-American upbringings throughout the 1990s and 2000s — we never experienced our parents or family members building altars in our California homes. Not until maybe around Pixar’s “Coco” (2017), that is.

That tradition has quickly spread. Within the past decade, it has become more commonplace to see altares, ofrendas and Día de Muertos-themed households worldwide. Of course, it existed long before “Coco,” but it wasn’t as ubiquitous as it is today.

When my son was born in 2023, my wife and I had already spent significant time in Mexico, including traveling to Oaxaca for a month during Día de Muertos season and fully immersing ourselves in its wondrous spirit of parades, parties and gravesite visits.

We had learned, while exploring Mexico’s vast regional scenes and lodging with family members in various states across the span of multiple summers, about the importance of Día de Muertos as a form of intimate ancestral remembrance. In contrast to the candy-collecting rampage we’d always known the end of October to be, we’ve been able to incorporate those important elements of Día de Muertos into our lives — and in our son’s understanding of this time of the year.

Now, having fully transplanted our lives to Veracruz, we get to experience the best of both worlds as a young family: the playful, goofy costumery and decorations of Halloween, combined with the artisanal charms and spiritual connectivity of Día de Muertos.

I wouldn’t have it any other way.

Building core memories

Undoubtedly, our son’s autumnal memories will be completely different than ours: Instead of knocking on doors in a cul-de-sac with a group of neighborhood kids, he’s going to a field of cempasúchiles in a mountainous pueblo to get his photo taken on a horse that is whimsically painted like a calavera. Instead of visiting the pumpkin patch and riding a train through cornstalks and bales of hay, his abuela and bisabuelo are coming over to our house to eat pan de muerto and build a collective family altar with photos of family members that he, or even I, will never meet.

Each has their own joys and core-memory-building functions, and I enjoy them both. I hope he does, too.

It’s true that our current community doesn’t offer much traditional Halloween vibes, in the Americanized sense. You may see a decorative witch or black cat dangling from a window, here and there. Earlier this week, I walked past a large inflatable ghost on someone’s balcony, but it was awkwardly angled to avoid the mess of wires that complicate our narrow, colonial streets.

It’s just a different atmosphere in these smaller Mexican cities and towns, and the sidewalks don’t really allow for large groups of children to roam around without parents losing their minds over incessant traffic safety.

Trick-or-treating vs. Día de Muertos parades

In 2024, we flew to Mexico City for Halloween and Día de Muertos. It was noticeably different from our experience in Veracruz. A local group of parents organized families online for a neighborhood walk, with designated homes that had registered in advance, so we knew who would be giving out candy.

Similarly, we went to a mercado in Mexico City that weekend for a “calaverita” — a Mexican version of trick-or-treating, where kids dress up and go stall to stall asking for treats.

In those instances, my son, wife and I got to experience some of that old-school Americana by walking around Mexico City with strangers — some, but not all of them, international — and knocking on doors (or wandering shop aisles) together. That version of Halloween offers a communal, neighborly bonding that isn’t always seen during other holidays, which more often than not take place inside homes with close family members, rather than out in public and in the streets. We certainly could use more of it.

Then, there’s the other side of it all: attending a Día de Muertos parade and being part of a collective throng of spectators, while ceremoniously dressed performers and various forms of alebrijes dance, flutter and chant around you. (It’s worth noting that Día de Muertos parades, like the one in Mexico’s capital, are relatively new traditions in many areas; they weren’t commonplace when I was growing up, but are a part of Día de Muertos’ increasing popularity.)

I’m glad my son will get to be immersed in those cultural experiences in ways my wife and I weren’t for Halloween.

Fusing traditions in an ever-connected world

Having access to those dual experiences is a life hack, really. That’s not to say that Halloween has never existed in Mexico, or that Día de Muertos is nonexistent in California. In each case, the cultural traditions are becoming more fused than ever before, largely thanks to social media, travel access and other global factors.

You no longer have to be in Oaxaca’s Centro to experience Día de Muertos, nor do you have to reside in a U.S. suburb to appreciate Halloween. Depending on where you are, you may not be able to fully replicate the magic of the other — but you learn to salvage whatever aspects you can.

By being in Mexico, we are reminded that we will always have generous access to, and understanding of, both celebratory worlds. That’s ultimately the beauty of being a Mexican-American binational family, no matter the seasonal holiday or time of year.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Do Mexicans celebrate Halloween? It’s not what you’d expect
World.content:
I have to be honest here. Growing up, I did get excited about Halloween parties at school.

Although some colleagues might be flabbergasted by this, as a kid, my friends in elementary school did organize trick-or-treat evenings — which were mostly about the treats, honestly — and children invited each other to their houses to play dress-up and paint their faces as pumpkins and skeletons.

However, for the November festivities, my family always made a point to put a special emphasis on building our Día de Muertos altar at home. It kind of felt more important, in a way, than just getting your pumpkin or vampire disguise. Still, as the air grows colder and the moons appear larger at night, the question arises: Do Mexicans celebrate Halloween? Well, it’s a bit more complicated than you might expect.

When the barrier between the two worlds grows thin

As the November festivities draw closer, you might come across the debate on social media. More nationalist and opinionated Mexicans will defend our millennia-old traditions over the hyper-Americanization of our fall festivals. Incidentally, there is a similar debate among our fellow countrymen regarding why pan de muerto should only be eaten during this time of year, and we have discussed it at length on MND before.

And the people who share this point of view do have a point. Setting up the altar for the dead, waiting for our deceased relatives to return and share a meal at home once more, is something we inherited from our parents, who in turn inherited it from their grandparents, and so on.

The pre-Hispanic roots of this ritual are enough to warrant an article in their own right — covering the spiritual light of the cempasúchil flower and the way the barrier between the two worlds seems to grow thin at this time of year. But that is not all. Although it is a custom with distinctly Mexica origins, it manifests in widely diverse cultural ways across the country: The massive ofrenda created annually at UNAM is vastly different from the long nights people spend in Pátzcuaro, Michoacán, awaiting the return of their departed loved ones.

We even have a word for them: nuestros muertitos, our beloved deceased. The suffix -ito or -ita in Mexican Spanish implies not only a diminutive form, but also a relationship of affection and respect inherited from Nahuatl -tzin, the honorific suffix used for high-ranking officials as well as for our mothers and fathers.

In preparation for their return, we prepare the favorite foods of our dearly departed — like mole de olla for a dear auntie, or the Diet Coke my grandma used to enjoy so much. Some people leave cigarettes for a brother who has passed away, or even traditional candies like Pulparindo or Pelón Pelo Rico.

So, yeah, you can see how these festivities might weigh a lot more on us than simply going trick-or-treating. Why then, why do we see children running around dressed as skeletons, ghosts and pumpkins as Oct. 31 approaches?

Día de Muertos vs. Halloween: Is there a disagreement about this in Mexico?

First of all, it is worth emphasizing that Mexico is an incredibly culturally diverse country. Even taking into account the legacy of the Mexica Empire — which spread many Day of the Dead practices across the nation — and the overwhelming influence of contemporary globalization, one cannot truly generalize about how the tradition is observed throughout the country. To do so would almost be disrespectful to the 68 official Indigenous languages (with their 364 linguistic variants) and the unique ways in which each culture shows respect and affection for its departed loved ones.

What I mean by this is that there is no single way to celebrate Day of the Dead in Mexico — or Halloween, for that matter.

That said, how right Porfirio Díaz was when he said that Mexico was very far from God, but very close to the United States. Given the geographic, commercial and political proximity we share with our northern neighbors — who are increasingly coming to share our country with us — it is only natural that Mexicans also join in the Halloween festivities.

We love dressing up, eating candy until we’re stuffed and having an excuse to run through the streets dressed as pumpkins. Who doesn’t, right?

Why the answer is complex

We could easily say, however, that both celebrations coexist today — and even engage in a dialogue. On more than one occasion, I have seen jack-o’-lanterns on Día de los Muertos altars. You can even hear children on Oct. 31 asking, “¿Me da mi calaverita?” — the hyper-Mexican version of “Trick or treat!”

Now, while all this is true, it would be somewhat simplistic to say, “Yes, in Mexico we celebrate everything.” Although it is true that we never lack reasons to throw a party here, the reality is that Halloween celebrations are more of a recreational activity than a cultural one. Day of the Dead is something we collectively look forward to and honor with greater solemnity — ranging from our intimate family traditions at home to the grand public displays we see in the streets year after year.

So yeah, if you ask a Mexican if they celebrate Halloween, they’ll probably say they do — but that they observe Día de Muertos.

Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have to set out a Coke for my grandma; she’s on her way back from the other side.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the Mexico News Daily Features desk. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams anthropology. Or yoga. Or both.

The Knesset, Israel’s parliament, in Jerusalem. (File photo)

Prediction Markets: Israel

Key Facts Prediction markets. Polymarket, a crypto-based platform: Eizenkot 47% to be prime minister, up 14 points in 24 hours. 1:25 p.m. ET, 1 Nov.

Kalshi. Kalshi, a US-regulated exchange, has Eizenkot at 34%, up more than 10 points, and Netanyahu at 16%.

Trigger. Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister, said his party will back Eizenkot to form the government.

Count. Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc holds 53 of 120 seats; his rivals plus Arab parties hold 67.

Next. President Isaac Herzog, who picks who tries to form a government, starts talks Wednesday 4 November.

Israel’s main challenger has jumped back to the front of the betting, and traders now see a real chance that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu loses power.

Traders on Polymarket, a crypto-based betting platform, now give Gadi Eizenkot a 47% chance of becoming Israel’s next prime minister. That is up 14 points in 24 hours, and it puts him ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at 34%, who fell 10 points.

It matters to US readers because Israel is the largest cumulative recipient of US foreign aid since World War II, according to the Congressional Research Service, the research arm of the US Congress. Who governs Israel shapes what Washington can ask on Gaza, Iran and arms.

Eizenkot, 66, is a retired general who once led the Israeli army and now heads Yashar, a new party. His 21 seats make it the second-largest party in the Knesset, Israel’s 120-seat parliament.

What Prediction Markets Say

Three markets were read at about 1:25 p.m. ET on 1 November 2026. These are bets, not polls.

Polymarket, next prime minister after the election: Eizenkot 47% (up 14 points in 24 hours, down 5 points in 7 days), Netanyahu 34% (down 10 in 24 hours), Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party, 5%, Bennett 5%. The market has traded about US$83 million overall and about US$1.1 million in the last 24 hours.

Eizenkot 47% (up 14 points in 24 hours, down 5 points in 7 days), Netanyahu 34% (down 10 in 24 hours), Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party, 5%, Bennett 5%. The market has traded about US$83 million overall and about US$1.1 million in the last 24 hours. Kalshi, prime minister after the 2026 election: “No one” 42%, Eizenkot 34%, Netanyahu 16%. Kalshi is a US exchange regulated by the CFTC, the federal derivatives regulator. About 8.7 million contracts have traded overall and about 235,000 in the last 24 hours.

“No one” 42%, Eizenkot 34%, Netanyahu 16%. Kalshi is a US exchange regulated by the CFTC, the federal derivatives regulator. About 8.7 million contracts have traded overall and about 235,000 in the last 24 hours. Kalshi, who succeeds Netanyahu: Eizenkot 45%, Bennett 6%. Only about 140,000 contracts have traded in total, so this market is thinly traded.

The Eizenkot line on the main Kalshi market is thin: about 24,000 contracts changed hands in 24 hours, so a few large bets can move it. The Polymarket market is far deeper, and both point the same way.

On the main Kalshi market Eizenkot traded at about 51% before the vote, then fell sharply after the count. Sunday’s jump is a rebound, not a new high.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Why the Odds Moved

The clearest trigger came on Sunday 1 November. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad (Together) party, which won 12 seats, said it will recommend Eizenkot to form the next government.

The Joint List and Ra’am, the two main Arab parties with 19 seats between them, are expected to recommend Eizenkot as well, according to senior party officials. Ahmad Tibi, a Joint List lawmaker, said on Saturday 31 October that his party would back an Eizenkot-led government from outside, without taking ministries.

Eizenkot said on Saturday that more than half a million more Israelis voted against Netanyahu’s government than for it. He promised to use the new Knesset majority quickly, starting with a state commission of inquiry, an independent official investigation, a long-running demand linked to the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023.

No bettor has said why they traded, and markets show the move, not the reason. The timing matches Bennett’s announcement, but we cannot prove it caused the jump.

The Arithmetic Behind the Bets

Israel held its election on Tuesday 27 October. Netanyahu’s Likud party won 27 seats, the most of any party, and his bloc of right-wing and religious parties holds 53 of 120.

His opponents hold 48, and the Arab parties add 19. Together that is 67, above the 61 needed for a majority, but only if parties that rarely sit together agree.

That is why Kalshi still gives “No one” 42%. Traders see a long road from recommendations to a working coalition.

What Happens Next

President Isaac Herzog is due to begin talks with every party that won seats on Wednesday 4 November. His office is largely ceremonial, but he decides who gets the first chance to build a government.

That person has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. If they fail, the president can turn to someone else, and repeated failure can send voters back to the polls.

Before the election, reports said Herzog had floated a unity government of Likud and Yashar. His office denied that he had discussed any such deal, and Eizenkot has ruled out serving under Netanyahu.

What It Means for US Readers

A new prime minister would not change Israel’s need for US weapons and diplomatic backing. It could change the tone of talks on Gaza and on Iran, though Eizenkot has not published a full platform that we could confirm.

For investors, the practical risk is delay. A coalition fight can postpone budgets and security decisions, and a failed attempt could mean a seventh election since 2019.

What It Means for Latin America and Africa

Our market data does not price a direct link to either region. The clearest channels are oil, where Israel–Iran tension moves prices for exporters such as Brazil and Nigeria, and diplomacy.

Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 under a US-brokered deal, so a new Israeli government could shape that relationship. We have not confirmed any specific policy change.

What Is Not Known

How Likud will respond to Bennett’s move, and whether any party switches sides.

Whether Bennett’s party and the Arab parties could sit in one coalition, and whether Eizenkot would accept a government that depends on their votes.

Whom Herzog will pick for the first attempt once he hears every party.

What each trader reacted to; the markets show the move, not the reason.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do prediction markets expect in Israel now?

On Polymarket, Gadi Eizenkot has a 47% chance of becoming prime minister and Benjamin Netanyahu 34%, read at 1:25 p.m. ET on 1 November. Kalshi gives “No one” 42%, Eizenkot 34% and Netanyahu 16%.

Why did Eizenkot’s odds jump?

Naftali Bennett’s party said on 1 November it will recommend Eizenkot to form the government. The Arab parties are also expected to back him, though no trader has explained the move.

Has Israel’s new government been decided?

No. Netanyahu’s bloc has 53 of 120 seats and his rivals 67 including Arab parties, but 61 are needed and President Herzog starts talks on 4 November.

How long does a coalition take to form?

The person chosen by the president gets 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. Failure can lead to another candidate or a new election.

Are prediction markets the same as polls?

No. They are real-money bets, not surveys of voters. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the CFTC, the federal derivatives regulator.

World.title: Venezuelan Deportation Shield Nears Return
World.content:
Venezuelans queue on the Rumichaca bridge between Colombia and Ecuador to have their passports stamped, pictured in August 2018. Photo: UNICEF Ecuador / Arcos / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Venezuela · US Immigration

Published Sunday, November 1, 1:30 p.m. ET (2:30 p.m. Caracas) · Source: federal court records; ACLU of Northern California

This story is part of our coverage of the venezuela us tensions. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. For hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans living in the United States, a court has just opened the door back to legal status, and now everything depends on the next five days. A federal appeals court, the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco, refused on Friday, October 30, to keep their Temporary Protected Status (TPS) switched off, so the protection is set to return on Friday, November 6, unless the U.S. Supreme Court steps in first.

The ruling is the latest turn in the long fight over Venezuela US tensions, which now reach into the lives of ordinary families. TPS is a program created by Congress that shields people from deportation when their home country is in turmoil, and lets them work legally.

Key Facts

Alignment group: Closer to Beijing. Some pillar data are incomplete for Venezuela; see the index notes. WatchSovereign in selective default; inflation of 252%; public debt at 309% of GDP. What happened: A federal appeals court (the Ninth Circuit) denied the government’s request to keep Venezuela’s TPS termination in force.

A federal appeals court (the Ninth Circuit) denied the government’s request to keep Venezuela’s TPS termination in force. Who is affected: The ACLU says hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans lost status when TPS ended.

The ACLU says hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans lost status when TPS ended. What happens next: Protection returns November 6, 2026, unless the Supreme Court acts first.

Protection returns November 6, 2026, unless the Supreme Court acts first. Why it matters for US readers: Employers and families may soon see work permits and deportation protection return.

In plain English TPS lets people from countries in crisis live and work in the United States without fear of deportation. The Trump administration ended it for Venezuelans, a lower court said the move went too far, and the appeals court has now refused to pause that decision.

What the Court Decided

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, based in San Francisco, unanimously denied the Trump administration’s request to keep the termination of Venezuelan TPS in force while the case continues. The panel also turned down a fallback request for a short administrative pause of at least 21 days.

The case is known as National TPS Alliance v. Mullin. The ruling is not a final verdict on the merits, and the litigation continues on an expedited schedule.

File photo: Venezuelans at a rally in Florida in 2019. Photo: VOA / Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why November 6 Matters

The plaintiffs say TPS will be restored on that date unless the Supreme Court intervenes. November 6 is when the Supreme Court’s emergency pause of the lower-court order, granted on October 3, 2025, is due to expire.

If the government asks the Supreme Court to step in before then, the justices could suspend the order again. No such filing had been confirmed as of Sunday, November 1.

How the Case Got Here

On September 5, 2025, Judge Edward Chen of the U.S. District Court in San Francisco found that former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem exceeded her authority when she cancelled an extension of Venezuela’s TPS and ended the designation. The Supreme Court then paused that order on October 3, 2025, which is why Venezuelans have been without protection.

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), a civil-liberties group that represents the plaintiffs, says hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans were affected. The plaintiffs’ side also includes the National Day Laborer Organizing Network, an immigrant-worker advocacy group.

What It Means for US Readers

Venezuelans who held TPS could regain protection from deportation and the right to work on November 6. Holders and their families would be the clear winners; the administration would be the loser if the order stands. A Supreme Court filing in the coming days is the main way it could change.

Holders should wait for official guidance from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) before relying on any restored status.

What Is Not Known

The government has not said whether it will appeal to the Supreme Court. No statement from DHS or the White House responding to the ruling was found.

It is also unclear exactly how many people will qualify again. The ACLU speaks only of hundreds of thousands who lost status.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has Venezuelan TPS been restored?

Not yet. Protection is set to return on November 6, 2026, unless the Supreme Court intervenes.

Is this the final ruling?

No. The court refused to pause a lower-court order, and the case on the merits continues.

World.content:
File photo: the Hôtel de Matignon in Paris, office and residence of the French prime minister. (Photo: ScareCriterion12, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Published Sunday, November 1, 10:30 a.m. ET (4:30 p.m. Paris) · Source: Paris prosecutor’s office, French Interior Ministry, Paris police prefecture

A homemade firebomb burst at a gendarme’s feet as France’s Saturday protest ran down, and by Sunday the country was asking who threw it. Paris prosecutors have opened an inquiry, for attempted homicide.

The attack came at the close of the latest round of France protests over living costs and public services. Student groups are now calling blockades before a national strike on Thursday, November 5.

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: France Protest Day Ends With 500+ Arrests

In plain English A gendarme is a soldier-police officer; France’s gendarmerie is a military force that works as police. A Molotov cocktail is a bottle filled with fuel and lit. Paris prosecutors investigate crimes in the capital. The inquiry only starts the search for whoever threw it; nobody has been charged.

A Firebomb at Porte de Charenton

The device exploded at the end of the Paris march on Saturday, October 31, at the Porte de Charenton, a city gate in the 12th arrondissement, a district in eastern Paris. It set the leg of a mobile gendarme alight, and the scene was filmed.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who runs the national police, called it an attempted murder on Saturday. He said the officer was only lightly injured and did not stop working.

The Paris police prefecture counted five officers hurt in the capital, four police officers and one gendarme.

File photo: riot police outside a looted shop on Boulevard Voltaire in Paris on 17 October 2026. (Photo: Jorge Jaramillo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Turnout Tops 300,000, With 779 Arrests

Authorities counted 320,000 marchers nationwide on Saturday, while organisers claimed 500,000. Police made 779 arrests across France.

Earlier tallies are in our report France protest day ends with 500+ arrests.

File photo: high-school and university students march in Paris on 6 October 2026. (Photo: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Students Call Blockades Before the Strike

The Union étudiante, a university students’ union, called blockades of high schools and universities for Tuesday, November 3, and Thursday, November 5. Thursday is also the day unions have called a national strike and march.

Our explainer on why France is protesting sets out the grievances.

What Prediction Markets Say Polymarket, a crypto betting exchange, priced a French state of emergency by December 31 at 7.5% on Sunday morning, with more than US$2.6 million traded. These prices are bets, not polls. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. What It Means for US Readers

Travellers in Paris should expect school-area disruption on Tuesday and a day of strike and marches on Thursday, which can slow metro and rail lines. Our guide on whether it is safe to travel to France is updated as dates change.

The attack gives security a larger place in the run-up to the 2027 presidential vote. A calm November 5 would ease that pressure, while fresh violence would harden it.

What Is Not Known

Nobody knows who threw the device or when an arrest might come.It is also unclear how many devices were thrown in total.Crowd counts also differ, 320,000 by authorities against 500,000 by organisers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who threw the Molotov cocktail in Paris?

Nobody has been identified or arrested for the throw. Paris prosecutors opened the inquiry on Sunday, November 1, for attempted homicide.

What happens in France next week?

Student groups call blockades on Tuesday, November 3, and Thursday, November 5. Unions plan a national strike and march on Thursday, November 5.

World.title: Cabo Verde Picks a President on 15 November
World.content:
Cabo Verde, an Atlantic archipelago off West Africa, elects its president on Sunday, 15 November, and the sitting president is the heavy favourite in prediction markets, where traders bet real money on outcomes. Our Cape Verde presidential election 2026 coverage tracks every update.

A candidate needs more than 50% of valid votes to win outright, or the top two meet in a runoff on Sunday, 29 November. Polling stations have usually been open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. local time, which is 4 a.m. to 2 p.m. ET.

Vote: Sunday, 15 November; stations usually open 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. local time, 4 a.m. to 2 p.m. ET.

Rules: Over 50% of valid votes wins; otherwise a runoff follows on Sunday, 29 November.

Field: Six candidates, led by President José Maria Neves and former justice minister Joana Rosa.

Voters: About 420,000 were registered for May’s parliamentary vote, roughly 72,000 of them abroad.

Prediction markets: Polymarket, a crypto-based market, gives Neves 87.5% and Rosa 3.9% (1 November, 8:22 a.m. ET), with US$34,544 traded.

This story is part of our coverage of the Cape Verde presidential election 2026. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Cabo Verde Campaign Opens, Odds Favor Neves

Six Candidates on the Ballot

José Maria Neves, the incumbent president, seeks a second term with the backing of the African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde (PAICV), which now leads the government. Joana Rosa, a former justice minister, is backed by the Movement for Democracy (MpD), which led the previous government.

Four others are on the ballot: Gilson Alves, Casimiro de Pina, Antero Tavares and Loisito Tavares de Sousa. The field was admitted by the Constitutional Court of Cabo Verde, which vets candidacies, and de Pina finished third in 2021.

In 2021 Neves won the first round with 51.8%, ahead of Carlos Veiga, a former prime minister and MpD founder, on 42.4%. Abstention reached 52%.

The Presidential Palace in Praia, the capital of Cabo Verde. File photo: Ji-Elle, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What Has Changed Since Our Earlier Reports

The official campaign opened on Thursday, 29 October, and ends on Friday, 13 November, under the calendar of the National Elections Commission (CNE), the body that administers the vote. Votes are cast on Sunday, 15 November, and a runoff would follow two weeks later.

Neves’s party took over the government after the May parliamentary election, so the vote also tests whether voters want president and government from one camp. In 2021 Neves won while the MpD governed, a pairing known as cohabitation.

What It Means for US Readers

In presidential elections, Cabo Verdeans abroad vote in person rather than by mail, and the United States forms part of the Americas diaspora constituency. Cabo Verde has a large diaspora in New England, especially around Boston and Providence.

Official information is on the CNE site, cne.cv. See our guide for US visitors to the election and our report on the campaign opening.

When is the Cabo Verde presidential election?

The first round is Sunday, 15 November 2026. A runoff is set for Sunday, 29 November if no candidate wins more than 50%.

Who are the main candidates?

World.title: Democrats Lead US Midterm Polls and Odds
World.content:
Voters wait in line for early voting at the East Bank Regional Library in Metairie, Louisiana, in October 2024 (file photo; Photo: Infrogmation, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Americans vote on Tuesday, 3 November, in midterm elections that will decide whether President Donald Trump’s party keeps control of Congress. Our 2026 US midterm elections hub tracks every update.

Democrats enter the final weekend ahead in national polls and in prediction markets, and early voting is running far above 2022. Polls begin closing at 6 p.m. ET on Tuesday.

Election Day: Tuesday, 3 November, with all 435 House seats and 35 of 100 Senate seats up.

Polls: Democrats lead national congressional polls 51.4% to 43.2% in RealClearPolling’s polling average.

Prediction markets: Polymarket, a prediction market, gives Democrats 94.5% for the House and 72.5% for the Senate (1 November, 8:22 a.m. ET).

Early voting: More than 43 million ballots were cast with five days to go, nearly 10 million above 2022.

Poll closings: From 6 p.m. ET Tuesday to 1 a.m. ET Wednesday, 4 November.

This story is part of our coverage of the 2026 US midterm elections. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: US Judge Bars Threats to Election Staff

Democrats Hold a National Lead

Democrats lead Republicans by 8.2 points, 51.4% to 43.2%, in RealClearPolling’s average of national polls for Congress as of 31 October. RealClearPolling is a site that averages published public polls.

A late-October Economist/YouGov survey, run by the YouGov polling firm, found 44% of registered voters expect Democrats to win the House of Representatives, against 31% who expect Republicans to keep it. On the Senate, 39% expect a Democratic majority and 36% a Republican one.

An early voting booth at the Madison Parish Courthouse in Tallulah, Louisiana. File photo: Ktkvtsh, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, gave Democrats 94.5% for the House and 72.5% for the Senate on 1 November at 8:22 a.m. ET. Across both sides, US$35.3 million has been traded on the House market and US$13.7 million on the Senate market.

Its Balance of Power market put a Democratic sweep of both chambers at 71.5%, with US$49.6 million traded. Those prices are bets, not polls, and they can move within minutes.

Democrats need 51 Senate seats for a majority, while Republicans need 50 because the vice president breaks ties. A Republican Senate with a Democratic House is the next most likely outcome in that market, at 22.5%.

Early Voting Runs Ahead of 2022

More than 43 million Americans had voted in person early or returned mail ballots with five days to go before Election Day. That is nearly 10 million more than at the same point before the 2022 midterms.

Early voting rose by more than 30% in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas. The figures do not show which candidates voters chose.

The Final Push in Contested States

President Donald Trump campaigned in Florida on Friday, 30 October. Sunday rallies in Iowa and Kansas were cancelled on Thursday, 29 October, and restored on Friday.

In Iowa he is expected to back Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate candidate. In Kansas he will appear with Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who trailed Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, 45% to 43% in a September poll by Emerson College, a university polling centre, within the margin of error.

In Texas, Senate candidates Ken Paxton, a Republican, and James Talarico, a Democrat, are focusing on Houston and Harris County, the state’s most populous. Start times for Trump’s Sunday rallies were not available.

What It Means for US Readers

The first scheduled poll closings come at 6 p.m. ET on Tuesday in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. The last are at 1 a.m. ET on Wednesday, 4 November, in Alaska’s Aleutian Islands.

Results arrive in waves because closing times and ballot-counting rules differ by state. Check your state election office for official figures, and use your own polling place’s local deadline rather than an Eastern Time conversion.

For more, see our guide to midterm poll closing times and our look at midterm odds. Our report on Latino voters in the midterms covers a key group.

What Is Not Known

Market prices change by the minute, and no poll or market is a forecast of the result. Early-vote totals are independent tallies, not official final turnout counts.

We did not confirm the full state-by-state poll-closing schedule with every state election office. Start times for Trump’s Sunday rallies were not available.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the 2026 US midterm election?

Election Day is Tuesday, 3 November 2026. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot.

What do the latest polls show?

RealClearPolling’s average, as reported on 31 October, has Democrats ahead 51.4% to 43.2% on the generic congressional ballot. an Economist/YouGov survey found 44% of registered voters expect a Democratic House, against 31% who expect a Republican one.

When do polls close?

The first scheduled closings are at 6 p.m. ET on 3 November in parts of Indiana and Kentucky. The last are at 1 a.m. ET on 4 November in Alaska’s Aleutian Islands.

World.title: Colombia Town Bombing Kills Police Officer
World.content:
Key Facts Blast. A bomb went off in the nightlife district of Algeciras, Huila, killing one police officer and injuring seven.

Cause. Reports say a motorcycle loaded with explosives was used; officials have not confirmed this.

Status. No arrests, no claim of responsibility and no official attribution have been reported so far.

As of 1 November 2026, 13:00 GMT

A bomb blast in a nightlife district in Algeciras, in Colombia’s Huila department, killed a police officer and injured seven people.

A bomb blast outside a nightlife venue in Algeciras, a town in Huila department in southern Colombia, killed one police officer on the night of Saturday 31 October 2026. Seven other people were injured, according to reports on Sunday morning.

The attack matters to US readers because it hit a nightlife district, the kind of place visitors go, in a country where security conditions shape travel decisions. It also feeds into the security picture that frames US-Colombia cooperation.

Six of the injured were civilians and one was a police officer. The blast hit while the area was busy with people out for the evening.

What We Know

The explosion happened in the zona rosa of Algeciras, the local term for a nightlife and entertainment district. It was near a commercial venue called Las Palmitas, close to the town entrance.

Huila is a department, Colombia’s equivalent of a province, in the south of the country. Algeciras is one of its towns.

National Police officers were carrying out surveillance and control in the area when the device went off. Reports on Sunday morning said a motorcycle loaded with explosives had been used in the attack.

The use of a motorcycle has not been officially confirmed. It remains under investigation.

One police officer died and seven people were injured. Six of the injured were civilians and one was a police officer.

The injured were taken to the Municipal Hospital of Algeciras. Early reports said transfers to hospitals in Neiva, the departmental capital, were being considered.

Algeciras has seen repeated explosive attacks this year. On 12 August 2026, an explosive ambush on soldiers in a rural area of the town killed two soldiers and wounded at least 16.

Authorities preliminarily blamed the Iván Díaz Front for that August ambush. The Front is a dissident group that broke away from the FARC, the former guerrilla army, and nothing reported so far links Saturday’s attack to it.

Separately, at about 6 a.m. on Saturday 31 October, a motorcycle bomb destroyed the El Mango toll booth on the Pan-American Highway, the main north-south road, in La Sierra in Cauca, south-west Colombia. Colombian authorities attributed it to the Carlos Patiño structure, a FARC-dissident unit, and no injuries were reported.

What Is Not Known

No official statement had named the dead officer or given a final toll at the time of the first reports. The Huila Police, the Huila governor’s office and the Algeciras mayor’s office were expected to report on the officer’s identity, the injured and new security measures.

No one has been arrested, and no group has claimed responsibility. Authorities have made no official attribution.

Investigators have not said who was targeted. They have also not confirmed how the explosives were delivered.

It is also unclear whether any of the injured needed transfer to larger hospitals. Their condition has not been described in detail in the reports available.

File photo: Colombian security forces at a ceremony. It does not show the Algeciras attack or its victims.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

Anyone planning a trip to Colombia should check official government travel advisories before they go, including the advice issued by their own country. This report does not rely on any advisory, so the current wording for each region should be read directly.

The attack took place in a town in Huila, and reports so far describe a local incident. Nothing in the confirmed facts says that foreign visitors were targeted or hurt.

Visitors in smaller towns may wish to follow guidance from local police and municipal authorities, especially around nightlife areas. Updates are expected from the Huila Police and local officials.

For US readers, the attack adds to a pattern of explosive incidents in Huila this year, with a separate attack in Cauca the same day. Colombian authorities will show whether the incidents are connected, and so far none has said they are.

Government travel advisories can change quickly. Checking them close to departure is the safest habit.

The coming days should bring official statements on the toll, the officer and the investigation. Those statements will show how the inquiry is developing.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Algeciras?

A bomb blast in the nightlife district on the night of 31 October 2026 killed one police officer and injured seven people. Six of the injured were civilians and one was a police officer.

Where is Algeciras?

Algeciras is a town in Huila department, in southern Colombia. The blast was near a venue called Las Palmitas, close to the town entrance.

Who is responsible for the attack?

No one has been arrested and no group has claimed responsibility. Authorities have made no official attribution.

Is it safe to travel to Colombia?

Conditions vary by region, so travellers should check official advisories before any trip. No confirmed report says foreign visitors were hurt in this attack.

For earlier security reporting, see our coverage of the Cúcuta explosion that wounded police and civilians and of Colombia’s order to militarise Cúcuta. More is on our Colombia news page.

Sources: Colombian Army attribution for the Cauca attack; Colombian local and national news reports of 1 November 2026. Huila and Algeciras authorities had issued no detailed statement at the time of writing.

Final Saturday 17 July 2027; the Confederation of African Football (CAF) has not named the stadium. The field 24 national teams; Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda qualify automatically as the three hosts. Watch in the US No US broadcaster announced; East Africa is seven hours ahead of New York in June and July. The Africa Cup of Nations 2027 opens on Saturday 19 June 2027 and ends with the final on Saturday 17 July 2027. It is the first time the continent’s biggest football tournament is shared by three countries, Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. The Africa Cup of Nations 2027 opening match falls on Saturday 19 June 2027, which is Juneteenth. In Plain English CAF is the Confederation of African Football, the continental governing body that owns the tournament and sets the schedule. Its official name for the 2027 edition is PAMOJA, a Swahili word for “together”, which refers to the shared hosting. A qualifying group is a mini-league of four national teams, and the best teams advance to the finals. The three hosts are already in the finals, but they still play in the qualifying groups. Dates and Times in East Africa and US Eastern For the Africa Cup of Nations 2027, CAF has confirmed the opening on Saturday 19 June 2027 and the final on Saturday 17 July 2027. Other match days, kick-off times and venues have not been published. Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda all use East Africa Time, which is three hours ahead of UTC all year. In June and July New York is on daylight time, four hours behind UTC, so East Africa is seven hours ahead of US Eastern. That means a 4 p.m. kick-off in Nairobi, Dar es Salaam or Kampala is 9 a.m. Eastern, and a 7 p.m. kick-off is noon Eastern. West Coast fans would start at 6 a.m. Pacific for the earlier game and 9 a.m. for the later one. Treat these examples as a guide to the arithmetic only, because CAF has not set any kick-off time. Do not book flights around a match until CAF publishes the full schedule. How the 24 Teams Are Decided For the Africa Cup of Nations 2027, 48 teams, including the three hosts, are in 12 qualifying groups of four. Most groups send their top two teams to the finals, but a group with a host sends only its best non-host team. Matchdays 1 and 2 ran from 21 September to 6 October 2026, and matchdays 3 and 4 follow from 9 to 17 November 2026. Our guide to the resumption of the qualifiers on 11 November covers the next round. Matchdays 5 and 6 follow from 22 to 30 March 2027, and CAF expects the full line-up of 24 teams by the end of March. Until then, big names such as Nigeria, Egypt, Senegal and Morocco are not guaranteed a place. The final draw, which sets the groups for the finals, comes only after the line-up is known. Pay by card where possible, and never send money to a social media seller or a person who offers a ticket in a private message. CAF has not said how the 2027 sales will work, whether by match, by stadium or by ticket category. Do not rely on a pattern from earlier tournaments. Demand for the opening match and the final is likely to be high. A fan who wants the final should book flexible flights and a hotel with free cancellation until the tickets are in hand. Where the Matches Will Be Played CAF has not confirmed the host cities or the stadiums. The three countries are building and renovating grounds, and our report on Tanzania’s stadium progress shows one host’s work. The largest cities in the host countries are Nairobi in Kenya, Dar es Salaam in Tanzania and Kampala in Uganda. They are the likeliest bases for visitors, but no city is confirmed as a host until CAF says so. Because the three countries are joint hosts, a team may travel between countries from one match to the next. Fans who follow a single team should wait for the final draw before booking a base city. Entry Rules and Safety for US Visitors Each host sets its own entry rules, and a US citizen needs a separate visa or permit check for Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. Check each country’s official immigration site before you book, because rules and fees change and CAF does not cover them. For Kenya the US State Department advises “Exercise increased caution”, and it lists the border counties with Somalia as Level 4, “Do Not Travel”. It also lists the Nairobi districts of Eastleigh and Kibera as Level 3 for crime and kidnapping. For Tanzania the State Department advisory is Level 3, “Reconsider Travel”, raised from Level 2 on 31 October 2025, and it adds an unrest warning. It says authorities may limit or ban large gatherings, and demonstrations sometimes break out around large events. Read the current State Department page for each country in the week before you travel, because advisories can change before June. Use registered taxis or hotel cars after dark, and avoid political demonstrations near stadiums. How to Watch in the United States No US broadcaster or streaming service is announced for the Africa Cup of Nations 2027, and CAF has not published a US rights list. Check CAF’s official channels and your usual sports service in spring 2027, once the schedule is out. The kick-off arithmetic above shows that most matches will be morning or midday games on the US East Coast. Whether live games will be available in the United States at all is not confirmed. What It Means for You If you plan to attend the Africa Cup of Nations 2027, wait for the draw and the ticket announcement before you book flights. The only fixed dates are 19 June and 17 July 2027, so keep those weeks free and watch for news. To follow the Africa Cup of Nations 2027 from home, note the qualifiers on 9 to 17 November 2026 and 22 to 30 March 2027. The March games decide who joins the three hosts. If you want a safari too, book lodges early. A major football tournament will raise demand for hotels in the host cities. It has also not announced ticket prices, sales dates, official sellers or the date and place of the final draw. The US broadcaster is not announced, and the 36th-edition numbering is described by CAF as expected. Twenty-one of the 24 finalists are still to be decided in the qualifiers, and we will update this guide when CAF publishes the schedule. World.title: Fixing an Invoice in Costa Rica Can Now Reopen a Tax Return You Already Filed
World.content:
Starting today, fixing a mistake on an electronic invoice in Costa Rica can reopen a tax return you already filed. New invoicing codes from the Ministry of Finance took affect today and changes how you correct, cancel or replace an invoice. If you bill anyone in Costa Rica, whether you run a company, work freelance or rent out property, this applies to you.

The key change is timing as when you correct an invoice because of a material error, such as a wrong amount, the correction now belongs to the month the original invoice was issued, not the month you catch the mistake. So, an invoice from January that you correct in August sends you back to January. If the fix means you owed more tax that month, you pay the difference plus interest. If you paid too much, the difference becomes a credit in Tribu-CR, the tax administration’s online platform.

The point is to keep income and tax tied to the month they actually belong to. A correction filed months later could blur that line, and the new codes tell the tax administration exactly what kind of fix you made and which invoice it touches. Tax attorney Raymundo Volio said the update does not change tax rates or create new taxes, and is designed to improve tracking and the accuracy of the data.

Your invoices still run on version 4.4 of the electronic invoicing system, which became mandatory in September 2025. What changes today is the set of codes your billing software must use when it issues credit and debit notes. Three new codes cover material errors. One cancels an invoice (code 13), one corrects an amount (code 14) and one replaces an invoice entirely (code 15).

If you cancel an invoice and need to issue a new one, the replacement code must also be recorded so the two documents stay linked. Two more codes handle other situations. Code 16 is for replacing an invoice the tax administration rejected, and code 17 records a payment against an invoice through the electronic payment receipt.

An existing code for credit notes on tax exemptions granted after a sale has also been adjusted, and in that case the accounting effect lands in the month the credit note is issued. Silvia Castro, a tax partner at the firm Despacho Carvajal, said a correction that looks simple, like changing the amount on an invoice, can end up affecting taxes you already declared.

If you use private billing software, ask your provider whether the November codes are active. If an accountant handles your filings, ask how corrections will be flagged so the right months get amended. If you rarely correct or cancel invoices, you may notice little difference. The businesses that will feel it most are those that frequently adjust amounts, cancel sales or reissue rejected receipts.

The tax administration announced the changes on April 22 and let businesses switch early, so many billing platforms may already be updated. It is the latest in a series of moves to tighten tax monitoring, including a requirement for businesses to register the phone numbers they use to receive payments.

Another change is on the way. The National Registry plans to begin issuing new companies legal identification numbers that include letters, in a format such as 3-101-A00001. No start date has been set, though it is expected before the end of 2026. Invoicing systems will need to accept the new format, while existing companies keep their current numbers unless they request a change.

For anyone who invoices in Costa Rica, the practical step is the same. Make sure the software you bill with is current, and keep records that let you trace every correction back to the original sale. Questions about how a correction affects your tax obligations are best taken to an accountant.

World.title: Costa Rica Court Asked to Halt Shark Fishing Near Cocos Island
World.content:
A Costa Rican environmental attorney has asked a court to temporarily prohibit the capture of several types of sharks in waters surrounding Cocos Island, arguing that the government has failed to establish the fishing regulations needed to protect threatened marine species. Attorney Walter Brenes filed the request with Costa Rica’s Administrative Court, seeking an immediate suspension of both intentional shark fishing and the accidental capture of sharks during commercial fishing operations in the Bicentennial Marine Management Area.

The protected area surrounds Cocos Island, one of the most important marine conservation sites and a destination internationally known for its large populations of hammerhead sharks and other marine wildlife. At the center of the dispute is the absence of a specific fisheries management plan that would establish how commercial fishing can operate within the protected waters.

Brenes argues that without clear rules governing fishing activities, sharks remain vulnerable despite the area’s protected status. The request covers eight categories of sharks, including hammerheads, silky sharks, blue sharks, blacktip sharks, thresher sharks, Galápagos sharks, tiger sharks and shortfin makos.

Several of these species face serious conservation threats, particularly from commercial fishing operations that use longlines, which are fishing lines carrying hundreds or sometimes thousands of baited hooks. Although longlines are commonly used to catch tuna and other commercially valuable fish, sharks can also become hooked and brought aboard.

Brenes maintains that this type of fishing continues inside the marine management area without adequate safeguards for vulnerable species. He also questions provisions in the area’s general management plan that allow fishing activities in waters extending hundreds of meters below the surface.

According to the attorney, those rules fail to adequately protect sharks that regularly swim through the same depths where commercial fishing gear operates. He is also challenging portions of the general management plan, arguing that more of the protected area should be closed to fishing.

His proposal calls for substantially expanding the waters where fishing would be prohibited, although that remains part of the legal dispute rather than a requirement already accepted by authorities.

Costa Rica Already Faced a Court Order

The latest legal action follows a November 2025 ruling by Costa Rica’s Constitutional Chamber (Sala IV), which found that environmental authorities had failed to complete several measures required to manage Cocos Island and the surrounding marine protected area.

The court ordered the Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) and the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) to complete outstanding management and regulatory measures within 12 months of notification. Those requirements included a fisheries management plan for the Bicentennial Marine Management Area, rules governing public use and improvements to the resources available for conservation.

Although a general management plan for the marine area has since been published, Brenes argues that the separate fisheries plan remains unfinished. The distinction is important because the general plan establishes broad conservation objectives and zones where different activities may take place, while the fisheries plan is intended to provide more detailed rules for fishing operations.

The new court request seeks immediate protection for sharks while the dispute over those regulations is resolved.

A Critical Area for Sharks

Cocos Island lies more than 500 kilometers (310 miles) off Costa Rica’s Pacific coast and is considered one of the most important locations in the eastern tropical Pacific for sharks, rays and other migratory marine animals. Its surrounding waters attract large schools of hammerhead sharks, making the island a major destination for scientific research and recreational diving.

In 2021, Costa Rica significantly expanded its marine protection around Cocos Island, creating a larger national park and the neighboring Bicentennial Marine Management Area, which covers approximately 106,000 square kilometers (40,900 square miles). The expansion was intended to protect marine biodiversity while allowing regulated activities in designated areas.

However, conservation groups have repeatedly raised concerns about how fishing is managed and monitored in those waters. Sharks are particularly vulnerable because many species grow slowly, mature relatively late and produce fewer offspring than other fish. Heavy fishing pressure can therefore take years or even decades to overcome.

Their movements also make protection difficult, since sharks regularly travel beyond the boundaries of national parks and other restricted areas. For Costa Rica, the issue goes beyond protecting individual animals. Sharks play an important role in maintaining healthy marine ecosystems, while Cocos Island’s wildlife has become part of the country’s international reputation as a leader in conservation and nature-based tourism.

The fishing industry also has an economic stake in the outcome, since restrictions on longline operations could affect access to commercially important fishing grounds.

Court Decision Still Pending

The new filing does not mean shark fishing has been prohibited in the Bicentennial Marine Management Area. A judge must first consider the request and determine whether temporary restrictions are justified while the underlying legal questions are examined. The outcome could influence how Costa Rica manages commercial fishing around one of its most important marine protected areas, particularly if the court requires additional safeguards before fishing activities can continue.

For now, the dispute highlights an unresolved question in Costa Rica’s marine conservation efforts: whether declaring an area protected is enough when the detailed rules governing fishing activities have yet to be completed.

World.title: Missing Caribbean Fishermen Found Alive in Colombia, Family Says
World.content:
Three fishermen from Costa Rica’s Caribbean coast who vanished at sea on Oct. 19 have been found alive in Colombia, a relative said Saturday, ending a 12-day search that drew in coast guard and air support from three countries. Rosemary Zárate, the aunt of one of the men, said that the three were very weak but already on dry land. No official statement on the discovery had been made public by Costa Rican authorities as of Saturday evening, and details of where and how the men were found had not been released.

The men were identified as Carlos Díaz, 27, a mechanic; Frederick Brown, 20, a hairdresser; and Michael González, 36. All three are from Cieneguita, a coastal community in the province of Limón. They left Cieneguita aboard the El Corrongo, a boat of about 10 meters (33 feet), at 3 a.m. on Monday, Oct. 19, and were expected back that evening. According to relatives, the engine had been giving trouble for days before the trip, and the crew carried food and water for a single day and no life jackets.

The crew later reported an engine failure and said they were stranded about 26 kilometers (16 miles) off the southern Caribbean coast, near the border with Panama. The first alert reached Panamanian authorities, who notified Costa Rica’s National Coast Guard Service. Commissioner Juan Carlos Alvarado, director of the National Coast Guard Service, said the search began the same day and continued without interruption. Coast guard boats from the Limón station patrolled the area while a U.S. aircraft flew overflights, with Panama’s National Aeronaval Service and the U.S. Joint Interagency Task Force South supporting the effort.

Search teams used a U.S. Coast Guard drift-modeling tool that weighs currents and wind to predict where a disabled vessel might travel. As the days passed, Alvarado warned that the search area was growing by the hour and did not rule out that the boat had drifted into international waters.

Relatives criticized the pace of the response during the search, saying they received few updates. Families also asked around coastal communities in Panama and Colombia for any sign of the men. Authorities are still looking into how the men reached Colombian territory and the condition of the boat, according to initial reports. No details on their return to Costa Rica have been announced.

It is the second time in roughly a month that Costa Rican fishermen have been found alive after drifting in the Caribbean. In late September, Panamanian authorities rescued three Costa Rican fishermen who had spent six days adrift.

World.title: Costa Rica Plans Blue Zone Seal and Wellness Tourism Push for Nicoya
World.content:
Costa Rica has laid out a timeline to develop the Nicoya Peninsula’s Blue Zone as a wellness tourism destination, with an official Blue Zone seal, three new tourism products by 2028 and national and international promotion campaigns. The plan runs alongside expanded care for the region’s oldest residents.

The measures are part of the Costa Rica Centenaria strategy, which President Laura Fernández Delgado announced on July 24 during a tour of Guanacaste. According to the Ministry of National Planning and Economic Policy (MIDEPLAN), the National Council for Older Persons (CONAPAM) will lead the strategy, which is still going through the administrative process to make it official.

The Nicoya Peninsula is one of a handful of regions worldwide known as Blue Zones, where an unusually high share of residents live into their 90s and past 100. Researchers have long debated whether that longevity advantage can survive among younger generations of Nicoyans.

The strategy covers health, social protection, tourism, infrastructure and local economic development. The announcement does not include budget figures for any of its components. On the tourism side, the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) plans to develop experiences tied to wellness, nature, culture and local traditions.

In 2026, the work centers on forming an interinstitutional team and carrying out a tourism carrying-capacity study, an assessment of how many visitors the area can absorb without damaging it. An inventory of the region’s existing wellness tourism offerings is due in 2027. A national promotion campaign is planned for 2027 and an international one for 2028, the same year three new tourism products are to be launched. The plan also calls for an official Blue Zone seal.

The push builds on the country’s broader effort to market itself as a wellness destination, including a national wellness route launched last December and growing demand from older travelers seeking health-focused trips. The care measures center on the people behind the Blue Zone’s reputation. CONAPAM is to create a National Registry of Centenarians between 2027 and 2030 to keep updated information on Costa Ricans aged 100 and older.

A national support program delivered through the National Care Network aims to reach 100% of the country’s centenarians and to strengthen daytime care services. The Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS) plans to give each identified centenarian a comprehensive geriatric assessment and an individual care plan covering medical follow-up, home visits and disease prevention.

The Ministry of Health intends to bring the municipalities in the high-longevity area into its age-friendly cities and communities program, with a target of 80% participation in 2027 and 100% in 2028. The strategy also includes two community economic projects in rural Guanacaste.

In Pozo de Agua de Nicoya, a rural agritourism and agroecology project with technical support from the National Training Institute (INA) involves 22 women livestock producers and 16 women entrepreneurs in traditional cooking, with about 152 direct beneficiaries. In Pochote de Quebrada Honda, a project to strengthen artisanal fishing and community development involves 36 organized fishers and shellfish harvesters, with an estimated 140 direct beneficiaries.

The Social Protection Board (JPS), which runs the national lottery, has registered two projects to buy medical equipment for La Anexión Hospital in Nicoya, both still in the pre-execution stage. The plan also includes a four-wheel-drive vehicle for the Nandayure Pain Clinic and Palliative Care Association.

According to MIDEPLAN, the strategy is meant to help preserve the region’s longevity, strengthen public services and create sustainable development opportunities for the communities of the peninsula.

World.title: Chaves Calls TEC Rector a Terrorist as 417 Limón Students Face Campus Closure
World.content:
Former president Rodrigo Chaves, who now serves as minister of the Presidency and of Finance, called Costa Rica Institute of Technology (TEC) rector María Estrada a terrorist after she warned that a budget cut could force the immediate closure of the institute’s Limón campus, where 417 students are enrolled.

Chaves made the remark on the program No Mientas Show and, when asked, confirmed that he was referring to Estrada. He accused the rector of holding the Limón campus hostage over a reduction he put at roughly 0.4% of the institute’s budget. He also said university authorities were unwilling to give up their privileges.

The Limón Academic Center offers degrees in business administration, computer engineering and industrial production engineering. Estrada has said the campus would have to close at once if a ₡491 million ($1.08 million) reduction in the second extraordinary budget for 2026 takes effect.

Jorge Herrera, president of the National Council of Rectors (Conare), has linked the funds at stake to Law 9635, the 2018 public finance law that helps finance the universities’ regional campuses. Those campuses allow students outside the Central Valley to earn a degree without moving away from home.
