NEW DELHI: India has adopted new airfare rules where government will not interfere in the process except âin an extraordinary situation (where) it considers it necessary to do so in the public interest. â Notified under the Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026, which will be applicable from Jan 1, 2027, government has continued its policy of letting market forces determine airfares without government interference.TOI reported on Oct 17 that India has no plans to regulate or cap airfares in the free market under which airlines here operate under the new airfare policy being finalised. However, it will keep a âstrong leverâ on airlines to ensure they donât resort to very sharp surges in âexceptional and extraordinary circumstancesâ that see demand rising for certain routes.âEvery air transport undertakingâ¦ shall establish tariff based on factors including cost of operationâ¦. (They) shall submit tariff to the Director General (DGCA) in such form, manner and periodicity as may be specifiedâ¦. (They) shall publish tariff on their websitesâ¦ for wider public awareness and transparency,â says the gazette notification published Saturday (October 31).Airlines have been asked to give a break-up of tariff in terms of the total amount payable by a passenger and break-up of the same by displaying components like base fare, tax, fees, cancellation charges, refund conditions and any other charge separately.Regarding intervention in âextraordinary circumstances,â it says: âWhere the central government is of the opinion that (in) an extraordinary situation it may, by order in writing, issue such directions in public interestâ¦. such directions shall be proportionate to the circumstances and shall remain in force for the period specified only.â

World.title: ‘Nobody can touch this Kumaraswamy’: Union minister dares cops, Karnataka govt over sting row
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The mobile phone allegedly used in the sting operation targeting former Karnataka chief minister

was purchased in New Delhi and subsequently handed over at the official residence of Union minister

, Bengaluru Police Commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh said on Sunday.

Responding to the police claims, Kumaraswamy challenged the commissioner and said he would disclose details of the investigation on Monday.

According to Singh, the phone was purchased from a shop in Delhi's Karol Bagh by accused Ritesh Pandey and Vinod Sharma before being delivered to Prajwal Prasad at Kumaraswamy's official residence. The handover was allegedly made on the instructions of Prasad, who was present at the residence, the commissioner said, citing Pandey's statement to investigators.

Pandey, who was arrested in New Delhi on October 24, is the first accused to be apprehended in connection with the case. Police said technical evidence, including details establishing the phone's purchase and delivery location, supported parts of his account. Investigators have also found evidence of financial transactions between Pandey and Prasad, which are being verified.

Reacting to the commissioner's statement, Kumaraswamy told ANI, "Who is this police commissioner? Whatever statement was given today by the Police Commissioner, you will get the statement tomorrow from my side.





At what stage has the investigation reached? What steps is the Commissioner taking, and whose position is he trying to secure? I will explain everything tomorrow..."

He further questioned the state government's handling of the investigation and said, "What is happening in this state under this government? What is the state of governance? I will put all these details before you tomorrow. This government, the chief minister and the officials of this government- nobody can touch this Kumaraswamy. I will challenge them. They are afraid of me. World.title: International Digi Yatra trials to begin at 7 airports for Indian nationals this year for wider rollout in 2027: Government
World.content:
File photo: India will trial Digi Yatra for international passengers at seven airports over the next three months

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Travelling abroad from India could soon be a seamless experience just like taking domestic flights with Digi Yatra (DY). India will hold trials for international passengers at seven airports in the three months of this year, allowing eligible Indian nationals holding e-passports to use DY at designated airport touchpoints while travelling on select flights operated by Air India and IndiGo.The aviation ministry said trials are being conducted at Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Cochin, Mumbai, Chennai and Amritsar airports. âEligible passengers will be able to use the facility at terminal entry points, security hold areas (SHA) and boarding gates, wherever the required infrastructure is available. Feedback received during the trial period will inform the planning of a wider rollout in 2027,â it said in a statement.To access this facility, eligible Indian nationals will need to create an e-passport-based âverifiable credentialâ (VC) through DY mobile application. âThe process involves scanning the machine readable zone (MRZ) of e-passport, reading the embedded chip using the near field communication (NFC) feature of a compatible smartphone, capturing a selfie and verifying the details. The credential is stored in the passengerâs Digi Yatra wallet on the device and can be used at airport touchpoints enabled for the trials,â the statement said.The facility will complement, and not replace, existing travel processes. âPassengers must continue to carry their travel documents and complete all mandatory airline document checks, immigration procedures and other applicable travel formalities,â it added.IndiGo said eligible passengers can upload their boarding pass to the Digi Yatra app. After completing mandatory document verification at airline check-in counter, they can proceed through the security hold area and boarding gates using DY biometric face authentication.IndiGo chief digital and information officer Neetan Chopra said: âAt IndiGo, we are committed to redefining air travel by making it more seamless, efficient, and customer centric, and we believe that technology can be a key catalyst in this evolution. Having been a key part of the technical proof of concept earlier this year, we are pleased to partner with Digi Yatra for the launch of these international passenger trials. Expanding secure digital identity and biometric technologies to international departures is a significant step forward for Indian aviation. We are committed to delivering a seamless travel experience for our customers at every touchpoint. The successful deployment of this technology marks an important step in reimagining the airport experience, combining enhanced security, convenience and operational efficiency. As the aviation industry continues to evolve, such innovations will play a key role in shaping the future of passenger travel.âDigi Yatra Foundation CEO Suresh Khadakbhavi said: âDigi Yatra has demonstrated how digital identity can simplify domestic air travel. With the start of international passenger trials, we are taking an important step towards extending this experience to eligible Indian nationals travelling internationally.Interoperability with global frameworks such as IATAâs One ID and ICAOâs Public Key Directory (PKD) will be an important part of this journey, helping explore how e-passport-based digital credentials can enable more seamless and secure passenger journeys across borders, while keeping passenger consent, privacy and security central to the experience. âDigi Yatra platform has over 2.6 crore users at present and has enabled more than 11 crore journeys across 39 domestic airports, serving domestic airlines. A further 25 domestic airports are planned to be covered by 2027. âThe aviation ministry remains committed to leveraging technology to improve airport operations and facilitate seamless air travel, in line with govt's vision of Digital India and ease of flying. â

World.title: Democracy protest concludes peacefully outside BMC headquarters; organisers say objective achieved
World.content:
Opposition leaders, student organisations and civil society groups gathered outside the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) headquarters on Sunday (November 1, 2026) to protest alleged electoral irregularities and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The demonstration concluded peacefully after several political leaders addressed the gathering and protesters raised slogans, with organisers deciding to disperse without proceeding with the planned march towards Mantralaya.

The protest, held under the banner of ‘A Walk to Defend Our Democracy’, followed a call by Tushar Gandhi, leader of Hum Bharat Ke Log. Participants had assembled near the Sir Pherozeshah Mehta statue opposite Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT) at 4.30 pm, with plans to proceed to the Mahatma Gandhi statue near Mantralaya.

The gathering was held in solidarity with demonstrations taking place in Delhi and other parts of the country over allegations of electoral manipulation and concerns surrounding the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

Earlier in the day, Deputy Commissioner of Police (DCP) Maneesh Kalwaniya said, “Permission has not been granted for the protest.” Police did not intervene as protesters addressed the gathering near the statue, but personnel were prepared to detain participants if they attempted to proceed with the march.

A senior police officer said restrictions on demonstrations in south Mumbai were based on directions issued by the Bombay High Court following concerns over public inconvenience and disruption. The court had also emphasised the need for prior permission and adherence to designated protest locations during proceedings concerning Maratha reservation activist Manoj Jarange-Patil’s agitation in Mumbai. The officer said police were required to enforce the applicable restrictions, particularly in Zones 1 and 2.

Communist Party of India (CPI) Maharashtra Secretariat member Prakash Reddy said the gathering was intended as a peaceful demonstration in support of the wider protests. “We wanted to have a peaceful demonstration, and they allowed us. We appreciate that. We don’t want to disrupt traffic or create any chaos,” he said.

Reddy demanded Kumar’s resignation and arrest, alleging that the SIR exercise was being misused to exclude eligible voters. He also described the turnout as encouraging, saying, “People have responded beyond that symbolism. So, it’s a success.”

The restrictions on the proposed march prompted questions from civil society representatives about the right to protest in public spaces. Ali Bhojani of Hum Bharat Ke Log questioned Mumbai Police Commissioner Deven Bharti over what he described as unequal treatment of political demonstrations.

Referring to a march allegedly undertaken by Union Minister Piyush Goyal between Borivali and Malad, Bhojani asked why similar permission could not be granted to ordinary citizens. “The rule should be equal for everybody, whether it is a common man or a Central Minister. You have to work according to the Constitution, not according to your political boss,” he said.

Bhojani also criticised the restrictions confining demonstrations to Azad Maidan, arguing that the designated space had become inadequate and isolated from decision-makers. He urged the Bombay High Court to reconsider the restrictions and designate additional protest locations, including the area near the Mahatma Gandhi statue at Mantralaya, warning that protesters could approach the court through a public interest litigation.

Samajwadi Party Maharashtra president and MLA Abu Asim Azmi accused the BJP-led government of undermining democratic institutions and alleged that electoral malpractice had influenced election outcomes. He reiterated his party’s demand for elections to be conducted using ballot papers instead of electronic voting machines.

Student organisations also raised concerns over electoral transparency. Representatives of the All India Students’ Association (AISA) demanded a complete rollback of the SIR exercise, restoration of allegedly deleted voter names and the repeal of legal provisions they said protected election officials from accountability.

Sahil Parsekar, a CJP leader, highlighted the participation of younger protesters, saying students were increasingly using creative forms of expression, including poetry, satire and public performances, to raise political concerns. He said young people would continue demanding accountability from those in power.

Representatives of the CPI(M), Shiv Sena (UBT) and other organisations also expressed support for the demonstration.

CPI(M) Mumbai district secretary Shailendra Kamble thanked the police, particularly officers from Zone 1, for cooperating with the organisers during the gathering. He subsequently announced the conclusion of the protest and appealed to participants to disperse peacefully.

World.title: JU V-C orders probe into molestation complaint against staffer
World.content:
Kolkata

A first-year student of Jadavpur University’s (JU) Arts Faculty was allegedly molested by a non-teaching staffer on campus on Friday afternoon, prompting Vice-Chancellor Chiranjib Bhattacharjee to order a probe on Saturday.

According to a complaint submitted by the survivor’s friends to the V-C on her behalf, the incident took place at 3.20 p.m. when they were sitting at the staircase on the seventh floor of Technology Bhavan. The complaint stated that the accused staffer allegedly shouted at them and asked them to go downstairs. Following this, her two friends immediately rushed downstairs.

The accused then allegedly asked the survivor to accompany him to a classroom to explain why he does not allow anyone to sit there. He took her to the sixth floor where there were no lights. He showed her some locked rooms and told her that laptops had been stolen from there. He also asked her number, name, and department, the complaint said.

The complaint stated that the survivor told him that she would not sit there in future. When she turned around to leave, he pulled her by her hand and touched her inappropriately. In self-defence, she pushed him back, left the spot, and narrated the incident to her friends.

A little later, the accused acame down and started talking to the security guards. When she confronted him, he started defending himself aggressively. He kept asking for proof from her friends and kept on saying that “this was a small issue that was being unnecessarily blown out of proportion”, the letter read.

In the letter submitted to the Vice-Chancellor, 17 students who signed it also alleged that the accused had shown objectionable behaviour towards many students in the past.

They have demanded that the complaint be immediately forwarded to the Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) and action be taken at the earliest.

The students also demanded that the Gender Sensitisation Committee against Sexual Harassment (GS-CASH) be immediately implemented on the campus for the safety of women.

Soon after receiving the letter, Mr. Bhattacharjee forwarded it to the ICC and also directed the committee to launch an immediate probe into the matter. “This is a serious complaint. Based on the prima facie evidence, the accused should be defunct immediately from entering campus. The complaint letter be sent to the ICC for investigation and necessary action,” he said in his written note.

World.title: Even as unemployment falls, lack of ‘decent work’ in India
World.content:
India’sunemployment rate fell from 6.1% in 2017-18 to 3.2% in 2023-24. At the same time, female workforce participation increased for the first time in decades as has been widely reported in government documents. In light of these positive developments, it is the right time to ask what kind of jobs have been generated in India recently, and what working conditions accompany them.

Also read | Understanding inequality in India’s growth story

This is important because employment alone does not inherently ensure dignity, security, or a stable livelihood. A worker engaged in garment sewing without a formal contract, a gig worker without insurance coverage, or a construction labourer without paid leave may technically be considered employed, but they remain outside the promise of decent work. The International Labour Organization (ILO) defines ‘decent work’ as employment that offers equitable income, workplace rights, social security and dignity. This principle is integrated into Sustainable Development Goal 8 (SDG-8), which advocates “decent work for all”. Measured this way, India’s labour market persistently exhibits high levels of informality, insecure employment, and increasing inequalities.

Measuring decent work

Using two rounds of the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), 2017-18 and 2023-24, the quality of employment in India has been analysed. By constructing a multidimensional Decent Work Index (DWI) based on three subdimensions — employment status, employment opportunity, and social security — across five major industries (agriculture, manufacturing, construction, wholesale and retail, and transport), it was observed that India has made progress in improving work conditions over time. The overall DWI increased from 0.247 in 2017-18 to 0.302 in 2023-24. While this indicates some improvement in job quality, the overall level remains alarmingly low. More importantly, progress has been uneven across sectors, regions, gender and caste groups.

Manufacturing in the secondary sector and transport in the tertiary sector showed the highest improvement in decent work conditions during this period. The manufacturing sector’s DWI increased from 0.324 to 0.411 due to a gradual rise in formalisation and digitalisation. The transport sector also experienced significant progress (from 0.285 to 0.35), largely due to the expansion of urban logistics and app-based platform work.

The social security gap

However, these improvements also reveal an important concern. Even in sectors where employment conditions have improved, access to social security remains limited. A large number of workers still do not have written contracts, paid leave, provident fund benefits or insurance coverage. Though employment opportunities are increasing, labour protections and job security are not improving at the same pace. Agriculture, which continues to employ the largest share of India’s workforce, remains the lowest-quality employment generating sector. The agricultural sector’s DWI marginally increased from 0.211 to 0.267 during the study period; most agricultural workers continue to be self-employed or unpaid family workers without stable income or labour protections. The issue is not merely low productivity; rather it is the rise of informal jobs. Construction and retail sectors tell a similar story. Workers remain dependent on casual employment, subcontracting chains and insecure labour arrangements. Welfare schemes exist on paper but implementation gaps continue to exclude millions of workers.

Nearly 90% of India’s workforce remains informally employed, a share that has risen since 2019, according to the India Employment Report 2024 (ILO–IHD). It has expanded into supply chains, app-based work in the gig and platform economy, logistics, home-based production, and in even organised industries through contractualisation and outsourcing.

Who gets left out

The challenge becomes even more serious when viewed in the context of social inequality. The analysis by the authors shows that decent work outcomes improve significantly with education, formal enterprise employment and skill training. However, informalisation of jobs reduces decent work creation in India over time. Especially concerning is the growing intersection of caste and gender disadvantage: women from Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes experienced a decline in decent-work outcomes between 2017-18 and 2023-24, even as outcomes for men improved. The labour market penalty for being both female and socially marginalised has intensified after the COVID-19 pandemic. This shows that inequality in India’s labour market is not just economic, it is also structurally rooted in caste and gender hierarchies.

Regional disparities further expose the uneven nature of labour market progress. States such as Goa, Keralam, Tamil Nadu, and Haryana perform substantially better in terms of decent-work creation; in contrast, Bihar, Jharkhand, and Uttar Pradesh continue to lag behind.

The findings point to a serious policy concern: while India has been able to create more jobs, it is still struggling to ensure that these jobs provide decent working conditions and security.

Poor-quality employment generation has consequences for economic growth. Workers without social security spend less, save less and remain vulnerable to economic shocks. Moreover, informality depresses productivity, weakens tax capacity, and increases inequality. India cannot measure labour market success only through reduction in unemployment rates and income growth. A country aspiring to become Viksit Bharat by 2047 cannot rely indefinitely on insecure, low-paid and unprotected labour. Economic growth without decent work can create a workforce that may have jobs, but still lives with insecurity, instability and a lack of protection. India has to shift from a ‘job-counting approach’ to a ‘job-quality approach’.

The way forward

The findings point toward where policy should focus. First, social protection must extend to all workers — gig and platform workers, self-employed, farmers, and informal workers — through systems that are portable and accessible regardless of employment status. Platforms such as e-Shram are a good start, but registering alone does not guarantee protection; workers need real protection, not just a database entry.

Second, formalisation policies should focus on labour conditions, not just business registration. Enterprises receiving tax incentives or subsidies should be linked to mandatory worker protections such as written contracts, paid leave, and social security contributions.

Third, labour policies need to be more intersectional. Given that women from marginalised caste groups are the group whose outcomes worsened rather than improved, targeted measures — childcare facilities, safe transportation, skill training and safeguards against workplace discrimination — should not be an afterthought. Finally, labour reforms should be designed around the needs of workers first, rather than being framed primarily as a means of easing the cost of doing business.

The four Labour Codes were introduced in 2025 with the promise of simplifying labour regulation and expanding protections. However, implementation remains partial and inconsistent. Critics argue that while compliance has been eased for businesses, worker protections may have diminished with rising contractualisation.

The real test of development is not whether workers have some kind of work; it is whether that work provides dignity and security. Until then, India’s employment success story will remain incomplete — no nation can call itself developed while its workforce remains insecure.

Anukriti Negi is Research Scholar, Department of Economics, Banaras Hindu University, Varanasi. Priyabrata Sahoo is Assistant Professor in the Department of Economics, Banaras Hindu University, and visiting Research Fellow to University of Leeds, United Kingdom. Santosh Kumar Dash is Assistant Professor at IRMA, “Tribhuvan” Sahkari University, Anand

World.title: U.S. mid-term elections: How officials are facing the heat
World.content:
Americans vote tomorrow, November 3, to elect the Congress for the last two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. While Indian voters are used to a single counting day, with most results in by evening, a U.S. count can run for days, and in a close race for weeks. This year the worry is whether the outcome will be accepted at all. In 2020, doubts arose after the count, and Mr. Trump still has not accepted that defeat. This time, they are being raised before voting, with Mr. Trump stating that he will accept the result only “if the elections are honest”.

The U.S. does have a federal Election Assistance Commission (EAC), but its responsibility is limited to certifying voting machines and training election staff. The 50 States have thousands of county officials who man the booths, count the votes and declare results; India’s electronic voting machines can total crores of votes in a few hours. In the U.S., many votes come by post, and each envelope must be opened and its signature checked before the ballot is counted. Moreover, there is variance in the procedure followed by different States. California will accept a postal ballot up to a week after polling day if it was posted in time. Twenty-six States order an automatic recount when the margin is very narrow.

World.title: Slow recovery: On the ISRO’s GSLV-F18 mission
World.content:
With the successful launch of the GSLV-F18 mission and the NVS-03 satellite’s healthy status, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is on course to heave a sigh of relief. Its last 18 months have been constrained by the consequences of two launch failures involving PSLV rockets, which share some of their design aspects with GSLV, to the extent that the F18 mission was only the second successful launch of 2026. If the NVS-03 satellite is successfully manoeuvred into its final intended orbital slot and commissioned, ISRO will also have pulled off a rescue mission for the ‘Navigation with Indian Constellation’ (NavIC) programme, which has been at least one functional satellite short for the last six months and thus unable to meet its primary purpose of providing standalone positioning services over the Indian subcontinent. The three second-generation NVS satellites thus far are distinguished by having at least one indigenously made atomic clock onboard, in line with the recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee (PSC) on Science and Technology and India’s investments in quantum timekeeping, and away from the imported clocks onboard the first-generation IRNSS satellites.

The PSC had also flagged procurement bottlenecks across ISRO’s programmes, including difficulties with obtaining specialised components and ensuring vendor readiness on the timelines that NavIC needs. The ISRO Space Applications Centre’s ‘request for proposals’ in 2025 also specified a large lead time of nearly two years between a contract’s start and the first two flight models. The Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme and the programme to modernise the Semiconductor Laboratory can be tweaked to serve these needs, with the Electronics Ministry also setting aside dedicated funds for developing specialised components and their qualification tests in a five- to seven-year programme. In tandem, the government must allocate around ₹17,000 crore in the 2027-28 Union Budget for the Department of Space, against ₹13,705.6 crore in 2026-27, with the hike focusing on manufacturing launch vehicles, replacing satellites, and recruitment. Besides, NavIC also requires a dedicated operator, so that ISRO can be left to focus on its core mandate, and India needs a national space law addressing private participation in this enterprise, and liability. Two successful orbital missions in five-sixths of a year is unbecoming of a national space programme with imminent plans of human spaceflight, a space station, and reusable launch vehicle capabilities. Without significant measures, ISRO will lurch from one mission to the next as and when its inadequate workforce is able to make do with its inadequate allocation.

World.title: Dwindling support: On the U.S. and the Cuban embargo
World.content:
Nearly every year since 1992, the United Nations General Assembly has passed a resolution calling on the U.S. to end its decades-old economic embargo on Cuba. As a result, the outcome at the UNGA resolution titled the ‘Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba’ passed on October 30, was expected. Surprisingly, the support for the resolution this year was dramatically lower than previous years. For the preceding decade, more than 180 countries of the 193-member UNGA had expressed their support for ending the embargo, but the numbers dropped to 165 in favour in 2025; this year’s tally dropped sharply lower, with 130 in favour, 25 abstaining and 17 countries voting against the resolution. The trend clearly points to efforts by the Trump administration to use its pressure on countries to change their votes, and many appear to have succumbed to those threats. Among those were several Latin American countries, that have more recently grown closer to the U.S., particularly after the operation in Venezuela in January 2026, where U.S. marines abducted President Maduro and brought him to the U.S. for a trial. Countries in the region such as Costa Rica, Ecuador, Argentina, and Colombia that have downgraded ties with Havana, switched votes on the resolution. In addition, U.S. diplomats argued that Havana-Moscow ties emboldened Russia’s war in Ukraine, which led to several western countries switching their vote. Diplomats from Ukraine and Poland, for example, referred to Cuba’s ties with Russia while explaining their vote, and Germany and Italy switched for the first time in many years to abstaining on the resolution. While it is clear that the bulk of the Group of 77 and non-aligned states including India maintained their support on the resolution for Cuba, the vote by the others demonstrates a disquieting turn.

Amidst these turns, New Delhi must be credited for standing firm on the issue, opposing the embargo, and calling for “dialogue and diplomacy” in its statement. The vote came a month after the BRICS New Delhi declaration expressed “deep concern” over the tightening of unilateral blockade measures on Cuba, and the “worrying humanitarian impact” on the Cuban people. It is important that India continue to stand up to such unilateral measures and amplify the voice of smaller countries, particularly those in the Global South.

World.title: Cyclone Murasu LIVE update: Orange alert in six Telangana districts, yellow alert in five; holiday announced for schools, colleges in T.N., A.P. districts
World.content:
A deep depression over the Bay of Bengal on Sunday (November 1, 2026) intensified into a cyclone named “Murasu”, which means war drum. The latest storm is set to make landfall on the morning of November 3 between Nellore and Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh, with wind speeds of 100-110 kmph, gusting to 120 kmph, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).

Watch: Days after Cyclone Arnab, Cyclone ‘Murasu’ forms over Bay of Bengal

Chennai and Tiruvallur District Collectors have announced that schools and colleges of the districts will be closed on Monday (November 2, 2026) due a heavy rains. An orange alert was announced in six Telangana districts and a yellow alert in five districts in Telangana for Monday.

The cyclonic storm over Southwest and adjoining Westcentral Bay of Bengal moved west-northwestwards at a speed of 25 kmph during the past six hours.

Also read: A.P. seeks assistance from Tamil Nadu, Karnataka for cyclone power restoration

It lay centred about 350 km east of Chennai, 400 km east-southeast of Nellore, 430 km southeast of Machilipatnam, 420 km east-southeast of Kavali, 450 km southeast of Ongole, and 520 km south of Visakhapatnam, according to IMD.

World.title: Rebel leaders of AIADMK do not take part in district secretaries’ meeting chaired by Palaniswami
World.content:
The rebel leaders in the AIADMK, S.P. Velumani and Natham R. Viswanathan, did not take part in the meeting of party’s district secretaries chaired by general secretary Edappadi K. Palaniswami at the party head office in Chennai on Sunday.

The party’s performance in the recent bypoll in Dharapuram and Madurantakam Assembly constituencies, and preparations for its general council and executive committee meetings, expected to be conducted in December this year, were among the issues discussed at the meeting. Senior leaders A. Tamilmagan Hussain, K.P. Munusamy, and Dindigul C. Sreenivasan were among those who attended the meeting.

Earlier, Mr. Palaniswami issued a statement criticising the TVK-led government over the rates of medicines in Mudhalvar Marundhagams (formerly Amma Marundhagams). Citing a report from the All India Drug Action Network, he said medicines at Amma Marundhagams were being sold at rates higher than the prices fixed, which is affecting the poor.

Retired Additional Superintendent of Police S. Velladurai, who was known for his involvement in many ‘police encounter’ cases, joined the AIADMK in the presence of Mr. Palaniswami on Sunday.

World.title: ‘We’re technology-savvy’: DG ISPR says Pakistan ahead of India, Afghan Taliban in operational readiness
World.content:
Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has affirmed that Pakistan is “much ahead” in operational readiness compared to the Afghan Taliban and India, adding that the country’s military is adopting emerging technologies.

The military spokesperson’s remarks, shared by state media on Sunday, were made during Friday’s wide-ranging interview with an international outlet. The remarks aired today focused on the ongoing tensions between Islamabad and Kabul.

Replying to a query about whether Islamabad was worried about the use of drones by the Afghan Taliban, considering their increased use in the ongoing Middle East conflicts, the DG ISPR said, “It’s a narrow thing that I’ll be worried about the drones being used by Afghanistan.”

He noted that the Afghan Taliban had no military capabilities of their own, but those “provided by the sponsors”. He accused the Afghan Taliban of being a “proxy” of India, which he described as the “biggest terror sponsor”.

Lt Gen Chaudhry then recalled that during the May 2025 conflict with India, Pakistan had shot down dozens of highly sophisticated drones sent from across the eastern border.

“So those drones, wherever they were, turned them into dust everywhere. That was about two years ago. So we are much ahead where we stand in our own operational readiness,” he said, expressing confidence in Pakistan’s military capabilities compared to India as well.

The DG ISPR said that the Pakistani army was adapting itself in a “very professional, well-thought-out way with the changing character of warfare”.

“Whether it’s in non-contact [or] contact warfare, whether it’s in cyber, whether it is in drones, long-range missions, … we are very cognisant of what capabilities we need for the present and also for the future.

“But you have rightly pointed out that this proliferation of this non-contact warfare means to the non-state actors like the Taliban, Khawarij, and Houthis; they pose a threat to everyone. And the states will have to reconsider and re-evaluate their security architecture,” he stressed.

The Pakistani government uses the term “Fitna al-Khawarij” to refer to the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and its affiliates, and the term khariji (outcast) when referring to the perpetrators of terrorist attacks on Pakistan.

Asked whether Pakistan used artificial intelligence to help identify targets in Afghanistan, the DG ISPR said he could not discuss the specifics of how the military used AI, quantum technology, cyber technology, and multiple other technologies, but that they can and should be used.

“We are a technology-savvy army,” Lt Gen Chaudhry asserted.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

For their part, the Afghan Taliban have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while dismissing Islamabad’s stance that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan.

‘Afghanistan has only two products: terrorism and drugs’

Asked about allegations by the Afghan Taliban of Pakistan’s involvement in coordinating anti-Taliban elements, Lt Gen Chaudhry rejected them. “That’s how you play the victim card.”

The DG ISPR noted, “They are apt at using non-state actors, militias, mercenaries, for their objectives. So they think everyone does that. We are a state. Afghanistan is not a state. It is still being run by a non-state actor. It’s a regime.”

He noted decades of foreign interventions, including by the erstwhile Soviet Union and the United States, following which multiple “agencies and proxies” established roots in Afghanistan.

He said Afghanistan was perhaps the only country in the recent past that had been affected by interventions for 40 to 45 years.

Lt Gen Chaudhry said: “The forces are gone physically, but still that front of Afghan Taliban is a proxy to multiple parties. In the case of Pakistan, the prime contractor is India. And the proxies are TTP and the BLA (Balochistan Liberation Army).

“But there are others also,” he pointed out, naming East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM), Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan (IMU), Jaish al-Adl, Al Qaeda, and Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP).

“And this is not what I’m saying. [This] is what the United Nations reports and the intelligence assessments of the US and many other countries also say,” he stressed. “How could so many terrorist organisations, the whole alphabet, thrive over there?“

The DG ISPR further questioned, “Why would Reuters or anyone take the words of a non-state actor so seriously?”

He said the Afghan Taliban could “come out with anything”, recalling false claims made by them of capturing a Pakistani pilot and presenting their own tanks as captured Pakistani tanks.

Responding to a question about whether isolating the Afghan Taliban could further harm the neighbouring country, particularly its farmers affected by cuts in foreign aid, Lt Gen Chaudhry voiced Pakistan’s opposition to isolating Afghanistan.

“I fully agree. Who is saying that the world and the region need to isolate Afghanistan? No,” he said, adding that the international community should instead press them to “act like a state”.

“What Afghanistan is producing right now, it has only two products: terrorism and drugs,” he said. “Both are not good for the world and the region and everyone. So that requires engagement.”

The military spokesperson noted that Pakistan was also engaging with its neighbour.

“Pakistan is asking them that we have got nothing to do with you. You run your country the way you feel like. It’s for the Afghans to decide. We only ask you that don’t support terrorism inside Pakistan. Stop harbouring the terrorist leaders,” he reiterated.

‘Principal obstacle to normal relations’

A day earlier, the information ministry stressed that the “Taliban regime’s persistent refusal to address terrorism remains the principal obstacle to normal relations”, objecting to Kabul’s portrayal of the issue.

“The Taliban leadership continues to blame Islamabad’s policies while conveniently ignoring the single most important issue poisoning bilateral relations: its persistent failure to address terrorism emanating from Afghan soil,” it said.

Multiple rounds of talks between the two sides last year — facilitated by Qatar and Turkiye — failed to bring about any workable solution, with the Pakistani government saying the Taliban officials gave no assurances on the key issues. Efforts this year made with China’s involvement also resulted in no breakthrough.

Russia, the only country to have formally recognised the Taliban government, has also recently renewed its offer to facilitate a settlement if both sides request its involvement.

When asked about it earlier this month, Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said he was “not aware of any separate, formal Russian mediation initiative being under discussion”.

He said talks with Afghanistan could not be unconditional and rejected suggestions that Islamabad was unwilling to engage with its neighbour.

September witnessed another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

This was followed by drone incursions from across the border, which Islamabad said were shot down, and two further rounds of retaliatory airstrikes.

World.title: Pakistan responds to unprovoked firing from Afghan posts along border in Lower South Waziristan: DC
World.content:
Pakistani security forces have responded to unprovoked firing from the Afghan border posts, the deputy commissioner of Lower South Waziristan district said on Sunday.

In a post on X, the DC’s official account said, “Unprovoked firing from Afghan border posts onto Pakistani border checkpoints continues.”

It added that Pakistani security forces responded immediately and effectively, targeting “multiple Afghan border posts, mortar positions, and defensive checkpoints”.

“The Afghan Taliban were forced to abandon their posts and flee in response to the Pakistani forces’ strong response,” the post read.

It further said no reports of any casualties have emerged from the border areas on the Pakistani side.

“Pakistani forces remain prepared to deliver a full response to any kind of aggression,” the deputy commissioner affirmed.

The military’s media affairs wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), is yet to comment on the development.

The fresh exchange of fire follows Friday’s skirmishes, when Pakistan’s armed forces responded to unprovoked firing from the other side, state media reported, citing security sources. As a result, several Afghan Taliban posts in areas adjacent to South Waziristan and Parachinar were destroyed.

The Afghan forces had also opened fire along the Angoor Adda border area on Tuesday, which claimed the life of one local and injured a family of five.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi had condemned the firing, asserting that Pakistan would “never tolerate” attacks on its people or violations of its sovereignty.

Pakistan had also dismissed a statement by Afghanistan’s defence ministry regarding the incident that claimed that Pakistan was the aggressor, terming it a “fabrication of lies”.

The border at Angoor Adda is one of the most important and sensitive crossings along the Pak-Afghan border, serving as a key trade route and one of the main points of public movement between the two countries.

Amid the heightened tensions, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday said that Washington has “heard” Pakistan’s concerns about terrorism emanating from Afghanistan and if “there’s a productive role for us to play, we would play it”.

Asked about the conflict between the neighbouring countries, Rubio said, “We’ve heard the concerns that Pakistan has raised and we’ve seen some of those attacks that they point to. We’re against terrorism no matter where it emanates from and who it targets.”

Pak-Afghan tensions

Ties between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been strained in the past few years as Islamabad continues to voice its concern over cross-border terrorism.

Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded.

For their part, the Afghan Taliban have avoided taking a categorical position on the TTP and other groups, while dismissing Islamabad’s stance that Afghanistan is being used as a base for attacks against Pakistan.

A day earlier, the information ministry stressed that the “Taliban regime’s persistent refusal to address terrorism remains the principal obstacle to normal relations”, objecting to Kabul’s portrayal of the issue.

The recent wave of military conflict began in September, when Pakistan carried out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in KP. This was followed by drone incursions from across the Afghan border, which Islamabad said were shot down.

In retaliation to the drone incursion, Pakistan conducted “precision aerial and drone strikes” in 10 locations across Afghanistan, followed by another round of “calibrated” air strikes against terrorist hideouts in Afghanistan on Oct 1.

World.title: Polio case from KP's Khyber takes nationwide tally for 2026 to eight
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The National Emergency Operations Centre for Polio Eradication (NEOC) on Sunday confirmed the country’s eighth polio case of this year.

The latest case was from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Khyber district, where the affected child is a 13-month-old girl from Union Council Janbaz-B in the Bara tehsil, according to the Pakistan Polio Eradication Programme (PPEP).

Polio is a highly contagious disease that has no cure and can cause lifelong paralysis. It can, however, be prevented through safe and effective polio vaccines, which have been used safely in 195 countries, including all Muslim-majority countries.

“The case is a reminder of the importance of vaccinating every child,” read a statement from PPEP. It urged parents to ensure that all children under five receive the oral polio vaccine in the upcoming subnational polio campaign from Nov 2 to 8 and in subsequent campaigns.

“This is the second case reported from Khyber District this year — and the sixth from KP province — underscoring that no child will be safe from polio until all children are consistently vaccinated and protected across the country,” the statement read.

While overall wild poliovirus transmission has declined this year, the Peshawar Block, comprising the districts of Khyber and Peshawar, has reported positive environmental detections, indicating virus circulation and a continued risk to children’s health.

The Pakistan Polio Eradication Initiative (PEI) has launched a case investigation and is analysing the best science-based response to tackle and prevent further transmission, including targeted vaccination activities and support to strengthen routine immunisation.

In 2026 so far, Pakistan has already implemented four large-scale polio campaigns, protecting more than 45 million children multiple times, alongside smaller targeted campaigns to administer oral and injectable vaccines in high-risk areas, including the Peshawar Block.

The recent sub-national vaccination campaign in September protected over 29.3m children across the country, while the next vaccination round is scheduled from Nov 2-8 to protect nearly 24m in 97 districts, including Khyber. It will be conducted simultaneously in Pakistan and Afghanistan with strong cross-border coordination.

World.title: PIA's first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner arrives in Islamabad
World.content:
Pakistan International Airlines’ (PIA) first Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, acquired on lease last month, arrived in Islamabad from London as flight PK786 on Sunday.

A PIA spokesperson, in a statement, said that the carrier is the first Pakistani airline to have added a Boeing 787-9 to its fleet.

PIA Chief Executive Aamir Hayat, accompanied by his team, welcomed the Dreamliner at Islamabad airport, according to the statement.

The plane is equipped with modern technology, including in-flight entertainment, and features a spacious and comfortable cabin, PIA said.

“The inclusion of the Dreamliner is part of a strategy to modernise PIA’s fleet and strengthen its international network,” the spokesperson said.

Photo shows the inside of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday. — Photo courtesy PIA

“PIA’s objective is to provide international-standard travel facilities and a more comfortable air travel experience to passengers through modern aircraft.”

The Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is a long-range, twin-engine plane with up to 325 seats. Previously, PIA’s fleet consisted of 12 Boeing 777 jets, 15 Airbus A320 planes and five smaller ATRs.

Photo shows the inside of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday. — Photo courtesy PIA

Last month, PIA signed an ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance) lease agreement with Norse Atlantic Airways to acquire two state-of-the-art Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners, one of which arrived in Islamabad on Sunday.

A PIA spokesperson at the time said the addition of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner would mark the start of the airline’s expansion.

By expanding its fleet, the airline aims to meet rising demand with direct flights and broader global connectivity, he added.

The aircraft would operate direct long-haul flights from Pakistan to the United Kingdom, he said, adding that they would support PIA operations between different points in the UK and Pakistan.

The development also comes as the government in September clarified that it was not buying any aircraft for the former national carrier after reports emerged of a federal minister arranging and negotiating sovereign-linked financing for PIA jets.

World.title: Crew from Nasa's simulated Mars mission emerges after 378 days in isolation
World.content:
The four members of a crew who took part in a simulated mission to Mars have emerged after 378 days in isolation ​at the US space agency’s Johnson Space Centre in Houston, an endeavour designed to help prepare for a ‌possible future excursion by Nasa astronauts to Earth’s planetary neighbour.

“It’s been a hell of a year — analogue astronauts living in captivity of our own free will,” Ellen Ellis, the medical officer on the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analogue (Chapea) mission, said in remarks at Johnson Space Centre after ​emerging with her three crewmates on Saturday.

The four entered the 158-square-metre 3D-printed habitat on Oct 19, 2025, and performed ​tasks such as growing crops in simulated Martian soil and interfacing with Nasa officials with delays ⁠recreating those inherent in interplanetary communications.

Nasa, which has explored Mars with robotic rovers and orbiting spacecraft, has ambitions for a human mission ​to Mars as early as the 2030s, with plans before that to return astronauts to the moon for the first time since 1972.

“We ​have a narrowing window of opportunity to maintain US preeminence in space,” Ellis said.

Ellis mentioned the service academy for space-related operations pursued by United States President Donald Trump’s administration and plans for a lunar base.

“Let’s seize the initiative, lead with science that will benefit our economy and ensure our legacy in space for our ​children’s children,” Ellis said.

The other crew members were mission commander Ross Elder, science officer Matthew Montgomery and flight engineer James Spicer.

“For ​Mars, the risks are great,” Elder said in remarks after emerging from isolation.

“But through seeking understanding, strong vision and leadership, creativity, fortitude, hard work ‌and ⁠incredible foundation, the goal of putting humans on Mars is not only achievable, but rather inevitable.”

The crew is set to participate in two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefing with Nasa scientists. Nasa has said it is looking for insight into what it takes for astronauts to adapt to the routines and demands of daily life on long-duration missions beyond Earth to keep them healthy, productive, ​and connected.

This was Nasa’s second ​Chapea mission, with another four-person ⁠crew in isolation at Johnson Space Centre for 378 days spanning 2023 and 2024.

Vanessa Wyche, director of the Johnson Space Centre, greeted the crew members when they exited isolation. Wyche said they ​managed to live with limited resources, maintain their habitat, and carry out simulated Mars operations.

Wyche also ​noted how the ⁠crew dealt with the simulated interplanetary communications, with lag times between sending messages and receiving responses.

“These delays require patience, careful planning and greater independence — qualities that will be essential for future astronauts travelling millions of miles from home,” Wyche said.

Wyche said the lessons learned from ⁠the Chapea crew and their experiences will help pave the way for the missions first ​to the moon and “one day, Mars”.

World.title: Terrorist attacks drop by 37pc in October: PICSS
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan witnessed a significant improvement in several key security indicators during October, with terrorist attacks declining by 37 per cent compared with September, it emerged on Sunday.

According to statistics released by the Islamabad-based Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), the country experienced 143 terrorist attacks during October, compared with 226 in September. The decline reversed two consecutive months of increasing terrorist violence.

The improvement was particularly pronounced in Balochistan and mainland Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, while suicide attacks also declined substantially. However, an increase in kidnappings, particularly in Balochistan, remained a major area of concern.

Data gathered by PICSS showed that terrorist attacks claimed 111 lives in October, compared with 260 in September, representing a reduction of 57pc. The number of people injured in these attacks dropped even more sharply, from 242 to just 69, a decline of 71pc.

The improvement in the security situation was also reflected in the overall human cost of violence.

According to PICSS, terrorist attacks and security forces’ counterterrorism operations collectively resulted in deaths of 53 security forces personnel, 45 civilians and five peace committee members, while 169 terrorists were killed.

The 71 injured included 29 security forces personnel, 11 peace committee members, and 31 civilians.

A rolling 12-month comparison conducted by PICSS revealed several encouraging developments. Injuries resulting from terrorist attacks fell to their lowest monthly level in the past year. The combined number of injuries from terrorist attacks and security operations also reached a 12-month low, as did injuries among security forces personnel.

— Screengrab via PICSS report.

The number of suicide attacks was jointly the lowest recorded during the same period. However, the number of terrorists killed, at 169, was also the lowest monthly figure in the past 12 months, reflecting a decline in terrorist fatalities, the report noted.

Suicide attacks declined sharply during October, with only one such incident, compared with three in September. The October incident involved a vehicle-borne suicide attack but caused no fatalities or injuries.

In contrast, the three suicide attacks recorded in September, including two vehicle-borne attacks, resulted in 45 deaths and 138 injuries. Consequently, fatalities and injuries from suicide attacks both declined by 100pc during October.

According to PICSS, continued counterterrorism operations across the country by security forces resulted in the killing of 156 terrorists and the arrest of seven suspected terrorists during October. Two security forces personnel and three civilians lost their lives during these operations, while two security forces personnel were injured.

Balochistan

Balochistan recorded one of the most significant improvements, with terrorist attacks declining by 46pc, from 132 in September to 71 in October. Fatalities from terrorist attacks dropped from 136 to 44, representing a reduction of approximately 68pc, while injuries declined from 63 to 37, a decrease of 41pc.

Separately, security forces’ operations in the province resulted in the killing of 79 terrorists.

Three civilians lost their lives, and two security forces personnel were injured during these operations.

In October, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) had confirmed that an army major was martyred in an improvised explosive device (IED) attack in Balochistan.

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Mainland KP, excluding the formerly federally administered tribal areas, also witnessed a substantial improvement. PICSS reported 40 terrorist attacks in October, compared with 58 in September, representing a decline of 31pc. Fatalities from these attacks decreased from 90 to 38, a reduction of approximately 58pc, while injuries fell from 165 to 19, an improvement of 88pc.

Counterterrorism operations in the region resulted in the killing of 42 terrorists, while two security forces personnel lost their lives.

The erstwhile FATA region experienced a comparatively modest decline in terrorist violence, the report said. The think tank recorded 30 attacks during October, compared with 34 in September, a reduction of 12pc. Deaths resulting from terrorist attacks declined from 33 to 25, while injuries increased slightly from 11 to 13. Security forces’ operations in these districts resulted in the killing of 35 terrorists.

Sindh and Punjab

Punjab witnessed two terrorist attacks during October, compared with none in September. These incidents resulted in four deaths and no injuries.

Sindh recorded no terrorist attacks during the month. However, counterterrorism operations in the province resulted in the arrest of seven suspected terrorists. Islamabad, Azad Jammu and Kashmir, and Gilgit-Baltistan also remained free of recorded terrorist attacks during October.

— Screengrab via PICSS report.

Kidnappings ‘serious security concern’

Despite the overall improvement, kidnappings emerged as a serious security concern, particularly in Balochistan.

PICSS recorded 88 people kidnapped in terrorist incidents nationwide during October, compared with 72 in September, an increase of 22pc. This was the highest monthly kidnapping figure recorded during the preceding 12 months. Balochistan accounted for 70 of these kidnappings, representing nearly 80pc of the nationwide total.

The increase suggests that, despite the reduction in attacks and casualties, kidnapping remained a significant tactic employed by terrorist groups, the report said.

While October’s figures indicate a significant month-on-month improvement, the longer-term security picture remains challenging.

According to the report, Pakistan experienced 1,376 terrorist attacks during the first 10 months of 2026. These attacks, alongside security forces’ counterterrorism operations, collectively resulted in 3,902 deaths, including 645 security forces personnel, 65 peace committee members, 595 civilians, and 2,597 terrorists.

Another 1,953 people were injured during the January–October period, including 639 security forces personnel, 62 peace committee members, 1,055 civilians, and 197 terrorists.

Compared with the corresponding 10-month period of 2025, the number of terrorist attacks increased by 53pc, while the combined death toll rose by 36pc.

World.title: Sialkot police say 6 held as TikToker nominated in case over stampede at mehndi event
World.content:
NAROWAL: Sialkot police on Sunday said they had arrested six suspects and registered a case after a stampede at a TikToker’s mehndi (henna) event, the deaths from which have risen to two.

TikToker Muhammad Ansar Jatt, known as “Mr Pattlo”, had announced holding a mehndi event and prize-distribution ceremony at Faraz Cricket Ground on Daska Road on Friday night.

With hundreds gathered at the site, a stampede occurred when the stadium gates opened. While Rescue 1122 initially said one man had died and 13 others were injured, residents had put the number of injured higher because many were taken to nearby hospitals by attendees at the event.

On Sunday, Sialkot Police said 18 people were injured in the stampede. One of them succumbed to his injuries at a government hospital, taking the deaths to two, the public relations officer for the district police officer (DPO) confirmed.

Noting that Jatt had immediately fled the scene after the incident, police said their investigation and raid teams were conducting operations to apprehend the TikTok influencer.

The police statement added that they had taken 50 motorcycles and a car — intended for Friday’s lucky draw — into their custody.

Sialkot DPO Dost Muhammad confirmed the arrest of six individuals involved in managing the event.

He added that police teams have been constituted to apprehend the remaining suspects with the help of modern technology, human intelligence sources, and traditional policing methods.

The retired captain noted that according to preliminary police investigations, organisers had invited a large number of people by advertising a lucky draw featuring prizes such as motorcycles, a car and other valuable items via social media.

During the event, an announcement was made over the loudspeakers instructing all attendees to enter the grounds simultaneously. This simultaneous entry into the sports stadium triggered a severe stampede, the DPO said.

He stated that the organisers violated the terms of their permit, as well as established safety standard operating procedures (SOPs). The stampede also disrupted the flow of traffic on the main Daska-Sialkot Road.

Noting reports of unruly behaviour by attendees and damage to public and private property, DPO Muhammad emphasised that protecting citizens’ lives and property is the police’s primary responsibility.

“Negligence regarding safety arrangements at any public gathering or event which puts human lives at risk cannot be permitted,” he said.

The Sialkot DPO declared that legal action would be taken against all those responsible for the incident, without any discrimination.

NOC revoked

According to a spokesperson for the Sialkot district administration, a no-objection certificate (NOC) had been issued to the TikToker for holding a mehfil-i-samaa (a gathering for devotional music/poetry) during a private event within an enclosed space in Daska.

The spokesperson stated that the event was cancelled before it could even begin, due to violations of the stipulated terms and conditions. According to the spokesperson, the NOC specified that the programme was to commence after the Isha (night) prayers on Friday.

However, reports were received regarding alleged irregularities in the event arrangements by the organisers as early as 4pm.

Upon reviewing the reports, Sialkot Deputy Commissioner Awais Mushtaq took immediate preemptive action and revoked the previously issued NOC.

FIR registered

The first information report (FIR), dated Oct 31 and available with Dawn, was registered at the Motra Police Station on the complaint of Inspector Mubeen Ahmed.

The FIR names Jatt, his brother, the owner of Faraz Cricket Ground, and six others who were organisers of the event, as well as 40-45 unidentified security guards.

It invoked sections 322 (punishment for qatl-bis-sabab), 188 (disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant), 148 (rioting, armed with deadly weapon), 149 (every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object), 431 (mischief by injury to public road, bridge, river or channel), 440 (mischief committed after preparation made for causing death or hurt), and 109 (abetment if the act abetted committed in consequence) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), along with Section 16 of the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) Ordinance.

In the FIR, the inspector accused the suspects of violating the terms of the permit granted by the Sialkot district administration, as well as the established SOPs.

The alleged violations included the misuse of loudspeakers, the blocking of a main road, the vandalism of citizens’ motorcycles, and the infliction of loss of life and property.

The FIR noted that a large crowd managed to enter the Faraz Sports Stadium due to inadequate security arrangements at the venue.

According to the FIR, dozens of attendees at the mehndi and prize distribution ceremony reported that their mobile phones had gone missing and unidentified thieves picked their pockets, depriving them of cash and important documents.

World.title: Pakistan's embassy in Tehran refutes rumours of people 'attacking' its ambassador to Iran
World.content:
Pakistan’s embassy in Iran on Sunday refuted rumours of an attack on Ambassador Imran Ahmed Siddiqui in Tehran, terming them “baseless”.

In a post on X, the embassy said it had taken note of “certain reports circulating in social media and other forums” concerning the Pakistani ambassador to Iran.

The embassy shared a post from another X account, which had posted a video showing a commotion amongst a large crowd of people in an unidentified building, with several people appearing to engage in physical altercations.

The account that posted the video alleged, citing reports, that the Pakistani ambassador had been attacked in Tehran at an unspecified event where he had been invited. It did not specify the nature or origin of the reports.

The account claimed that Siddiqui was taken to a nearby hospital for medical treatment.

“The embassy categorically clarifies that these reports are baseless and factually incorrect,” the post by Pakistan’s embassy in Tehran said.

The ambassador himself has not made any statement on his X account about the rumours.

Pakistan appointed Ambassador Siddiqui as its envoy to neighbouring Iran in February. Before assuming his current post, he served as Pakistan’s ambassador to Bangladesh.

Last month, the information ministry refuted rumours that Pakistan’s envoy in London was “confronted and attacked with a white powder-like substance”.

It said the video being shared on social media was “fake and is being circulated with a misleading caption”.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks.
