In January 2023, Russian occupying forces removed a monument to Taras Shevchenko from the center of occupied Melitopol, in the Zaporizhzhia region. The dismantling took place late in the evening. The city’s mayor, Ivan Fedorov, reported the removal, adding: “They probably took him to the basement. That’s the only way they know how to deal with those they don’t like.”

He knew about basements from personal experience. In March 2022, he was abducted from his office, a bag was pulled over his head, and a week later he was exchanged for nine very young Russian conscripts captured by Ukrainian forces. By May 9, 2025, a bust of Stalin had been installed on the pedestal in Melitopol where Shevchenko’s monument had stood.

Shevchenko has repeatedly reappeared in Ukrainian territories soon after Russian forces were driven out. A short video, filmed by Ukrainian Air Force assault troops in the liberated city of Balakliia, in the Kharkiv region, during the autumn 2023 counteroffensive, was shown on what seemed like every television channel in the country.

In the footage, soldiers tear down a Russian tricolor banner from a roadside billboard. It bears the words “We are one people with Russia.” Beneath it, a portrait of the Kobzar is revealed, along with a famous stanza from his poem The Caucasus. The banner had been put up in the last year before the invasion that could still be described as relatively peaceful, to mark another anniversary of Ukraine’s independence.

One soldier reacts in disbelief: “Holy f—!” Another orders him: “Read it!” And he reads the stanza aloud:

“Fight on – and you will prevail! God is with you! For you are truth, for you are glory, and holy freedom!”

Serhiy Nihoyan, a student who became one of the first people killed during the Maidan protests, had recited the same passage aloud against a backdrop of barricades.

Today, in Kyiv’s Lukianivka district, where little remains untouched, a banner bearing Shevchenko’s portrait and the words “We are fighting. We will prevail” covers the facade of a damaged building. Ukrainians immediately recognize the reference: the call to “Fight on – and you will prevail!” is etched into their collective memory.

Shevchenko’s lines are continually adapted to the moment. At Barbara, a coffee shop near the author’s home, one version reads: “Get out of our home. We are free forever. There will be no Muscovy here. Glory to Ukraine!”

Chernecha hill under the tsars

The hill near Kaniv, overlooking the Dnipro River and its green slopes, became a place of pilgrimage almost immediately after Shevchenko’s remains were transferred there from St. Petersburg in May 1861, in accordance with his Testament.

In 1884, local residents raised funds to erect a cast-iron cross. Nearby, at the edge of the woods, they built a simple hut.

One half became an improvised folk museum called Tarasova Svitlytsia (“Taras’s Chamber”); the other served as the home of a caretaker. The exhibits included a copy of Kobzar, an oil portrait of the poet with a halo above his head, brushes belonging to an unknown artist, a kobza, a traditional Ukrainian stringed instrument, and an old visitors’ book lying on a table.

Embroidered Ukrainian towels, known as rushnyky, hung on the walls, including some bearing Shevchenko’s image. Many of those who brought them could neither read nor write, yet knew his poems by heart.

Secret reports from the Kaniv gendarmerie on visitors to the site have survived in the State Archives of the Kyiv Region. People came to Chernecha Hill not only from neighboring villages but from far away. Surveillance intensified ahead of major anniversaries.

The authorities refused to permit either accommodation for pilgrims or the establishment of an association to maintain and protect the grave. A document dated April 8, 1910, from the Kyiv provincial authority responsible for public associations explained why. Such an association, it warned, “would provide a convenient means of bringing together activists and adherents of the Ukrainophile party, allowing them to gather in an isolated place, difficult for the administration to observe and monitor.”

The association’s activities, officials cautioned, “would be directed toward strengthening propaganda for the cultural and political autonomy of Little Russia.” They even found evidence of suspicious intentions in the application’s failure to specify the language to be used for official business. The implication was clear: the language in question might not be Russian.

The Moscow art theatre at Shevchenko’s grave

The warnings from the gendarmerie and the authorities’ fears of “advocates of autonomy” did not deter prominent figures in Russia’s artistic and intellectual circles.

Zinaida Tarakhan-Bereza, the oldest living staff member of the Shevchenko National Reserve, cites historical accounts in her scholarly chronicle The Shrine (Kyiv, 1998). In May 1912, a steamer decorated with Shevchenko’s portrait, embroidered towels and flowers arrived at the Kaniv landing.

“No speeches, politically charged songs or other demonstrative performances!” the “tourists” were reminded once again as they came ashore.

Only two wreaths were permitted at the poet’s grave.

One came from the Ukrainian Club, a national and cultural association headed by the composer Mykola Lysenko. The other was an elaborate wrought-metal wreath decorated with oak leaves, symbolizing eternity, a laurel branch and a bronze plaque bearing the inscription: “A bow to the ground before the genius Shevchenko from the Moscow Art Theatre.”

The Moscow Art Theatre was touring Kyiv at the time. From then on, its actors spent every summer living communally at a nearby hamlet beside Taras Hill, drawing inspiration from the place. Among them were Ivan Moskvin, Yevgeny Vakhtangov and Mikhail Chekhov.

The Ukrainian Club was shut down in 1912.

I examined the leaves from the theatre’s wreath in a museum display case. They have survived two world wars and are now enduring Russia’s invasion.

The Museum in a bomb shelter

Few original exhibits remain on display at the museum. The most valuable surviving objects have been moved to a secure location to protect them from bombing.

“Kaniv, and particularly the Kaniv Hydroelectric Power Plant, has come under fire more than once. But our academic council collectively decided not to evacuate anything outside the country,” says Hanna Manzhara, the museum’s senior collections curator.

She is 80 and cannot imagine her life apart from the museum.

“We resumed work in July 2022 because the number of visitors kept growing. That was such an incentive! We moved the exhibition to the basement, which had been converted into a bomb shelter. At the beginning of this year, we returned to the surface, to the galleries.”

Unlike monuments in Kyiv, Shevchenko’s memorial in Kaniv has not been covered with sandbags. It is not simply a sculpture but a burial mound with a crypt inside, a place where people come to pay their respects.

Yet Russian forces have also struck cemeteries: in Cherkasy in July 2025, in Odesa in October 2024 and in Kramatorsk in April 2023.

Hanna Ivanivna Manzhara, senior collections curator. Photograph: Olga Musafirova

Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow

The conversation naturally turns to Russia. The Moscow and St. Petersburg periods of Shevchenko’s life and work cannot simply be erased from his story.

Hanna Manzhara recalls taking part in Ukrainian Culture Days in Moscow in 2003, together with Vita Dzyma, a senior researcher.

“The Ukrainian Center on Arbat Street asked us to take part.

“We brought an exhibition featuring lifetime editions of individual poems, as well as publications from 1911 and 1914, marking the 50th anniversaries of his birth and death. We added woven Ukrainian folk towels made by Marуsia Vasylashchuk, a traditional craftswoman. The response was fantastic! Teachers from Moscow came, along with members of the Ukrainian diaspora. Our fellow museum professionals were particularly remarkable in the attention they gave us.”

“And, of course, there were collectors,” Dzyma continues. “I won’t name them; we lost contact a long time ago. But copies of Moscow newspapers reporting on Taras Shevchenko’s funeral found their way to Kaniv through antique shops on Arbat Street.

“The museum was preparing for reconstruction, and we were trying to build up our collection.”

Manzhara adds: “You see, the life and work of the Kobzar are far broader than anything we ourselves could convey to an audience.”

Dzyma has a similar story. In the family of the St. Petersburg literary scholar Ieremiya Aizenshtok, a self-portrait of 16-year-old Taras was discovered, dating from the time he served as Engelhardt’s personal attendant, or kazachok. Research and evidence suggested it was the earliest portrait of the Kobzar.

“But Aizenshtok’s relatives asked for a very high price. The Kaniv museum simply couldn’t afford it. What happened to the portrait, and who owns it now, is unknown.”

At that moment, the author’s phone begins to vibrate: an air-raid alert has been issued in Kyiv.

On social media, Russian military personnel who have spent nearly five years launching missiles, including at Ukrainian museums, are sarcastically dubbed “Pushkinists.” Among the institutions hit have been the Hryhorii Skovoroda Museum in Skovorodynivka, the Kupiansk Museum of Local History and the Odesa Fine Arts Museum.

A Shrine to an Icon: The Museum Under Soviet Rule

“Now the working people of Ukraine and the Soviet Union will be able to become more familiar with the great legacy of the poet-revolutionary, a fighter against the social and national oppression that weighed so heavily on the peoples of the former tsarist Russia,” the republican newspaper Kommunist wrote in 1936.

The newspaper recalled that in 1923, a temporary monument had been erected over Shevchenko’s grave “in place of the cross so hated by the poet and all working people,” and that a temporary exhibition had been set up nearby in 1934. At the same time, construction of a museum was underway on Taras Hill.

Visitors often ask why the Soviet authorities invested so heavily in the project during the Holodomor, the famine that devastated Ukraine. It was the first building in Ukraine designed specifically to house a museum. Until then, museums had generally occupied historic aristocratic or manor houses.

Vita Dzyma offers an explanation:

“Look around: every home had a portrait of Shevchenko – embroidered, painted, burned into wood or assembled from straw. Kobzar lay beside the Bible, or took its place when the campaign against religion began.

“The villages at the foot of Taras Hill were being starved to death. People hired themselves out to work on the construction site for a piece of bread. They carried stones by hand, as in ancient Egypt. Yet they were proud of their work. The Shevchenko Museum was no less than a temple.

“Arguing with Ukrainians about this is a losing battle. Taras is both a father and a prophet!”

Vita Dzyma, senior researcher at the museum. Photograph: Olga Musafirova

A sculptural composition of Lenin and Stalin was installed in the entrance hall, while Shevchenko’s bust was moved to the second floor so that it would not compete with them. According to Dzyma, whose account is supported by research, Soviet propagandists in the 1930s seriously pursued the idea of finding a physical resemblance between Lenin and Shevchenko.

The burial mound was given an upgrade, too. Behind a granite balustrade at the base of the monument, a platform was built resembling the speaker’s tribune at Lenin’s Mausoleum, intended for members of the Ukrainian Communist Party’s Politburo.

In 1939, marking the 125th anniversary of the Kobzar’s birth, Nikita Khrushchev, the first secretary of the Communist Party of Ukraine, spoke at the opening of the museum and the unveiling of the new monument.

“The tradition of placing microphones beside Shevchenko and addressing the community as if speaking on his behalf, from his elevated position, has survived to this day,” Hanna Manzhara explains.

The museum under nazi occupation: Director Dmytro Lebedko

In mid-August 1941, the last train carrying mobilized troops left Kaniv across the bridge over the Dnipro. The bridge was bombed, and its ruins can still be seen from Taras Hill.

There was no time to evacuate the museum before the Nazi occupation. Its staff scattered. The women I spoke to avoid going into detail about what happened next. “It would be disrespectful to the local residents,” they say.

Dmytro Lebedko, a former librarian at the reserve who had been mobilized into the Red Army and survived the bombing of his train, found himself in two roles at once: collaborator, having agreed to work with the occupying forces, and preserver of the museum’s collection.

The Nazis did not close the museum. Instead, they ordered it to be put in order and kept open. Visitors, mostly German soldiers, were brought through in formation. For the first time, not a single entry appeared in the visitors’ book.

The local population was afraid to visit Taras Hill, even though in the nearby district center of Horodyshche, the Nazis had toppled a statue of Karl Marx and replaced it with one of Shevchenko.

Archival documents preserve Lebedko’s testimony: “In 1941, I managed to recover from the village of Pekari 15 chairs, about 2,000 books, two carpets embroidered with portraits of Shevchenko, six silk curtains and a number of other valuables.”

After becoming director, he carried out a full inventory of the museum’s collection, cataloguing 4,000 items. He was not afraid to compile a list of paintings and drawings that the local Nazi district commissioner had supposedly taken for “temporary use.” He also recorded every vase and carpet appropriated by yet another official with an interest in “Slavic exoticism.” Then he took a risk that could have cost him his life: he moved the most valuable objects into a hiding place, sealed it behind a wall and went into hiding himself.

After Soviet troops arrived, Lebedko still managed to help restore the museum, which the Nazis had ransacked shortly before retreating. He voluntarily admitted in court to having been involved in a “Ukrainian nationalist Bandera organization.”

The authorities demanded that he strengthen his self-incriminating statement. “I thought Soviet rule would no longer exist in Ukraine and that Ukraine would become independent. I now understand the serious political error in my views,” he was made to say.

He was convicted of treason and sentenced to the maximum term. Three years later, he died in the Norilsk labor camps from a perforated stomach ulcer.

Dmytro Lebedko was 47, the same age as Taras Shevchenko. His name was erased from the history of the reserve for decades. Museum staff emphasize that only 10 exhibits from the prewar collection have survived to this day.

Yanukovych’s makeover

Toward the end of Leonid Kuchma’s presidency, plans emerged for a major restoration project in Kaniv. A nationwide fund was established specifically to restore historical and architectural heritage sites, and UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya, a Ukrainian research and design institute specializing in restoration, was selected to develop the project. Its specialists proposed returning the building to its original appearance, based on the drawings of architect Vasyl Krychevsky.

In the 1930s, Krychevsky had been unable to realize his full vision. His design was deemed “too Ukrainian,” and both he and his closest student, Petro Kostyrko, were removed from the project. The construction was completed by more compliant hands. As a result, museum staff, whose building had received no major restoration since World War II, were afraid even to express their hopes aloud.

The project stalled, then resumed under President Viktor Yanukovych. According to those involved, the massive, even pompous building made a strong impression on him. If the museum was to host the annual Shevchenko National Prize ceremony, Ukraine’s highest state award for achievements in culture and the arts, it had to meet the president’s aesthetic standards.

Few understood Yanukovych’s tastes better than Hanna Herman, one of his closest allies, a member of parliament from the Party of Regions and head of its humanitarian policy team, and her protégé, architect Larysa Skoryk.

“History repeated itself,” Vita Dzyma says. “At the final stage, UkrNDIproektrestavratsiya was removed from the project, and the national character of the design was discarded. ‘No painted decoration on the exterior – this isn’t some village hut!’ they said. But the preparatory work for the majolica facade had already been completed. The same was true of the alfresco work – the decorative painting in relief.

“The Ministry of Culture’s scientific and methodological council convened and decided: whitewash it!”

Hanna Manzhara adds: “Even the surviving fragments of Krychevsky’s original work, which had miraculously survived the previous war and were rediscovered during the restoration, were covered up again.”

Skoryk developed a stripped-down design concept. The polychrome landscape inspired by the poem Haidamaky was replaced with a monochrome version.

The original coffered ceiling was concealed behind a stretch ceiling. Red lines of Shevchenko’s poetry ran across the gray fabric like information scrolling through a subway station. Glass replaced the wooden mosaic partitions in the entrance hall, while granite slabs took the place of parquet flooring.

“We wanted at least to restore the unique botanical and floral patterns on the columns.

“Both museum staff and Krychevsky’s relatives wrote to Yanukovych. It made no difference. What we got was a gray-and-white renovation,” Dzyma concludes.

She asks whether the author noticed the granite boulder at the entrance, in the center of the lobby. The author is puzzled. Surely this is not a geological museum.

▇ “Shevchenko is the cornerstone of the national idea. It’s a metaphor!”

Photographs From 1944 and a Forced-Labor Camp in the Museum

The author’s attention was drawn to two framed photographs on the wall, dated the last day of January 1944. Yakov Davidzon, a frontline correspondent, arrived at Taras Hill immediately after Kaniv was liberated. He found the museum surrounded by barbed wire, with burned books, torn paintings and shattered sculptures. Sixteen shrapnel wounds had been counted on the pedestal of Shevchenko’s monument.

“We learned only in 1981 that a forced-labor camp had operated inside the museum during the final months of the occupation,” says Valentyna Avramenko, head of the Tarasova Svitlytsia section.

She recalls a visitor from Moscow who wandered through the galleries as if he knew every corner of the building. It turned out that he was a native of the area who, as a teenager, had been caught in a roundup.

Young people were deported to the Reich for forced labor, while children as young as 13 or 14 were made to dig trenches and build fortifications. Several hundred schoolchildren were held inside the building, half-starved, sleeping on damp, rotting straw alongside horses. A toilet had been hacked directly into the parquet floor. Armed guards marched the children to the banks of the Dnipro with shovels and forced them to work under gunpoint. If one escaped, the others were beaten almost to death.

Staff at the reserve began tracking down the former child prisoners and recording their testimonies. Those who had survived long enough were later helped to submit applications for compensation from Germany. Why had no one spoken about the camp sooner?

The author found the answer herself in an archival leaflet issued by the Taras Shevchenko partisan unit, which operated in the forests of the Cherkasy region:

“We will find and kill everyone who helps the Germans build defensive lines along the Dnipro!”

Makohon’s bust: From Kaniv to Volodarka

In Davidzon’s second photograph, Shevchenko’s bust has a bullet hole in its forehead. The resemblance to the monument in Borodianka, shot up by Russian forces in 2022, is chilling.

The author was told that Ivan Makohon, a prominent Soviet Ukrainian sculptor, had created the plaster bust in 1937 specifically for the opening of the museum in Kaniv. But the work’s fate after World War II remains unknown. It is held neither in the museum’s exhibition nor in the collection of Ukraine’s National Art Museum.

The sculptor’s son, Ihor Makohon, himself a painter, sculptor and graphic artist, is now 90 and lives in Italy. He was surprised to hear the story of the wounded, missing Kobzar.

“There must be some misunderstanding! I visited Kaniv in the mid-1950s and took photographs. The bust was on the second-floor balcony, completely undamaged.

“In 1961, my father decided to modify the composition slightly, adding shoulders. The new version was more monumental. Two plaster casts were made in the workshop at the Kyiv Art Institute, where Professor Makohon taught, and the mold was preserved.”

More than 60 years passed. In 2024, Ihor Makohon received a request from Volodarka, a district center in the Kyiv region. Local residents wanted to install a “historic” Shevchenko monument by Makohon and asked for his permission.

Ihor Ivanovych not only found the original mold but also arranged for the bust to be produced.

“We cast the bust in concrete with the lads and took it to Volodarka. There was enormous interest, and a lot of people gathered,” he recalls.

The unveiling took place on the Feast of the Intercession of the Holy Mother of God, which Ukraine also celebrates as the Day of Defenders and Defendresses. The project fulfilled an idea conceived by Oleksandr Ushynskyi, a local resident, environmentalist, researcher of the Holodomor, Maidan protester and war veteran.

In 2014, Ushynskyi volunteered for the front, defended Donetsk airport and later established a community museum dedicated to the Russian-Ukrainian war in his hometown. The monument in Volodarka became the 1,385th monument to Shevchenko in Ukraine and around the world.

The nazis, the communists and Russian propaganda

“Both the Nazis during World War II and the Soviets used Shevchenko to manipulate Ukrainians’ minds for propaganda purposes,” says Ihor Solovey, head of the Center for Strategic Communications and Information Security under Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture.

“The Nazis tried to exploit our national sentiments under the guise of ‘friendship.’

“They took passages from Kobzar and amplified them to turn people against Soviet rule. The message was supposedly about resistance to Russian oppression, mixed with all sorts of vile nonsense about ‘Jewish Bolshevism.’ They even put Taras’s words on posters – the familiar line: ‘Muscovites are strangers; they bring you harm.’

“To present themselves as benefactors, the Nazis deliberately published his poetry and prose during the occupation and ran articles about Shevchenko that served their purposes. They wanted people to believe that Ukrainian culture was free and flourishing under the Reich.”

“The Communists did exactly the same thing. They just dressed it up differently to persuade Ukrainians to fight the Germans. Think of the famous rallying cry: ‘Drench freedom in the enemy’s blood!’” Solovey continues.

Eighty years have passed. In June 2026, Ukraine’s Security Service announced that a 57-year-old woman from Kaniv had been formally notified of suspicion over the dissemination of “materials justifying and denying the Russian Federation’s armed aggression against Ukraine.”

The woman reportedly referred to the invasion as a “special military operation,” urged support for the Russian army and openly promoted pro-Kremlin narratives among acquaintances and colleagues. According to investigators, she was one of the deputy heads of the Shevchenko National Reserve.

Modern Russian propaganda reproduces methods first used under the Russian Empire and later adopted by the Soviet Union. One is to present Shevchenko primarily as part of Russian culture, pointing to the fact that he wrote his diaries and prose in Russian.

Another is to portray him as a “pan-Russian poet,” downplaying the importance of his work in shaping Ukrainian national identity.

But those carrying out Russia’s full-scale war on Ukrainian soil increasingly see Shevchenko, his monuments and his museums not as shared cultural heritage, but as an adversary and a source of resistance.

World.title: Mayor and entrepreneur: Transparency International calls for dismissal of Georgian officials over business ties
World.content:
TI identifies 24 officials heading private companies

Transparency International Georgia (TI) has identified 24 serving public officials who simultaneously hold directorships at 30 private companies, in violation of anti-corruption legislation.

The officials include mayors, deputy mayors, heads of municipal councils and representatives of state agencies.

Georgian law prohibits public officials from simultaneously engaging in business activities. TI says officials whose violations are confirmed must be dismissed.

Under the law, newly appointed officials have 10 days to relinquish their positions as directors of commercial organisations. Failure to comply requires them to leave public service.

According to the list published by Transparency International Georgia, the officials named include:

Merab Bekaia – deputy head of Tbilisi’s Isani district administration and director of private company Hydraulic Service +.

Solomon Gorashvili – head of Dedoplistskaro City Hall’s Infrastructure, Spatial Planning, Architecture and Construction Department and director of private company Mirzaani.

– head of Dedoplistskaro City Hall’s Infrastructure, Spatial Planning, Architecture and Construction Department and director of private company Mirzaani. Roland Abuladze – head of Khulo City Hall’s Healthcare and Social Protection Department and head of the Adjara Clan cooperative.

– head of Khulo City Hall’s Healthcare and Social Protection Department and head of the Adjara Clan cooperative. Bidzina Mekvevrishvili – deputy chair of the Georgian Dream party faction in Akhmeta Municipal Council and head of the Magraani agricultural cooperative.

What the law says

Article 13 of Georgia’s Law on Combating Corruption restricts public officials from engaging in business activities and managing private companies. The aim is to separate public and private economic interests and reduce the risk of conflicts of interest.

At the same time, the law allows public officials to own shares in commercial enterprises, which gives them a different legal status from that of a company director.

Transparency International Georgia argues that simultaneously holding public office and managing a private company creates corruption risks. The organisation calls on the government to take action in accordance with the law.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: November 2, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 2. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day second Karabakh war ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Chronicle of the 37th day of the Second Karabakh War:

- President Ilham Aliyev shared a publication in connection with the liberation of several more villages of the Jebrail, Zangilan and Gubadli regions by the Azerbaijani army from the occupation.

- President Ilham Aliyev received a delegation led by former Prime Minister of Turkey Binali Yildirim.

- President Ilham Aliyev received the Secretary General of the Turkic Council and other officials.

- The list of destroyed military equipment of the Armenian Armed Forces was published.

- The Armenian Armed Forces fired at the territory of Aghdam and Aghjabadi districts. Armenia violated the ceasefire at the state border. Armenian troops retreated, suffering losses of up to 30 people.

- The Armenian Su-25 attack aircraft was destroyed. Four more "GRAD" missile launchers of the Armenian Armed Forces were destroyed.

- The Armenian Armed Forces intensively fired at the territory of the Terter and Goranboy regions. Armenia again fired at Gubadli from the territory of Armenia.

- The Ministry of Defense of Azerbaijan has disseminated a video of the destruction of enemy personnel.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry has disseminated a video of the destruction of the KUB anti-aircraft missile system of the Armenian Armed Forces.

World.title: First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva watched "Thikra: Night of Remembering” dance production (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 1. On November 1, the dance production "Thikra: Night of Remembering" was performed at the Azerbaijan State Academic National Drama Theater as part of the Baku International Arts Festival (BIAF-2026).

First Vice-President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva, along with her family members, watched the performance.

"Thikra: Night of Remembering", the latest work by acclaimed director and choreographer Akram Khan, was commissioned by Wadi AlFann, a global destination for contemporary art based in Al-Ula, Saudi Arabia.

Created in collaboration with award-winning visual artist Manal Al-Dowayan, Akram Khan Company’s final touring production draws on the ancient landscapes, mythology and cultural heritage of Al-Ula.

Through sacred rituals and shared recollections, an all-female ensemble transcend the boundaries of time, bridging past and present to invoke an act of spiritual renewal.

The production features an original score by Indian-American singer and composer Aditya Prakash.

The visual aesthetics of the play were created by "Wadi AlFann" artist Manal Al-Dowayan, renowned for her large-scale multimedia installation featured at the Saudi Arabian pavilion during the 60th Venice Biennale.

In the Thikra project, the artist blends traditional craftsmanship with contemporary forms. Natural dyes mirror the color palette of the desert, while geometric motifs rooted in Al-Ula’s heritage highlight the symbolic role and significance of each character.

The production draws on the ancient landscapes, mythology and cultural heritage of Al-Ula. The site-specific world premiere of the play was presented in January 2025.

World.title: Live: Albanese to seek tighter rules for British backpackers in meeting with UK PM
World.content:
Tanya Plibersek has again defended the federal government's budget tax changes, after new data was released showing the value of homes has dropped.

Cotality data says national house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, with the speed of the decline in home values tracking at the fastest pace seen over the past 40 years.

Its latest national Home Value Index (HVI) was down 1.2 per cent in October and is now 6.7 per cent below its March peak, equivalent to a decline of about $63,400 in the value of the median Australian dwelling.

But speaking to Channel Seven alongside One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce, the social services minister says she thinks the changes have made housing more affordable.

"The fact that the growth in house prices is moderated, I think that means that housing will be affordable for my kids and my grandkids one day," Plibersek says.

Plibersek has also been asked about polling showing Treasurer Jim Chalmers has an approval rating of minus 16.

The social services minister has thrown her support behind Chalmers, saying the treasurer is getting the "tough stuff" done.

World.title: Live: Wall Street sinks on AI fears, ASX on edge ahead of RBA meeting
World.content:
Wall Street closed the week, maybe not in a blind panic, but there was certainly a disquieting dumping of stocks as investors fled to the exits and the weekend.

All three key indices fell sharply, the tech-centric Nasdaq fell the hardest and is down almost 8% from its record high of just three weeks ago.

S & P 500: 1.8%

1.8% Dow: -1.1%

-1.1% Nasdaq: 2.9%

The dump saw the global MSCI down 1.5% for the day, while the pan-continental Eurostoxx 600 fell a comparatively modest 0.4%.

The tech-lite ASX is unlikely to be as affected by anxieties over cash-burning AI investments as Wall Street was on Friday.

When trading closed on Saturday morning (AEDT) ASX 200 futures were flat, or to be precise 4 points (0.04%) lower.

The tech rout was sparked by disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon released late on Thursday.

While Amazon pared losses as the session progressed, Intel shares cratered, down almost 30%

Chip stocks veered sharply lower, with Nvidia down more than 4%.

The broader chips index shed 7.2%, slumping to a monthly loss of more than 15%. Server makers Dell and HP dropped 10.8% and 9.6%, respectively.

"It's fair to say that this week, not just today, has been very much about the future of AI and what that's going to look like, whether there will be a positive return on investment and if so, how quickly," Wealthspire Adivors Oliver Pursche told Reuters. "Companies that are performing and meeting the very lofty expectations that have been set are doing well," Mr Pursche said. "Those that are falling short and seem to be missing the mark or not executing as expected are getting punished."

On the subject of being punished, cryptocurrency related firms all got walloped on the news that hackers nicked a lazy $US6.3 billion ($9 billion) worth of various stable coins, such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, while no one was looking at the world's biggest crypto exchange Binance.

Listed crypto firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robin Hood all fell between 7 and 11%. All said they were safe, but they would say that.

Putting aside the Binance contretemps, it's worth noting that hackers have made off with around $US3 billion in cryptos in around 150 incidents last

US Treasuries were one of the beneficiaries of the tech rout as investors decided they were a safer bet at the moment, which is saying something.

The benchmark 10-year yield closed the month with its biggest monthly drop in nearly three years.

Gold, once also considered a safe haven, didn't benefit from the conniptions — indeed, it slumped (-3.5%) to a one-year low, along with other precious metals. Silver shed 6.5% and palladium shed 3.0%.

"The sky is falling," independent metals trader Tai Wong told Reuters with a dramatic flourish. "Metals will not be able to escape the gravity well of a nasty stock correction. Earnings have been the foundation of the AI rally and now that pillar is showing some cracks."

Oil seems to be blithely ignoring Mr Wong's "gravity well". The key benchmarks both gained more than 2% on Friday.

Brent crude futures: +2.4% to $US117.64/barrel

+2.4% to $US117.64/barrel WTI crude futures: +2.1% to $US113.43/barrel

For the month, Brent finished almost 14% higher, while WTI rose even more, up 15%.

On Friday, a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by explosive devices, believed to be limpet mines attached by a small boat, according to UKMTO, the British maritime security service.

It is believed to be the first successful use of limpet mines since the war began in February. Probably not the last either.

With Reuters

World.title: NSW push to revert to pen-and-paper NAPLAN tests backed by experts
World.content:
Education experts have backed a push to return NAPLAN writing tests to pen and paper, eight years after the national test first moved online.

The New South Wales government will today ask national education ministers to scrap computer-based writing tests for year 5, 7 and 9 students from 2028.

Currently, only year 3 students complete the writing test on paper, while older students sit it on a computer.

NAPLAN moved to online testing in 2018. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Reading, numeracy, spelling, grammar and punctuation are tested online for all year levels.

NAPLAN first moved to online testing in 2018 to allow more precise testing and faster results.

NSW Deputy Premier and Education Minister Prue Car said recent results showed a national decline in writing skills and argued prolonged technology use in schools was affecting learning.

In a statement, she said building "strong foundational writing skills" would set students up for "long-term success".

"We're listening to teachers and families who want a sensible, balanced approach to technology use in schools," she said.

The proposal needs the support of the Commonwealth, states and territories to go ahead.

Prue Car says parents and teachers want schools to take a "sensible, balanced approach to technology". (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

'Counterproductive'

University of Sydney associate professor Marian Vidal-Fernandez supported the proposal, but said the move to online testing should not have happened in the first place.

"Then we would not be here again," she said.

The economist said most primary classroom work across the country was still done by hand, and students should be tested the same way.

"Doing the exam in the same way that they work in class should … benefit the average student," she said.

Marian Vidal-Fernandez says the move to online testing should not have happened. (Supplied: University of Sydney)

Overseas research from Portugal and the United States, she added, showed results tended to fall when the same children moved from handwritten to computer-based tests.

"We are actually asking the children about some skills that they might not be trained for," she said.

"This typing is going to be harder the younger you are."

NAPLAN results 'national tragedy' Experts say it is the fourth straight year that hundreds of thousands of students are not meeting the mark.

Edith Cowan University associate professor Anabela Malpique, who has for a decade researched how writing is taught, also agreed with the move.

She said research showed handwriting was important for learning and memory.

"Thinking with a pencil, as we used to say, is very, very critical," she said.

Cost, timing and typing

Dr Vidal-Fernandez said the cost of marking handwritten papers could be a barrier to rolling out the change nationally.

But she suggested AI tools could now read handwritten work, with humans checking results that were unclear.

"It should be doable with the technology that we have at the moment," she said.

Dr Malpique said the change would be easier in primary schools, where handwriting remained the focus, but that secondary schools would need more planning because students were more likely to work on computers.

Anabela Malpique says implementing the change will be easier in primary schools. (Supplied: Anabela Malpique)

She said a return to paper-based testing could also affect how typing was taught in schools.

Her national surveys of primary teachers found only nine minutes a week were spent teaching keyboard skills, compared with 31 minutes a week for handwriting.

"We need to support students to become hybrid writers," she said.

Both experts said students with learning difficulties and additional needs should be considered and would need accommodations.

"We should not do a one-size-fits-all type of policy," Dr Vidal-Fernandez said.

World.title: 'Despicable betrayal': Democrat backs GOP candidate in key midterms race
World.content:
The Democrats' messy Michigan Senate campaign has again been marred by friendly fire, with defeated primaries candidate Haley Stevens breaking ranks and endorsing the Republican nominee in Tuesday's midterm elections.

Analysts are expecting the Democrats to perform well against Donald Trump's Republican Party in many parts of the United States during this week's votes, which could reshape the Congress.

But the Democrats' efforts to retain their Senate seat in Michigan have been disrupted by an internal feud between the party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Ms Stevens, his rival in the primaries, which has included allegations of antisemitism, racism and xenophobia.

The pair's relationship plumbed new depths at the weekend, when Mr El-Sayed announced Ms Stevens was no longer invited to join him at a church service in Detroit on Sunday, local time.

The campaign event was supposed to be a show of party unity after several months of jibes, but it ended up exposing how deep their rift had become.

Loading

Mr El-Sayed justified the decision by saying he did not want any "distractions", although any hope of that crumbled when Ms Stevens turned up at a different church with the Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday morning.

Later that day, she went a step further and held a joint press conference with Mr Rogers in which she said she was a "proud Democrat".

"This is a very close election. We all know that," she said.

"But Abdul made very clear that I wasn't welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there that he didn't want me and at some point you gotta look at who’s standing for country."

The Democrats need to retain all of their current Senate seats, and flip four more, in order to wrest control of the chamber.

Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader and one of the most senior Democrats in the country, described Ms Stevens's decision as a "despicable betrayal".

In a social media post, Mr Trump praised Ms Stevens: "Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did."

Despite president's plummeting approval ratings around the country, the Republicans are hopeful of a strong showing in Michigan.

Mr Rogers is considered a moderate candidate, and the party has attempted to style Mr El-Sayed, who is attempting to become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, as a radical socialist (a label he denies).

Mr El-Sayed's combative style has earnt him plenty of admiration, particularly by left-wingers who believe the Democrats should do more to stand up to Mr Trump, although it has also sparked criticism from opponents and from some within his own party.

Mr El-Sayed is an outspoken critic of Israel and the US military and financial support for the country.

Abdul El-Sayed's supporters believe Democrats should do more to stand up to Donald Trump. (Reuters: Rebecca Cook)

Ms Stevens, a four-term congresswoman who gave up her seat to run for the Senate, is widely described as being among the most pro-Israel Democrats on Capitol Hill, and has accused Mr El-Sayed of not denouncing Islamic extremist groups strongly enough.

She has accused Mr El-Sayed of being antisemitic and spreading "hate", which he denies. Mr El-Sayed has argued he has faced racist and Islamophobic attacks from Republicans over the course of the campaign.

Several of her staff reportedly resigned after her decision to back Mr Rogers.

Speaking on Sunday, Mr El-Sayed batted away questions about Ms Stevens's decision.

"I’m not in the business of driving clicks for you. I’m in the business of trying to solve problems for the people of my state," he told reporters.

"None of this matters. The rest of this is just a distraction."

Mr Rogers said he was "honoured" to have Ms Stevens support.

"This is courage in politics in America today," he said.

World.title: FOI says Gold Coast mayor took Mar-a-Lago invoice out of the office
World.content:
Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate's troublesome trip to US President Donald Trump's holiday retreat at Mar-a-Lago has thrown up another twist, after a key invoice could not be found within council.

The mayor's office has explained the absence by saying the feisty politician only brought a paper invoice about the Florida trip into the office once, then took it away with him and no-one took another copy.

The invoice is an important part in how Mr Tate had nullified conflict of interest concerns about a proposed $1.5 billion Trump Tower on Gold Coast beaches earlier this year.

He had faced an outcry after initially declaring having received free accommodation at Mar-a-Lago from the Trump Organization, while the controversial tower was proposed within council boundaries.

A rendered image of The Trump International Hotel & Tower Gold Coast development before the project collapsed. (Supplied: Altus Property Group)

But Mr Tate later changed his declaration to say he had personally paid for accommodation during his three-day trip in February at the exclusive club based on 20 acres of landscaped gardens alongside the Atlantic Ocean.

The politician maintained he had always intended to pay himself but an invoice "was not received promptly".

"When I asked for the invoice on check out, they didn't have it," he said in September.

"I followed it up, I got the invoice, and we got it paid."

The four-term mayor has declined to hand over the invoice and now proclaimed the trip — for which he was invited as mayor and for which ratepayers paid airfares — was "private".

An aerial view of the Mar-a-Lago estate. (AP Photo: Steve Helber)

Council has twice rejected ABC right to information requests for the invoice. In an internal appeal, a council officer explained no copy was found in any council systems, emails or physical records.

"The office of the mayor further advised that the mayor brought a physical copy into the office, retained it with him when he left, and that it was not printed, copied, saved or otherwise managed by the office of the mayor staff," they wrote.

They indicated they would not demand it either: "I do not believe [council] has a present legal right or practical ability to require production of that privately held copy."

Gold Coast mayor swears at journalist Tom Tate has been asked questions about conflicting accounts of his dinner with US President Donald Trump.

Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore said that ideally some record of the invoice should be recorded for record-keeping purposes.

"Otherwise, it could be perceived as the old 'the dog ate my homework' excuse," he said.

"There is clearly a lot to explain about this trip, the nature of the hospitality, the costs, and the extent that the mayor was there on official, private or personal business."

Outstanding questions include about how much the mayor was charged. He has declined to say the amount but insisted he did not get "mate's rates".

His office issued a single line in response to questions: "The office of the mayor has fulfilled all (right to information) requirements."

The Trump Organization says the president did not have dinner with Gold Coast mayor Tom Tate. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

Other private information about the February trip has been released previously: Council has detailed how Mr Tate spent more than $13,000 personally upgrading flights.

The whole trip proved controversial after the mayor initially boasted of dining with the president at Mar-a-Lago, describing an evening of tomahawk steaks and expensive wine at the club, founded by Mr Trump in 1995.

But the ABC later revealed a sparsity of documentation and that the White House said the president "did not have dinner" with the mayor. The Trump Organization further branded Mr Tate's account as a "complete fabrication", saying the president only briefly said hello to the mayor's table from the patio.

Do you know more? Contact Liam Walsh on encrypted email or Signal. Please note end-to-end encryption is only possible with your own encrypted email system like Protonmail or Signal account.

Mr Tate at a press conference maintained: "Recollections may vary."

During questioning at that conference about the trip accounts and his payments, a frustrated Mr Tate eventually told a journalist to "f—k off", twice, and stormed out.

The Gold Coast mayor had also said he was invited to Mar-a-Lago by the Trump Organization, and not the Queensland developer working with the organisation for the proposed $1.5 billion tower.

No record of the invitation turned up in right to information requests. The mayor's office said that was because the "invitation was issued verbally".

The Trump Tower proposal, which had attracted almost 100,000 objection petitioners, eventually collapsed.

World.title: 'Annoying' Alcaraz denies de Minaur Vienna Open title in final
World.content:
Alex de Minaur served up some brilliant tennis, but it still wasn't enough for him to break his dispiriting duck against his "annoying" and virtuoso nemesis Carlos Alcaraz in the Vienna Open final.

In their seventh meeting, Australia's No.1 did his utmost to earn a first-ever win over the great young Spaniard in Sunday's championship match, but despite dragging him into some breathtaking rallies, he invariably came off worse as Alcaraz scorched to a 6-1, 6-4 victory.

"It's great to have you back on tour," de Minaur told the Spaniard afterwards in the Wiener Stadthalle, but couldn't resist adding with a smile: "I will say one thing though: it is very annoying to play against you!"

"But you're one of the good ones, one of the great guys on tour … As for myself, it's been a great week too."

Indeed, de Minaur could find plenty of consolation after a tournament in which he knocked out the new world No.1 Alexander Zverev in the semis, earning his first victory over the German in an individual rather than team tournament, and played perhaps his best tennis of the season.

Now he will fly straight off to Paris for the Masters tournament there, the crucial last qualifying event for the ATP Finals, also knowing he's in the eighth and final spot to be part of the Turin end-of-season men's championship.

"I'm proud to be standing up here and still fighting," said de Minaur, who'll move back to No.8 in the world from No.10 after reaching his third final of the year.

Carlos Alcaraz (pictured) had too much class for Alex de Minaur in the final of the Vienna Open. (Getty Images: Jakub Porzycki/Anadolu)

"So I'm excited for what's left for this year, and hopefully I can continue pushing and have a longer year."

Still, though, de Minaur couldn't cope with the brilliance of 23-year-old Alcaraz, who lifted his fourth title of the season and the 28th of his ‌career, sweeping to victory without dropping a set all week.

After the wrist trouble that ripped a hole in his season, he really is looking back to something like the world-beater who lifted the Australian Open crown at the start of 2026.

Alcaraz, who has dropped only two sets to de Minaur in their seven contests, never looked back again after a scintillating start when he caught the Aussie cold by breaking in the first game, before uncorking a champagne cross-court backhand winner to earn a second break en route to a 4-0 lead.

Happy just to eke out a single game in the opener, de Minaur was stubbornly competitive in the second, producing three sensational points when at break point and 3-4 down just to stay in the fight.

But serving to stay in the match at 4-5, the seven-time grand slam champ went into overdrive, and after applying the pressure to grab match point, played a fittingly wonderful final rally, delivering a drop shot, a lob and then a killing forehand, his 14th of the match, which clipped the baseline to seal the deal.

"He's really fast, you have to earn every point. You might have a winner against everybody — except him," said Alcaraz, acknowledging his opponent's excellence.

AAP

World.title: DV survivor told to pay child support to abuser she says earns $300k
World.content:
Canberra mother Chloe separated from her husband to escape domestic and family violence (DFV), but years later, the father of her children is still perpetrating financial abuse.

Beginning this month, Services Australia has told her she must make child support payments to her perpetrator, despite him currently owing her more than $15,000 in unpaid child support, and both children being under her roof.

"It's extremely tiring and debilitating, just getting up and going to work every day, having to do your best and keep a smile on your face because you're no longer going home to [DFV], but you're still living a probably worse hell," Chloe said.

"I actually can't afford to feed the kids," she said.

Here is how situations like Chloe's can occur.

Dragging out separation to financially punish

Chloe's family home was sold by a bank because no one was paying the mortgage. (ABC News: Tahlia Roy)

Chloe, as she has asked to be called to protect her identity, said after fleeing her perpetrator, he was able to use the legal system to "drag out the divorce for a couple of years to make it financially harder for me".

"I agreed to stupid things in the divorce, like keeping debt that was in both our names just to try and get him to be done with it," Chloe said.

And when she first sought legal help, she said several family law firms said they could not represent her because her ex had already contacted them.

She said more than half of the financial settlement money she eventually received was swallowed up by her lawyer's fees "because he would constantly get his lawyer to write letters or demands".

Do you know more about this story? Email roy.tahlia@abc.net.au

Chloe's family home was sold by a bank because no one was paying the mortgage.

"Then all of the house sale funds went into the trust with the lawyers," she said.

"He wouldn't let any funds be released, even though both my lawyer and his lawyer did suggest releasing a small portion each, like $10,000 each, so that we could go on about trying to sort out our lives.

" So I had to sleep in my car. I got a gym membership so I could shower and get ready at the gym for work. "

Her children lived with her perpetrator while Chloe was homeless.

Financial documents weaponised

Chloe's financial separation left her feeling "exposed". (ABC News: Tahlia Roy)

During the financial settlement, Chloe said her ex refused to disclose documents.

"Even though it was court-ordered, the court just brushed it off, and he never had to do it. I had to provide bank statements; even though he was asked, he never did," she said.

"And he used that to kind of bully me, harass me, see where I was spending money so he knew what shopping centres I was going to.

"[He] would make comments to the kids about seeing things that I bought on my bank statement. So just literally to use it as another tool to stalk and harass me.

" I'm constantly nervous. I'm watching my back. I just feel like I've been completely exposed and chucked out there and not protected. "

Underreporting taxable income by 93pc

Chloe has little confidence in Services Australia's assessors determining her ex's true income. (ABC News: Tahlia Roy)

The mother, who works full-time, said the latest front she was fighting came after Services Australia said she would have to start paying her perpetrator child support from this month.

She said the assessor told her:

"'Don't stress [about] the money you owe him because you're employed. We will either garnish it from your pay, if you refuse to pay, or we can do a debt offset of the money that he owes you.'"

According to parenting orders, she has custody of one child full-time and the other child half of the time, and earns a salary of about $80,000. Though, she said both children prefer to be under her roof, which they currently are.

Chloe had previously disputed the amount of taxable income the father of her children had reported in a past disclosure period, and said about seven months later Services Australia's assessors calculated his annual taxable income to be above $300,000.

In his most recent disclosure, he has estimated his taxable income to be below $20,000, which is why Chloe must now pay him.

She has little confidence in the assessors determining his true income, as she believes he has now discovered a loophole in which he has added other people to his bank accounts so they cannot be viewed by Services Australia.

"When we were married, I helped run his business. So I knew exactly what was coming in and going, and then obviously during the divorce, all of a sudden it was a lot less," she said.

"I've lost a ridiculous amount of weight because I can't afford to eat, over 50 per cent of my pay goes on rent plus the bills.

"The kids have sporting activities, which he doesn't go half in. [He] just refuses to reply to messages or pay, and I don't want my kids to miss out. I'm on payment plans with everyone," she said.

What's being done?

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek's office was asked whether Services Australia's handling of Chloe's case was appropriate, whether she had a message for the woman and what could be done.

A federal government spokesperson who responded did not comment on Services Australia's approach but pointed to reforms to child support announced in the May budget.

"This includes improvements to data sharing between Services Australia and the Australian Taxation Office to validate the income estimates for parents and flag more quickly when these estimates are wrong," the statement read.

"This will help catch people who deliberately under-estimate their income and ensure more parents, like in this case, receive the right amount of child support and debts are less likely to be accrued."

System designed around 'utopian ideal'

Dr Amira Aftab says the child support scheme is mistakenly based on assumptions that separated parents are always amicable. (Supplied)

Dr Amira Aftab, a senior lecturer at Macquarie Law School who has studied family law and gendered violence, said: "With the government's response, I suspect there'll still be this burden placed on the victim-survivor".

Dr Aftab believes there are incorrect assumptions underpinning the child support system that need to change.

"I see it as designed around this utopian ideal that separated parents will cooperate and that it's amicable.

"It really fundamentally overlooks … that family law is such a highly personal and emotive area of law, especially where children are involved," she said.

Calls to break 'nexus'

Care Financial and Consumer Law Centre chief executive Amy Kilpatrick says the child support scheme needs to cut financial ties between parents. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Care Financial and Consumer Law Centre chief executive Amy Kilpatrick said the proposed reforms failed to sever the child support-facilitated links between perpetrators and victim-survivors.

She said Care Financial counsellors commonly heard from clients who were being financially abused through the child support scheme.

"We believe that a reset is needed on the system whereby the nexus between someone who has left an abusive relationship in particular is broken with the perpetrator," Ms Kilpatrick said.

"And the only way to do that is for the survivor to not be dependent on the payments coming in from the perpetrator. So, once someone is assessed as needing child support … Then the money comes from the government. They should just receive the funds."

She said the paying parent would still be required to pay what they owed into the system, but crucially, it would create financial separation.

World.title: Protesters loot shops, 100 officers injured as riots spread to Germany
World.content:
Looters and rioters have damaged stores and injured more than 100 police officers in the German city of Frankfurt, prompting ministers to warn of a crackdown.

The central German city emerged as the main flashpoint on Saturday after tens of thousands of people rallied in dozens of cities to demand better education and lower living costs in protests organised by campaign group "Gen Z regelt", which translates roughly to "Gen Z takes charge".

Hooded rioters damaged 17 stores, of which five were looted, Roman Poseck, interior minister of the state of Hesse, told a press conference on Sunday.

The protests across Germany were organised by campaign group Gen Z regelt, or "Gen Z takes charge". (Reuters: Kai Pfaffenbach)

He said police deployed 1,300 officers, with more than 100 injured in clashes. Police arrested 54 people aged between 13 and 29.

"I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: Things cannot go on like this," Mr Poseck said.

Mr Poseck said most of those arrested were German nationals, adding that many of those involved in the disturbances were of an immigrant background, citing information from the police.

"Police currently estimate that they are dealing with between 1,000 and 1,500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from an immigrant background," he added.

Many protests across Germany were peaceful, with younger voters calling for government action to improve their lives. (Reuters: Kai Pfaffenbach)

Protesters throw petrol bombs at police

Frankfurt police reported violent disturbances including windows being smashed and petrol bombs, rocks and bottles being thrown at the emergency services.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a member of the conservative Christian Social Union, said perpetrators would be identified and held to account.

"I expect there to be severe penalties. We are not prepared to accept, in the slightest, that such incidents and such rioting should take place here," he told reporters on Sunday.

Police are vowing a harsher response to similar violence in the future. (Reuters: Kai Pfaffenbach)

He accused "troublemakers from the immigrant community" of acting alongside left-wing extremists and other far-left groups, but did not provide evidence to support the claim or say which groups had joined the demonstrations.

Mr Dobrindt said a policing strategy based on a large security presence and deployments across multiple locations had proved effective.

In France, protests continued largely peacefully for a third weekend after extensive riots and looting on October 17 damaged shops, public buildings and businesses.

Mr Dobrindt said that border controls had been tightened ahead of the protests out of fear extremist groups from abroad could exploit them to stir riots.

World.title: My suburb is split between grotty sharehouses and ritzy family homes. That’s its charm
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Every afternoon at 4pm, at the St Lucia and Taringa roundabout, a man sits on his balcony and waves at everyone who passes by. His name is Franky, and the restaurant beneath him, Franky’s, has been closed for as long as I’ve lived here. I’m not quite sure it ever opened. Still, every afternoon, there he is. Franky is one of St Lucia’s colourful local celebrities, and the sight of him up on his porch with his afternoon drink is one I got to know well while living at Union College at the University of Queensland. Like most at college, I was not from Brisbane, and I picked St Lucia as my base camp for four years without knowing how grateful I’d be that I did. The roundabout where Franky waves to passers-by. He’s there every day, but camera shy. Morgan Roberts There’s a saying at the University of Queensland: if you haven’t started studying by the time the jacarandas bloom, you will fail your exams. Rhea Anand Living and studying at UQ meant my whole world existed inside a one-kilometre radius. Everyone talks about the European walkable city as if it only exists in Paris or Berlin or Amsterdam. But I found it in a suburb built on hills, where the only thing standing between me and the gym was a steep walk home. St Lucia’s two halves are easy to map. On one side, UQ and a few thousand 18-year-olds living away from home for the first time. On the other, the St Lucia Golf Links and the leafy green streets around it, where people golf, marry and settle into middle age. But even the fairways weren’t off limits to us: we held college balls at The Hillstone, ran along its paths, and took our first dates on picnics on its grass.



The Women’s College at the University of Queensland. Morgan Roberts The uni’s picturesque lake. Morgan Roberts We would often hang out at the golf club as students. Morgan Roberts If St Lucia is a suburb consisting of two generations then Hawken Drive Village is where the two intersect. You have college kids buying cartons of Great Northern from Liquorland, and Ironside State School parents buying steak and macadamia milk from the IGA. My first-ever job was at A Salt & Battery Fish & Chips, located in the “Ville”, as everyone called it. And one of my housemates had the shortest commute in Brisbane: a three-minute walk down the road where she opened Yonder Espresso at 5am. Her customers: all students on weekdays, and all families on weekends. Then the college kids go home for summer, and the suburb finally exhales. No more drunk, rowdy students ravenous for late-night kebabs from the institution that is Mr Deno Kebab & Pizza. My second job was at Wordsmiths Cafe on the UQ campus. For three years I served coffee to students who couldn’t really afford a triple-shot coffee but needed one, then lecturers at lunch who could. By then, most of my social circle worked and lived in St Lucia. I knew the bartenders at the uni bar, The Redroom, and the baristas at If You Say So and Saint Lucy. I don’t think I ever paid full price for an oat cappuccino or a pint of Stone & Wood in those four years of my degree.



My suburb is a bubble you never had to leave. Then the 2022 floods made it an island. At first, it felt like a snow day: classes were cancelled, and most of us stayed in, watching movies, playing games and drinking, waiting it out. The Munro Soccer Fields became a mini-lake with kayakers and stand-up paddleboarders floating gracefully over the goalposts. A lake grows on UQ Sports Field 1 next to Union College during the 2022 floods. Rhea Anand The flood’s aftermath: ruined belongings lined up during the community clean-up. Rhea Anand Hawken Drive housemates. Rhea Anand With catering staff cut off by the floods, students stepped up to cook and serve dinner for all 300 of us. The menu was the same comforting college classic: frozen veggies steamed in bulk, and tray after tray of chicken parmis popped into the oven. The mood was closer to a party than a disaster. But the bubble popped on Coleridge Street when we saw cars sitting underwater, and ground-floor neighbours who had lost everything. We joined the community clean-up, hosing out garages and salvaging belongings. I recall one elderly man whose garage was full of random memorabilia. His eyes went misty as we played with his old cowboy bullwhip; I think it had been years since anyone had.



Living and studying at UQ meant my whole world existed inside a one-kilometre radius. Morgan Roberts Yonder Espresso at the Ville on Hawken Drive. Morgan Roberts Drinks on the balcony at The Redroom. Rhea Anand Moving from Union College into my first sharehouse was a hungover blur. My three friends and I hauled our things onto Hawken Drive and into a spacious house with front and backyards, and a sunroom that became the centre of our lives. We ate, cooked and hosted parties, always coming and going through our weird blue and off-yellow kitchen. St Lucia has both sharehouses and stately family homes. Morgan Roberts Established residents rent out houses to uni students, of which there’s a steady stream. Morgan Roberts The grotty sharehouses of 19 and 20-year-olds are only a few streets from people who’ve owned their homes for decades. We walked dogs, house-sat and cleaned for the wealthy families nearby. One mansion paid so well that all three of us went shoe shopping the next day.

World.title: Highgate Hill townhouses await court approval after half a decade of delays
World.content:
NationalQueenslandProperty development Highgate Hill townhouses await court approval after half a decade of delays Julius Dennis November 2, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
