A triple block of premium Highgate Hill townhouses could finally be finished more than half a decade after going on the market. The lengthy build has mystified locals in Brisbane’s inner south, but owners are still unable to move into the seemingly complete homes while they await approval through the planning court. Advertised for more than a million dollars a pop in 2020, the seven triple-storey units have sat almost finished and empty for years after an investment fund was forced to take over the project when its builder defaulted on its mortgage in 2021. The site appears complete but remains empty. Julius Dennis A retail space at 45 Gladstone Road below two of the units was sold to a real estate agent earlier this year after being listed for $500,000.



But the space, and the units, remain empty, with Trilogy Private – the fund – locked in a planning court fight with Brisbane City Council. Built around a towering hoop pine, the communal decks of the units are now covered in clumps of needles, and some of the timber floorboards are soft underfoot. The decks are covered in pine needles. Julius Dennis The ceilings on some of the units are unfinished, and paint cans are stacked in the empty shopfront, but otherwise the site appears finished. On the street outside, neighbours shrugged their shoulders in exasperation about what’s happened with the construction.



The project hit the market in 2020 as Tree Haus, with agents asking for $1.25m for potential owners to have a piece of the “boutique enclave of architecturally designed residences”. “These townhomes represent an unrivalled low maintenance inner-city lifestyle in one of Brisbane’s best performing growth suburbs, the opportunity exists for you to choose your new home today,” the Ray White ad read. The ceiling on unit 6’s deck is unfinished. Julius Dennis The original plans were approved for a material change of use in the planning court in 2019 after it was denied by the council in 2018. The better part of a decade later, the final changes must be ticked off in the same court.



The council argued some of the units, and the driveway and visitor parking, were below minimum flood heights and are yet to agree with the changes, which have already been built. But Trilogy said the habitable floor levels were “generally in accordance with the approved plans”, and the whole project had been ticked off by a building certifier. The units have been a subject of interest for locals for years. Julius Dennis In his affidavit, town planner Ben Russell said the parking heights had been approved by a flood expert. At a hearing on October 16, Judge Michael Williamson KC gave the council until November 2 to tell Trilogy if it remained opposed to the townhouses.



The matter will be reviewed on November 6. A Trilogy spokesperson said the company’s primary objective was to complete the project and get the purchasers in. “The homes are now built and practical completion has been achieved,” they said. The shopfront is empty. Julius Dennis “Our focus is on finalising the remaining planning and administrative steps needed so settlements can proceed.”



They said they could not go into detail while the matter was before the court. “We appreciate this has been a lengthy journey for purchasers and remain focused on achieving the best possible outcome for them, which is to see them move into their homes as soon as possible,” they said. Also referencing that it was a court matter, council declined to comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Airport rail study was doctored to ensure Sunshine ‘won’ shortlist of routes, commission told
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Airport rail study was doctored to ensure Sunshine ‘won’ shortlist of routes, commission told Chip Le Grand November 2, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Financial estimates were doctored and a senior public servant threatened with the sack to ensure the proposed Melbourne Airport Rail Link ran through Sunshine instead of a more direct route to the city, the Big Build royal commission has been told. The allegations challenge the integrity of the business case for Premier Ben Carroll’s priority project, call into question a $12 billion joint funding commitment by the state and federal governments, and plunge the Big Build into fresh scandal a month before the state election. Jacinta Allan, pictured next to Daniel Andrews, announces Sunshine as the preferred route for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link before the 2018 election. Paul Jeffers A confidential submission to the royal commission by a planning expert who advised on the airport rail link reveals that a secret working group was established in late 2017 or early 2018 at the direction of then-public transport minister Jacinta Allan to allegedly bake in the case for the Sunshine route. It says the small group, which included public servants within the Transport Department and outside consultants, was told to not discuss its work with any of their colleagues, including direct reports, or diarise their meetings. All instructions were given verbally.



The group’s brief, according to the submission, was to study four shortlisted routes for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link (MARL) and build evidence supporting the state government’s politically favoured outcome – that the new train line, if ever built, would have to go through Sunshine. “The task was to produce a document, or set of documents, prior to the 2018 election so that after that election there would be no further consideration of any alternative routes for the MARL other than through Sunshine,” the submission reads. Allan denies the allegations and is expected to be called as a witness before the commission. The submission is one of four to the royal commission raising concerns about the integrity of the current MARL project. All were provided to this masthead by their respective authors.



The most serious allegation raised by the planning expert is that, to make an iron-clad case for Sunshine, the estimated cost of a more direct route through Maribyrnong was intentionally inflated by exaggerating the amount of tunnelling required. The Maribyrnong route would have run beneath Highpoint shopping centre and opened up disused defence land for residential development. And the winner is – Sunshine. The state government announced its preferred route in 2018. Paul Jeffers An earlier 2012 study, commissioned by the then Liberal state government, top-scored Maribyrnong, known at the time as the “direct tunnel” option, out of 22 possible routes, with Sunshine ranked a close second. The allegation that costings were deliberately inflated to rule Maribyrnong out of contention is contained in a separate, contemporaneous file note made by a solicitor when the planning expert first sought legal advice about blowing the whistle.



The note, dated August 23, 2018, and seen by The Age, reads: “Untenable. Serious matters ignored, not acted upon. “4 options – one particular route better but more expensive (doctored to make it unviable).” The solicitor who wrote the file note confirmed its authenticity. The planning expert, who spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, decided against making a disclosure to the Victorian Ombudsman or IBAC due to fears of personal and professional recriminations. They subsequently quit the department, leaving the information buried for eight years.



“This is fraud on a billion-dollar scale,” they said. The planning expert, working with trusted former colleagues experienced in rail engineering and major project costing, has calculated that an unnecessary 3.5 kilometres of tunnelling was included along the proposed Maribyrnong route to add between $3.8 billion and $4.6 billion to the estimated cost. A price tag of $20 billion to $25 billion for Maribyrnong – double the estimated $8 billion to $13 billion cost of the Sunshine route – was included in a strategic appraisal of the airport rail link published by Transport for Victoria in July 2018 and built into the 2021 business case for the project. A truer, average cost estimate of the Maribyrnong route, according to detailed calculations provided to this masthead by the group of experts, is $16.5 billion in 2018 dollars.



Maribyrnong was the federal government’s preferred route when then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull came to Melbourne in April 2018 to announce $5 billion in funding towards the project. Related Article Public service Thrown in a loop: How Daniel Andrews’ biggest project was cooked up behind closed doors Then-premier Daniel Andrews, who did not appear at the funding announcement alongside Turnbull, was blindsided by the move. At the time, he was more focused on his government’s plans to unveil the Suburban Rail Loop, a project being developed in secret, as a vote-grabbing election promise. The Victorian government formally endorsed the Sunshine route for the airport rail link in August 2018 and the federal government followed suit three months later. The comparative cost of the Maribyrnong route was a critical factor in tipping the scales towards Sunshine in the published assessment. According to the Transport for Victoria analysis, Maribyrnong was the top-scoring route for the benefits it would bring to travellers using the line, Victorian businesses and the economic development of Melbourne’s inner north-west. Due to its prohibitive cost, it was ranked last for deliverability.



When the planning expert saw the assessment, he challenged an executive working in the department. “I just said to him, “How could you produce documents like this, and think this is OK?” the planning expert told this masthead. “He said to me, ‘The minister said to me that either these documents say Sunshine or I’ll sack you. So they say Sunshine.’” Allan, who is retiring from politics after losing the Labor leadership to Carroll in July, was the minister for public transport and major projects at the time the assessment was done. “The allegations made are incorrect,” a spokesman for the former premier said. “Ms Allan will co-operate with the important work of the royal commission. She will answer whatever questions the royal commission has for her about these allegations, but it is not appropriate to pre-empt the royal commission’s work.”



A colleague of Allan, who was unauthorised to publicly discuss the matter, said the former premier was furious at the suggestion she would coerce public servants to support a particular outcome. Allan made no secret during her time as a minister responsible for what became known as the Big Build that she wanted the MARL to run through Sunshine. The benefits of Sunshine, which Allan advocated within government and to her federal counterparts, was that it required no tunnelling, would accelerate Sunshine’s development as a second central business district, and would link the airport line with rail services to regional centres. A former cabinet colleague of Allan’s, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the former premier was insistent the airport rail line had to run through Sunshine so that people travelling to the airport by train from Ballarat or her home town of Bendigo only needed to change trains once. In December 2018, when defending the government’s decision not to make public a preliminary business case for the project, Allan hinted at a Sunshine bias. “We’ve released previously ... the strategic assessment of the four alignments, which is really what the preliminary business case was about, looking at those four alignments and giving [state and federal] governments the confidence that Sunshine stacked up the best,” she said.



Allan’s confidence in the strategic assessment was not shared by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office (VAGO). A 2022 VAGO report into the quality of government business cases used to support major projects was highly critical of the way that route options for the MARL were assessed, describing the work done as “not sufficiently rigorous” and lacking in transparency. The Big Build royal commission led by Chris Kourakis will begin public hearings next week. Joe Armao The auditor-general noted that the options assessments “significantly influenced” a state government decision to commit $5 billion to the project and were not “validated or revisited in any depth” before they were included in the published business case. The airport rail allegations go to the heart of a question that commissioner Chris Kourakis has flagged will be central to his inquiry into the Big Build – whether the state government’s $100 billion infrastructure program was primarily designed to advance the public interest or Labor’s electoral prospects.



In his opening address to the inquiry, Kourakis noted that “governments must select and design infrastructure projects around the socioeconomic needs of the Victorian public, and not party political interest”. The royal commission is scheduled to hold its first public hearings next week. William McDougall (pictured in 2019) worked on most of the major transport construction projects in Victoria since the late 1990s. Jason South William McDougall, an independent transport planner who has worked in Britain, the Middle East and on signature Big Build projects including the West Gate Tunnel, North East Link, Suburban Rail Loop and the MARL, has told the commission this is not his experience. “Throughout my career, I have seen an accelerating shift away from integrated, evidence-based planning towards politically selected and prioritised projects,” he writes in a submission provided to this masthead.



“The most egregious issue of all is that large projects are chosen for political reasons, announced and funded without the context of an integrated land use and transport plan.” McDougall, who is aware of the allegations about the development of the MARL now before the royal commission, believes the project is a case study of where Victoria’s planning for and delivery of major transport projects has gone wrong. Premier Ben Carroll, pictured with Anthony Albanese near Sunshine, has declared the MARL his “highest priority”. Jason South “A strategic assessment of options … was used to justify the Sunshine/Albion route, but it was a highly skewed assessment with direct, political interference aimed at ensuring that the Sunshine route was the best,” he writes in his submission. “Faster, shorter and cheaper routes were rejected.” Two further submissions to the royal commission, both made confidentially by former public servants, question the planning process and decisions taken that resulted in Sunshine being chosen as the route for a new airport line.



Carroll, since becoming Labor leader, has declared the airport rail link his “highest priority” major project. The government has selected a preferred bidder to redevelop Sunshine station, and Carroll last month was alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to announce forward plans to lay down airport rail tracks to a proposed new station in Keilor East, in the middle of his electorate of Niddrie. Related Article Analysis

Big Build royal commission Royal commission hints at original sin of Big Build Carroll did not address the allegations before the royal commission when questioned by this masthead. “The premier’s first act was to establish the toughest royal commission into the construction industry to leave no stone unturned,” a spokesman said. “The terms of reference are broad and expansive. Nothing is off limits. We won’t pre-empt its findings.”



The Victorian Coalition has also backed the MARL. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has promised to deliver the project, including a new station at Keilor East, if she becomes Victoria’s next premier. Both the Maribyrnong and Sunshine routes run through Keilor East. Wilson has promised to expand the royal commission’s terms of reference so that it examines whether “any project was conceived, selected, prioritised, expanded, re-scoped, funded or continued, wholly or partly, to confer an industrial, financial, organisational or political benefit” to a trade union or political party. World.title: ASX set to slip, Wall Street hit by tech rout; Binance sees withdrawals spike as it returns online
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip, Wall Street hit by tech rout; Binance sees withdrawals spike as it returns online Stan Choe November 2, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A selloff for tech stocks got even worse on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high. The S&P 500 tumbled 1.8 per cent for its worst day since June, and it closed out a third straight losing week. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 2.9 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572 points, or 1.1 per cent. Wall Street suffered more weakness in AI stocks on Friday. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to dip, with futures pointing to a slide of 4 points at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.29¢. The US stock market remains only 3.1 per cent below its all-time high, which has boosted the value of workers’ retirement accounts, but it’s become increasingly shaky as Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States approach. Worries about AI in general have already become a concern for voters across political parties, and President Donald Trump has historically used the stock market’s performance as a measure of his own success.



Intel’s stock led the way lower and plunged 28.6 per cent for its worst drop since 1974. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Related Article Analysis

Bonds The $315b debt binge that’s driving up the cost of borrowing Amazon fell 1.4 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through $US42.4 billion ($60.3 billion) of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $US94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology. A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record and dragged the S&P 500 down after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI. Worries are rising about whether all the hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centres have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centres.



“We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors. A drop of 4.2 per cent for Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, outweighing even Intel. In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell below $US77,000 from more than $US86,000 earlier this month, and a US-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $US6 billion worth of crypto at Binance. Coinbase Global fell 10.6 per cent even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4 per cent of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 7.8 per cent. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons. Binance customers pulled $US3.64 billion, or 2.1 per cent of its assets, as the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange went back online on Sunday after the hack. Binance said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained “substantial”. The exchange said it had now covered 95 per cent of the $US6.3 billion of stolen assets.



Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose within the S&P 500 index as fell. ExxonMobil climbed 2.2 per cent, and Chevron added 1.8 per cent after the oil giants reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Mondelez International rose 3.9 per cent after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth. Colgate-Palmolive climbed 2.3 per cent after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected. Expectations are high for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 140.32 points to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572.25 to 51,770.31, and the Nasdaq composite sank 747.73 to 25,437.00. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Thursday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier in the month. Related Article Superannuation Super funds slammed for ‘blaming customers for complaints’ Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields upward because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4 per cent to $US113.43. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following sharper swings in Asia.



South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5 per cent as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1 per cent after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: If you’re visiting Venice for the first time, this is the way to do it
World.content:
InspirationEurope If you’re visiting Venice for the first time, this is the way to do it Lee Tulloch November 2, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’ve been to Venice several times, but I’ve never seen it this way. From the top deck of Uniworld’s river ship SS La Venezia, I curl up on a day bed and watch Venice’s many islands pass in and out of view. For seven days, the SS La Venezia cruises to the distant reaches of the islands of Venice. It’s June, and the lightest of breezes brushes the deck. We’ve been slowly cruising around the Venetian lagoon all afternoon, one of only two ships – the other being the three-star Michelangelo – permitted to do so. From this bird’s-eye view, Venice’s archipelago is a cavalcade of beauty. The water sparkles like sequins and enormous seagulls fly alongside, then overtake our leisurely pace.



The Venice that is familiar to tourists, the historical centre of the city with St Mark’s Square at its heart, is a puzzle of 126 tiny islands connected by 472 bridges, which is why every turn leads to water. Less than 50,000 people live there. 



Over seven days, La Venezia will cruise to the most distant reaches of the archipelago, as far as the outer MOSE (Modulo Sperimentale Elettromeccanico) gates, which control flooding during high tides, and to Chioggia, the fishing village at the southern entrance of the lagoon. Some islands are covered in vineyards; others are little more than mud flats that disappear at high tide. We glide past a small island dominated by an old fortress. Another holds a ruined monastery. From another, a magnificent church basilica arises. A few islands, such as San Clemente Island and the Isola delle Rose, have been transformed into luxury resorts by Kempinski and JW Marriott respectively. Colourful Burano. iStock Only about 30 of these islands are inhabited. The Lido, a barrier island with a long, wide beach, has a population of 20,000. Tiny, colourful Burano, with about 3000 residents, is the most densely populated. It’s a real treat to see the entirety of Venice’s waters in one voyage. And because we dock overnight on Burano and along the Giudecca Canal, we simply walk off the ship in the evenings and wander around when the other tourists have deserted.



Most of my fellow passengers – Americans, Canadians, Brits and a few Aussies – have never been to Venice before; if I were travelling to Venice for the first time, this is absolutely the way I would choose to see it. Venice banned large ships from the inner lagoon and the Giudecca Canal in 2021. La Venezia has permission to cruise around it at leisure because the ship’s flat bottom doesn’t damage the shallow lagoon bed. If we keep our speed to 11km/h in the shallowest parts and 20km/h in the deepest, we can join the vaporetto, ferries, speedboats and barges through the busy waterway. Maritime authorities watch our progress very closely. Several areas are decorated with Venetian masks. Grand suite on La Venezia.



Venice has a modern terminal at San Basilio on the canal, which processed the large cruise ships until the ban. It’s extremely convenient, but only the river ships and some smaller cruise ships are allowed to dock there these days. The advantage for our 126-passenger river ship is that it doesn’t leave Venice so passengers can board without port formalities. I take a short water taxi ride to the port and roll my luggage directly onto the ship. There’s a vaporetto station at the port and the Alilaguna, the airport water bus, stops about 10 minutes’ walk away. La Venezia began life as Uniworld’s River Countess and had a major refit before it was relaunched in 2020 to specifically carry passengers on the seven-day Jewels of the Veneto itinerary. The bow is decorated with a whimsical Venetian mask, and the interiors are sumptuously furnished in Murano glass and Fortuny fabrics. The sense of place is strong. Mariano Fortuny (1871-1949) was an inventor, artist and designer whose beautiful fabrics are found in the world’s luxury interiors. We’re docked directly across the lagoon from the Fortuny factory on Giudecca.



From my deluxe stateroom on deck three, I sleep with Fortuny and the tower of the Hilton Molino Stucky Venice, a converted mill, out my window. At 14 square metres, the room is cosy and perfect for one. Its padded walls make it feel like a little jewel box with plenty of cupboard space, a sensibly organised marble bathroom with a good, hot shower, and a desk with a chair where I can work. Outside, vaporettos and other boats churn past at eye level. It’s an ongoing entertainment, wondering how on earth they don’t collide with each other. The long, low ship’s panoramic windows allow us to be continually immersed in Venice’s wonderful waterfront chaos without getting splashed. A stateroom aboard La Venezia. We glide past St Mark’s Square and the entire length of the canal several times during our voyage; the Gothic arches of the Doge’s Palace and the towering Campanile never fail to be heart-stopping, no matter how many times you’ve seen them.



The main dining room, Ristoranti Rialto, the casual Panini Bar and Hari’s Bar and Lounge, where we gather for drinks, daily briefings and lectures, all have great ringside views of the action. Even the small gym is low enough in the water for runners on the treadmills to feel like they’re racing with speedboats. The partly shaded upper Lido deck is where guests flock when they’re not taking one of the many tours on offer. The drinks waiter does a good business in spritzes, the local tipple. On our first night, the ship travels only a few kilometres along the canal to dock in Castello, one of Venice’s quieter districts, where you can experience the pace of real life. The upper Lido deck is where guests flock when they’re not taking one of the many tours on offer. Because there’s no port to negotiate, we can walk off the ship at any time after tapping our room cards on the scanner. Castello’s main street, Via Garibaldi, is full of restaurants and bars that locals patronise. It opens onto gardens and vistas, some of the best spots in Venice to capture sunsets. Several guests take the opportunity to join the locals in their evening passeggiata.



The days are a mix of guided tours and free time to explore individually. One morning, I team up with another guest and go shopping in Dorsoduro, an arty neighbourhood of little boutiques and famous museums such as the Peggy Guggenheim Collection and the Gallerie dell’Accademia. Related Article Opinion

My happy place This ‘impossible’ city doesn’t make sense, but it makes my heart soar Lee Tulloch Travel columnist I have enough free time to visit several churches and galleries I haven’t managed to visit before, including the exquisite Scuola Grande di San Rocco, within easy walking distance from the ship. La Venezia’s secret weapon is cruise manager Louisa Warman, a Brit who moved to Venice to study art in 2001, fell in love with the city, and stayed. She’s a fantastic source of high-quality knowledge on everything from art to shopping, and her lectures on lived experience, such as Venice’s floods and how Venetians cope with them (they check an app daily), are engrossing.



Classic experiences are among the included excursions, such as visits to the Doge’s Palace, St Mark’s Basilica, the glassblowers of Murano and the lace-makers of Burano. The excursion team can help negotiate the best price for a gondola ride. Guests can also 



I choose Vicenza, an elegant city, the highlight of which is the extraordinary Teatro Olimpico, considered Palladio’s masterpiece. It was built of wood, stucco and plaster inside a Roman amphitheatre and is the oldest Italian Renaissance theatre in existence. Related Article Cruises Port guide: Venice, Italy Chioggia is a fishing town on a small group of islands at the southern tip of the lagoon, connected to the mainland by a long bridge, and we can walk to its centre as we’re docked on the island. Built on canals, it’s like a mini Venice, although cars are allowed. The day we visit the main street is a riot of fairground rides and stalls due to a public holiday celebrating the town’s patron saints, the martyrs Felice and Fortunato – Happy and Lucky. They don’t sound so lucky. Chioggia has an impressive fish market and what’s widely considered the world’s oldest tower clock. At its port stands a small replica of the St Mark’s lion, known jokingly as “the cat of Chioggia”.



Before this cruise, I thought I knew Venice but there’s so much more to the Veneto than I ever imagined. In fact, so much more that I would happily get back on this cruise and do it all again. DETAILS Uniworld’s seven-night Jewels of the Veneto on the S.S. La Venezia costs from $5349 a person twin share in a Classic cabin and includes all meals, beverages, and 24-hour room service. Included shore excursions include after-hours visits to St Marks Basilica and Doges Palace. uniworld.com; From October 2026 Finnair flies Melbourne to Helsinki via Bangkok daily, with connections to 90 destinations in Europe, including Venice. World.title: Germany blames migrants and leftists as ‘Gen Z’ protests turn violent
World.content:
WorldEuropeProtests Germany blames migrants and leftists as ‘Gen Z’ protests turn violent Christoph Steitz and Tilman Blasshofer November 2, 2026 — 6:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Frankfurt: German ministers have threatened tough penalties for looters and rioters who damaged stores and injured more than 100 police officers in Frankfurt at the weekend, while praising security forces for preventing wider violence. Frankfurt became the main flashpoint after tens of thousands of people rallied in dozens of German cities to demand better education and lower living costs in protests organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt, or “Gen Z takes charge”. A person wearing a clown mask uses a traffic sign to smash shop windows in Frankfurt. DPA via AP In the financial hub, hooded rioters damaged 17 stores on Saturday, of which five were looted, Roman Poseck, interior minister of the state of Hesse, told a press conference on Sunday (German time). He said police deployed 1300 officers, and more than 100 were injured in clashes. Police arrested 54 people aged between 13 and 29.



“I am shocked by what I have seen, and there is no point in sugar-coating it. Let me make this very clear: things cannot go on like this,” Poseck said. Smashed glass lines a street in Frankfurt on Sunday. AP Poseck said most of those arrested were German nationals, adding that many of those involved in the disturbances were of an immigrant background, citing information from the police. “Police currently estimate that they are dealing with between 1000 and 1500 violent troublemakers, predominantly from an immigrant background,” he added. Petrol bombs thrown at police



Frankfurt police reported violent disturbances including windows being smashed and petrol bombs, rocks and bottles being thrown at the emergency services. Related Article Analysis

Protests Despair and decline: The risks for Europe behind the riots German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, a member of the conservative Christian Social Union, said authorities would identify the perpetrators and hold them to account. “I expect there to be severe penalties. We are not prepared to accept, in the slightest, that such incidents and such rioting should take place here,” he told reporters on Sunday. He accused “troublemakers from the immigrant community” of acting alongside left-wing extremists and other far-left groups, but did not provide evidence to support the claim or say which groups had joined the demonstrations.



Dobrindt said a policing strategy based on a large security presence and deployments across multiple locations had proved effective. In France, protests continued largely peacefully for a third weekend after extensive riots and looting on October 17 damaged shops, public buildings and businesses. Dobrindt said that border controls had been tightened ahead of the protests out of fear that extremist groups from abroad could exploit them to stir riots. World.title: My suburb is split between grotty sharehouses and ritzy family homes. That’s its charm
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Every afternoon at 4pm, at the St Lucia and Taringa roundabout, a man sits on his balcony and waves at everyone who passes by. His name is Franky, and the restaurant beneath him, Franky’s, has been closed for as long as I’ve lived here. I’m not quite sure it ever opened. Still, every afternoon, there he is. Franky is one of St Lucia’s colourful local celebrities, and the sight of him up on his porch with his afternoon drink is one I got to know well while living at Union College at the University of Queensland. Like most at college, I was not from Brisbane, and I picked St Lucia as my base camp for four years without knowing how grateful I’d be that I did. The roundabout where Franky waves to passers-by. He’s there every day, but camera shy. Morgan Roberts There’s a saying at the University of Queensland: if you haven’t started studying by the time the jacarandas bloom, you will fail your exams. Rhea Anand Living and studying at UQ meant my whole world existed inside a one-kilometre radius. Everyone talks about the European walkable city as if it only exists in Paris or Berlin or Amsterdam. But I found it in a suburb built on hills, where the only thing standing between me and the gym was a steep walk home. St Lucia’s two halves are easy to map. On one side, UQ and a few thousand 18-year-olds living away from home for the first time. On the other, the St Lucia Golf Links and the leafy green streets around it, where people golf, marry and settle into middle age. But even the fairways weren’t off limits to us: we held college balls at The Hillstone, ran along its paths, and took our first dates on picnics on its grass.



The Women’s College at the University of Queensland. Morgan Roberts The uni’s picturesque lake. Morgan Roberts We would often hang out at the golf club as students. Morgan Roberts If St Lucia is a suburb consisting of two generations then Hawken Drive Village is where the two intersect. You have college kids buying cartons of Great Northern from Liquorland, and Ironside State School parents buying steak and macadamia milk from the IGA. My first-ever job was at A Salt & Battery Fish & Chips, located in the “Ville”, as everyone called it. And one of my housemates had the shortest commute in Brisbane: a three-minute walk down the road where she opened Yonder Espresso at 5am. Her customers: all students on weekdays, and all families on weekends. Then the college kids go home for summer, and the suburb finally exhales. No more drunk, rowdy students ravenous for late-night kebabs from the institution that is Mr Deno Kebab & Pizza. My second job was at Wordsmiths Cafe on the UQ campus. For three years I served coffee to students who couldn’t really afford a triple-shot coffee but needed one, then lecturers at lunch who could. By then, most of my social circle worked and lived in St Lucia. I knew the bartenders at the uni bar, The Redroom, and the baristas at If You Say So and Saint Lucy. I don’t think I ever paid full price for an oat cappuccino or a pint of Stone & Wood in those four years of my degree.



My suburb is a bubble you never had to leave. Then the 2022 floods made it an island. At first, it felt like a snow day: classes were cancelled, and most of us stayed in, watching movies, playing games and drinking, waiting it out. The Munro Soccer Fields became a mini-lake with kayakers and stand-up paddleboarders floating gracefully over the goalposts. A lake grows on UQ Sports Field 1 next to Union College during the 2022 floods. Rhea Anand The flood’s aftermath: ruined belongings lined up during the community clean-up. Rhea Anand Hawken Drive housemates. Rhea Anand With catering staff cut off by the floods, students stepped up to cook and serve dinner for all 300 of us. The menu was the same comforting college classic: frozen veggies steamed in bulk, and tray after tray of chicken parmis popped into the oven. The mood was closer to a party than a disaster. But the bubble popped on Coleridge Street when we saw cars sitting underwater, and ground-floor neighbours who had lost everything. We joined the community clean-up, hosing out garages and salvaging belongings. I recall one elderly man whose garage was full of random memorabilia. His eyes went misty as we played with his old cowboy bullwhip; I think it had been years since anyone had.



Living and studying at UQ meant my whole world existed inside a one-kilometre radius. Morgan Roberts Yonder Espresso at the Ville on Hawken Drive. Morgan Roberts Drinks on the balcony at The Redroom. Rhea Anand Moving from Union College into my first sharehouse was a hungover blur. My three friends and I hauled our things onto Hawken Drive and into a spacious house with front and backyards, and a sunroom that became the centre of our lives. We ate, cooked and hosted parties, always coming and going through our weird blue and off-yellow kitchen. St Lucia has both sharehouses and stately family homes. Morgan Roberts Established residents rent out houses to uni students, of which there’s a steady stream. Morgan Roberts The grotty sharehouses of 19 and 20-year-olds are only a few streets from people who’ve owned their homes for decades. We walked dogs, house-sat and cleaned for the wealthy families nearby. One mansion paid so well that all three of us went shoe shopping the next day.

World.title: Highgate Hill townhouses await court approval after half a decade of delays
World.content:
NationalQueenslandProperty development Highgate Hill townhouses await court approval after half a decade of delays Julius Dennis November 2, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A triple block of premium Highgate Hill townhouses could finally be finished more than half a decade after going on the market. The lengthy build has mystified locals in Brisbane’s inner south, but owners are still unable to move into the seemingly complete homes while they await approval through the planning court. Advertised for more than a million dollars a pop in 2020, the seven triple-storey units have sat almost finished and empty for years after an investment fund was forced to take over the project when its builder defaulted on its mortgage in 2021. The site appears complete but remains empty. Julius Dennis A retail space at 45 Gladstone Road below two of the units was sold to a real estate agent earlier this year after being listed for $500,000.



But the space, and the units, remain empty, with Trilogy Private – the fund – locked in a planning court fight with Brisbane City Council. Built around a towering hoop pine, the communal decks of the units are now covered in clumps of needles, and some of the timber floorboards are soft underfoot. The decks are covered in pine needles. Julius Dennis The ceilings on some of the units are unfinished, and paint cans are stacked in the empty shopfront, but otherwise the site appears finished. On the street outside, neighbours shrugged their shoulders in exasperation about what’s happened with the construction.



The project hit the market in 2020 as Tree Haus, with agents asking for $1.25m for potential owners to have a piece of the “boutique enclave of architecturally designed residences”. “These townhomes represent an unrivalled low maintenance inner-city lifestyle in one of Brisbane’s best performing growth suburbs, the opportunity exists for you to choose your new home today,” the Ray White ad read. The ceiling on unit 6’s deck is unfinished. Julius Dennis The original plans were approved for a material change of use in the planning court in 2019 after it was denied by the council in 2018. The better part of a decade later, the final changes must be ticked off in the same court.



The council argued some of the units, and the driveway and visitor parking, were below minimum flood heights and are yet to agree with the changes, which have already been built. But Trilogy said the habitable floor levels were “generally in accordance with the approved plans”, and the whole project had been ticked off by a building certifier. The units have been a subject of interest for locals for years. Julius Dennis In his affidavit, town planner Ben Russell said the parking heights had been approved by a flood expert. At a hearing on October 16, Judge Michael Williamson KC gave the council until November 2 to tell Trilogy if it remained opposed to the townhouses.



The matter will be reviewed on November 6. A Trilogy spokesperson said the company’s primary objective was to complete the project and get the purchasers in. “The homes are now built and practical completion has been achieved,” they said. The shopfront is empty. Julius Dennis “Our focus is on finalising the remaining planning and administrative steps needed so settlements can proceed.”



They said they could not go into detail while the matter was before the court. “We appreciate this has been a lengthy journey for purchasers and remain focused on achieving the best possible outcome for them, which is to see them move into their homes as soon as possible,” they said. Also referencing that it was a court matter, council declined to comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Airport rail study was doctored to ensure Sunshine ‘won’ shortlist of routes, commission told
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Airport rail study was doctored to ensure Sunshine ‘won’ shortlist of routes, commission told Chip Le Grand November 2, 2026 — 5:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Financial estimates were doctored and a senior public servant threatened with the sack to ensure the proposed Melbourne Airport Rail Link ran through Sunshine instead of a more direct route to the city, the Big Build royal commission has been told. The allegations challenge the integrity of the business case for Premier Ben Carroll’s priority project, call into question a $12 billion joint funding commitment by the state and federal governments, and plunge the Big Build into fresh scandal a month before the state election. Jacinta Allan, pictured next to Daniel Andrews, announces Sunshine as the preferred route for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link before the 2018 election. Paul Jeffers A confidential submission to the royal commission by a planning expert who advised on the airport rail link reveals that a secret working group was established in late 2017 or early 2018 at the direction of then-public transport minister Jacinta Allan to allegedly bake in the case for the Sunshine route. It says the small group, which included public servants within the Transport Department and outside consultants, was told to not discuss its work with any of their colleagues, including direct reports, or diarise their meetings. All instructions were given verbally.



The group’s brief, according to the submission, was to study four shortlisted routes for the Melbourne Airport Rail Link (MARL) and build evidence supporting the state government’s politically favoured outcome – that the new train line, if ever built, would have to go through Sunshine. “The task was to produce a document, or set of documents, prior to the 2018 election so that after that election there would be no further consideration of any alternative routes for the MARL other than through Sunshine,” the submission reads. Allan denies the allegations and is expected to be called as a witness before the commission. The submission is one of four to the royal commission raising concerns about the integrity of the current MARL project. All were provided to this masthead by their respective authors.



The most serious allegation raised by the planning expert is that, to make an iron-clad case for Sunshine, the estimated cost of a more direct route through Maribyrnong was intentionally inflated by exaggerating the amount of tunnelling required. The Maribyrnong route would have run beneath Highpoint shopping centre and opened up disused defence land for residential development. And the winner is – Sunshine. The state government announced its preferred route in 2018. Paul Jeffers An earlier 2012 study, commissioned by the then Liberal state government, top-scored Maribyrnong, known at the time as the “direct tunnel” option, out of 22 possible routes, with Sunshine ranked a close second. The allegation that costings were deliberately inflated to rule Maribyrnong out of contention is contained in a separate, contemporaneous file note made by a solicitor when the planning expert first sought legal advice about blowing the whistle.



The note, dated August 23, 2018, and seen by The Age, reads: “Untenable. Serious matters ignored, not acted upon. “4 options – one particular route better but more expensive (doctored to make it unviable).” The solicitor who wrote the file note confirmed its authenticity. The planning expert, who spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity, decided against making a disclosure to the Victorian Ombudsman or IBAC due to fears of personal and professional recriminations. They subsequently quit the department, leaving the information buried for eight years.



“This is fraud on a billion-dollar scale,” they said. The planning expert, working with trusted former colleagues experienced in rail engineering and major project costing, has calculated that an unnecessary 3.5 kilometres of tunnelling was included along the proposed Maribyrnong route to add between $3.8 billion and $4.6 billion to the estimated cost. A price tag of $20 billion to $25 billion for Maribyrnong – double the estimated $8 billion to $13 billion cost of the Sunshine route – was included in a strategic appraisal of the airport rail link published by Transport for Victoria in July 2018 and built into the 2021 business case for the project. A truer, average cost estimate of the Maribyrnong route, according to detailed calculations provided to this masthead by the group of experts, is $16.5 billion in 2018 dollars.



Maribyrnong was the federal government’s preferred route when then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull came to Melbourne in April 2018 to announce $5 billion in funding towards the project. Related Article Public service Thrown in a loop: How Daniel Andrews’ biggest project was cooked up behind closed doors Then-premier Daniel Andrews, who did not appear at the funding announcement alongside Turnbull, was blindsided by the move. At the time, he was more focused on his government’s plans to unveil the Suburban Rail Loop, a project being developed in secret, as a vote-grabbing election promise. The Victorian government formally endorsed the Sunshine route for the airport rail link in August 2018 and the federal government followed suit three months later. The comparative cost of the Maribyrnong route was a critical factor in tipping the scales towards Sunshine in the published assessment. According to the Transport for Victoria analysis, Maribyrnong was the top-scoring route for the benefits it would bring to travellers using the line, Victorian businesses and the economic development of Melbourne’s inner north-west. Due to its prohibitive cost, it was ranked last for deliverability.



When the planning expert saw the assessment, he challenged an executive working in the department. “I just said to him, “How could you produce documents like this, and think this is OK?” the planning expert told this masthead. “He said to me, ‘The minister said to me that either these documents say Sunshine or I’ll sack you. So they say Sunshine.’” Allan, who is retiring from politics after losing the Labor leadership to Carroll in July, was the minister for public transport and major projects at the time the assessment was done. “The allegations made are incorrect,” a spokesman for the former premier said. “Ms Allan will co-operate with the important work of the royal commission. She will answer whatever questions the royal commission has for her about these allegations, but it is not appropriate to pre-empt the royal commission’s work.”



A colleague of Allan, who was unauthorised to publicly discuss the matter, said the former premier was furious at the suggestion she would coerce public servants to support a particular outcome. Allan made no secret during her time as a minister responsible for what became known as the Big Build that she wanted the MARL to run through Sunshine. The benefits of Sunshine, which Allan advocated within government and to her federal counterparts, was that it required no tunnelling, would accelerate Sunshine’s development as a second central business district, and would link the airport line with rail services to regional centres. A former cabinet colleague of Allan’s, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said the former premier was insistent the airport rail line had to run through Sunshine so that people travelling to the airport by train from Ballarat or her home town of Bendigo only needed to change trains once. In December 2018, when defending the government’s decision not to make public a preliminary business case for the project, Allan hinted at a Sunshine bias. “We’ve released previously ... the strategic assessment of the four alignments, which is really what the preliminary business case was about, looking at those four alignments and giving [state and federal] governments the confidence that Sunshine stacked up the best,” she said.



Allan’s confidence in the strategic assessment was not shared by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office (VAGO). A 2022 VAGO report into the quality of government business cases used to support major projects was highly critical of the way that route options for the MARL were assessed, describing the work done as “not sufficiently rigorous” and lacking in transparency. The Big Build royal commission led by Chris Kourakis will begin public hearings next week. Joe Armao The auditor-general noted that the options assessments “significantly influenced” a state government decision to commit $5 billion to the project and were not “validated or revisited in any depth” before they were included in the published business case. The airport rail allegations go to the heart of a question that commissioner Chris Kourakis has flagged will be central to his inquiry into the Big Build – whether the state government’s $100 billion infrastructure program was primarily designed to advance the public interest or Labor’s electoral prospects.



In his opening address to the inquiry, Kourakis noted that “governments must select and design infrastructure projects around the socioeconomic needs of the Victorian public, and not party political interest”. The royal commission is scheduled to hold its first public hearings next week. William McDougall (pictured in 2019) worked on most of the major transport construction projects in Victoria since the late 1990s. Jason South William McDougall, an independent transport planner who has worked in Britain, the Middle East and on signature Big Build projects including the West Gate Tunnel, North East Link, Suburban Rail Loop and the MARL, has told the commission this is not his experience. “Throughout my career, I have seen an accelerating shift away from integrated, evidence-based planning towards politically selected and prioritised projects,” he writes in a submission provided to this masthead.



“The most egregious issue of all is that large projects are chosen for political reasons, announced and funded without the context of an integrated land use and transport plan.” McDougall, who is aware of the allegations about the development of the MARL now before the royal commission, believes the project is a case study of where Victoria’s planning for and delivery of major transport projects has gone wrong. Premier Ben Carroll, pictured with Anthony Albanese near Sunshine, has declared the MARL his “highest priority”. Jason South “A strategic assessment of options … was used to justify the Sunshine/Albion route, but it was a highly skewed assessment with direct, political interference aimed at ensuring that the Sunshine route was the best,” he writes in his submission. “Faster, shorter and cheaper routes were rejected.” Two further submissions to the royal commission, both made confidentially by former public servants, question the planning process and decisions taken that resulted in Sunshine being chosen as the route for a new airport line.



Carroll, since becoming Labor leader, has declared the airport rail link his “highest priority” major project. The government has selected a preferred bidder to redevelop Sunshine station, and Carroll last month was alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to announce forward plans to lay down airport rail tracks to a proposed new station in Keilor East, in the middle of his electorate of Niddrie. Related Article Analysis

Big Build royal commission Royal commission hints at original sin of Big Build Carroll did not address the allegations before the royal commission when questioned by this masthead. “The premier’s first act was to establish the toughest royal commission into the construction industry to leave no stone unturned,” a spokesman said. “The terms of reference are broad and expansive. Nothing is off limits. We won’t pre-empt its findings.”



The Victorian Coalition has also backed the MARL. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has promised to deliver the project, including a new station at Keilor East, if she becomes Victoria’s next premier. Both the Maribyrnong and Sunshine routes run through Keilor East. Wilson has promised to expand the royal commission’s terms of reference so that it examines whether “any project was conceived, selected, prioritised, expanded, re-scoped, funded or continued, wholly or partly, to confer an industrial, financial, organisational or political benefit” to a trade union or political party. World.title: ASX set to slip, Wall Street hit by tech rout; Binance sees withdrawals spike as it returns online
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slip, Wall Street hit by tech rout; Binance sees withdrawals spike as it returns online Stan Choe November 2, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A selloff for tech stocks got even worse on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high. The S&P 500 tumbled 1.8 per cent for its worst day since June, and it closed out a third straight losing week. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 2.9 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572 points, or 1.1 per cent. Wall Street suffered more weakness in AI stocks on Friday. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to dip, with futures pointing to a slide of 4 points at the open. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.29¢. The US stock market remains only 3.1 per cent below its all-time high, which has boosted the value of workers’ retirement accounts, but it’s become increasingly shaky as Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States approach. Worries about AI in general have already become a concern for voters across political parties, and President Donald Trump has historically used the stock market’s performance as a measure of his own success.



Intel’s stock led the way lower and plunged 28.6 per cent for its worst drop since 1974. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Related Article Analysis

Bonds The $315b debt binge that’s driving up the cost of borrowing Amazon fell 1.4 per cent after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through $US42.4 billion ($60.3 billion) of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $US94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology. A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12 per cent to its worst day on record and dragged the S&P 500 down after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI. Worries are rising about whether all the hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centres have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centres.



“We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors. A drop of 4.2 per cent for Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, outweighing even Intel. In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell below $US77,000 from more than $US86,000 earlier this month, and a US-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $US6 billion worth of crypto at Binance. Coinbase Global fell 10.6 per cent even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4 per cent of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 7.8 per cent. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons. Binance customers pulled $US3.64 billion, or 2.1 per cent of its assets, as the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange went back online on Sunday after the hack. Binance said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained “substantial”. The exchange said it had now covered 95 per cent of the $US6.3 billion of stolen assets.



Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose within the S&P 500 index as fell. ExxonMobil climbed 2.2 per cent, and Chevron added 1.8 per cent after the oil giants reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Mondelez International rose 3.9 per cent after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth. Colgate-Palmolive climbed 2.3 per cent after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected. Expectations are high for US companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.



All told, the S&P 500 fell 140.32 points to 7,580.07. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572.25 to 51,770.31, and the Nasdaq composite sank 747.73 to 25,437.00. In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying US government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Thursday and from more than 5.30 per cent earlier in the month. Related Article Superannuation Super funds slammed for ‘blaming customers for complaints’ Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields upward because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4 per cent to $US113.43. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following sharper swings in Asia.



South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5 per cent as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5 per cent. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1 per cent after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank. World.title: If you’re visiting Venice for the first time, this is the way to do it
World.content:
InspirationEurope If you’re visiting Venice for the first time, this is the way to do it Lee Tulloch November 2, 2026 — 5:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I’ve been to Venice several times, but I’ve never seen it this way. From the top deck of Uniworld’s river ship SS La Venezia, I curl up on a day bed and watch Venice’s many islands pass in and out of view. For seven days, the SS La Venezia cruises to the distant reaches of the islands of Venice. It’s June, and the lightest of breezes brushes the deck. We’ve been slowly cruising around the Venetian lagoon all afternoon, one of only two ships – the other being the three-star Michelangelo – permitted to do so. From this bird’s-eye view, Venice’s archipelago is a cavalcade of beauty. The water sparkles like sequins and enormous seagulls fly alongside, then overtake our leisurely pace.



The Venice that is familiar to tourists, the historical centre of the city with St Mark’s Square at its heart, is a puzzle of 126 tiny islands connected by 472 bridges, which is why every turn leads to water. Less than 50,000 people live there. 



Over seven days, La Venezia will cruise to the most distant reaches of the archipelago, as far as the outer MOSE (Modulo Sperimentale Elettromeccanico) gates, which control flooding during high tides, and to Chioggia, the fishing village at the southern entrance of the lagoon. Some islands are covered in vineyards; others are little more than mud flats that disappear at high tide. We glide past a small island dominated by an old fortress. Another holds a ruined monastery. From another, a magnificent church basilica arises. A few islands, such as San Clemente Island and the Isola delle Rose, have been transformed into luxury resorts by Kempinski and JW Marriott respectively. Colourful Burano. iStock Only about 30 of these islands are inhabited. The Lido, a barrier island with a long, wide beach, has a population of 20,000. Tiny, colourful Burano, with about 3000 residents, is the most densely populated. It’s a real treat to see the entirety of Venice’s waters in one voyage. And because we dock overnight on Burano and along the Giudecca Canal, we simply walk off the ship in the evenings and wander around when the other tourists have deserted.



Most of my fellow passengers – Americans, Canadians, Brits and a few Aussies – have never been to Venice before; if I were travelling to Venice for the first time, this is absolutely the way I would choose to see it. Venice banned large ships from the inner lagoon and the Giudecca Canal in 2021. La Venezia has permission to cruise around it at leisure because the ship’s flat bottom doesn’t damage the shallow lagoon bed. If we keep our speed to 11km/h in the shallowest parts and 20km/h in the deepest, we can join the vaporetto, ferries, speedboats and barges through the busy waterway. Maritime authorities watch our progress very closely. Several areas are decorated with Venetian masks. Grand suite on La Venezia.



Venice has a modern terminal at San Basilio on the canal, which processed the large cruise ships until the ban. It’s extremely convenient, but only the river ships and some smaller cruise ships are allowed to dock there these days. The advantage for our 126-passenger river ship is that it doesn’t leave Venice so passengers can board without port formalities. I take a short water taxi ride to the port and roll my luggage directly onto the ship. There’s a vaporetto station at the port and the Alilaguna, the airport water bus, stops about 10 minutes’ walk away. La Venezia began life as Uniworld’s River Countess and had a major refit before it was relaunched in 2020 to specifically carry passengers on the seven-day Jewels of the Veneto itinerary. The bow is decorated with a whimsical Venetian mask, and the interiors are sumptuously furnished in Murano glass and Fortuny fabrics. The sense of place is strong. Mariano Fortuny (1871-1949) was an inventor, artist and designer whose beautiful fabrics are found in the world’s luxury interiors. We’re docked directly across the lagoon from the Fortuny factory on Giudecca.



From my deluxe stateroom on deck three, I sleep with Fortuny and the tower of the Hilton Molino Stucky Venice, a converted mill, out my window. At 14 square metres, the room is cosy and perfect for one. Its padded walls make it feel like a little jewel box with plenty of cupboard space, a sensibly organised marble bathroom with a good, hot shower, and a desk with a chair where I can work. Outside, vaporettos and other boats churn past at eye level. It’s an ongoing entertainment, wondering how on earth they don’t collide with each other. The long, low ship’s panoramic windows allow us to be continually immersed in Venice’s wonderful waterfront chaos without getting splashed. A stateroom aboard La Venezia. We glide past St Mark’s Square and the entire length of the canal several times during our voyage; the Gothic arches of the Doge’s Palace and the towering Campanile never fail to be heart-stopping, no matter how many times you’ve seen them.



The main dining room, Ristoranti Rialto, the casual Panini Bar and Hari’s Bar and Lounge, where we gather for drinks, daily briefings and lectures, all have great ringside views of the action. Even the small gym is low enough in the water for runners on the treadmills to feel like they’re racing with speedboats. The partly shaded upper Lido deck is where guests flock when they’re not taking one of the many tours on offer. The drinks waiter does a good business in spritzes, the local tipple. On our first night, the ship travels only a few kilometres along the canal to dock in Castello, one of Venice’s quieter districts, where you can experience the pace of real life. The upper Lido deck is where guests flock when they’re not taking one of the many tours on offer. Because there’s no port to negotiate, we can walk off the ship at any time after tapping our room cards on the scanner. Castello’s main street, Via Garibaldi, is full of restaurants and bars that locals patronise. It opens onto gardens and vistas, some of the best spots in Venice to capture sunsets. Several guests take the opportunity to join the locals in their evening passeggiata.



The days are a mix of guided tours and free time to explore individually. One morning, I team up with another guest and go shopping in Dorsoduro, an arty neighbourhood of little boutiques and famous museums such as the Peggy Guggenheim Collection and the Gallerie dell’Accademia. Related Article Opinion

My happy place This ‘impossible’ city doesn’t make sense, but it makes my heart soar Lee Tulloch Travel columnist I have enough free time to visit several churches and galleries I haven’t managed to visit before, including the exquisite Scuola Grande di San Rocco, within easy walking distance from the ship. La Venezia’s secret weapon is cruise manager Louisa Warman, a Brit who moved to Venice to study art in 2001, fell in love with the city, and stayed. She’s a fantastic source of high-quality knowledge on everything from art to shopping, and her lectures on lived experience, such as Venice’s floods and how Venetians cope with them (they check an app daily), are engrossing.



Classic experiences are among the included excursions, such as visits to the Doge’s Palace, St Mark’s Basilica, the glassblowers of Murano and the lace-makers of Burano. The excursion team can help negotiate the best price for a gondola ride. Guests can also 



I choose Vicenza, an elegant city, the highlight of which is the extraordinary Teatro Olimpico, considered Palladio’s masterpiece. It was built of wood, stucco and plaster inside a Roman amphitheatre and is the oldest Italian Renaissance theatre in existence. Related Article Cruises Port guide: Venice, Italy Chioggia is a fishing town on a small group of islands at the southern tip of the lagoon, connected to the mainland by a long bridge, and we can walk to its centre as we’re docked on the island. Built on canals, it’s like a mini Venice, although cars are allowed. The day we visit the main street is a riot of fairground rides and stalls due to a public holiday celebrating the town’s patron saints, the martyrs Felice and Fortunato – Happy and Lucky. They don’t sound so lucky. Chioggia has an impressive fish market and what’s widely considered the world’s oldest tower clock. At its port stands a small replica of the St Mark’s lion, known jokingly as “the cat of Chioggia”.



Before this cruise, I thought I knew Venice but there’s so much more to the Veneto than I ever imagined. In fact, so much more that I would happily get back on this cruise and do it all again. DETAILS Uniworld’s seven-night Jewels of the Veneto on the S.S. La Venezia costs from $5349 a person twin share in a Classic cabin and includes all meals, beverages, and 24-hour room service. Included shore excursions include after-hours visits to St Marks Basilica and Doges Palace. uniworld.com; From October 2026 Finnair flies Melbourne to Helsinki via Bangkok daily, with connections to 90 destinations in Europe, including Venice. See finnair.com The writer was a guest of Uniworld
