World.title: 'Effectively being cyber-bullied': Chlöe Swarbrick hits back against attacks
World.content:
Audio player for " Chloe Swarbrick responds to National's election attacks " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2295605%2Feffectively-being-cyber-bullied-chloe-swarbrick-hits-back-against-attacks

Chloe Swarbrick responds to National's election attacks Morning Report Download MP3 7m

Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick says the National Party's attacks on her in the election campaign amount to "nasty" hysterical cyber-bullying.

The National Party has repeatedly claimed Swarbrick would be finance minister if the government loses power.

According to an RNZ count, 37 of the party's 94 Instagram posts over the last six days feature the Greens or Chloe Swarbrick.

"lt's a pretty bizarre situation when I guess I'm effectively being cyber-bullied by the most powerful people in the country," Swarbrick told Morning Report.

"Very clearly, the National Party are hysterical, and they are throwing haymakers on the way down."

Audio player for " National targets Swarbrick while facing pressure from right " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2295605%2Feffectively-being-cyber-bullied-chloe-swarbrick-hits-back-against-attacks

National targets Swarbrick while facing pressure from right Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Swarbrick said she was more interested in debating policy, including the party's policy of a wealth tax.

Swarbrick said it was "100 per cent" reasonable to debate her aim to be finance minister, and she had already challenged National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis to a "good, clean" debate.

She said the attacks on her were now no longer just in social media platforms, but in every interview, with the Prime Minister "hammering" it in every speech.

Listen to Caucus: Top political commentators unpick and make sense of New Zealand's election campaigns with frank and forthright discussion.

"They are not talking about the substance of what we are proposing, they just keep trying to paint me a bogeyman."

National's campaign manager, Simeon Brown, declined Morning Report's request for an interview.

Former Prime Minister Sir John Key, told Morning Report, in his opinion the National Party campaign was doing a good job.

World.title: Netball NZ says plans to drop Mowbray-Williams private league leaked
World.content:
Netball New Zealand says it deeply regrets the way players found out about the future of the domestic game.

On Friday, RNZ broke the story that Netball NZ had pulled the pin on plans for a privately-run domestic league, with investors Anna Mowbray and Ali Williams.

In a statement on Monday morning, Netball New Zealand chief executive Jennah Wootten said confidential correspondence about the Board's decision to end negotiations on the proposed privatisation of the elite domestic competition was leaked to media on Friday, before NNZ had the opportunity to speak directly with those most affected.

She said their intention was always to speak with players before any public announcement, and to do so with as much clarity as possible about the pathway forward.

Wooten said she was sorry players instead had to learn of this decision through the media rather than direct from Netbball NZ.

World.title: Fijian PM Rabuka under pressure ahead of crucial vote on constitutional reform
World.content:
Fiji's Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka's coalition government is falling apart ahead of the crucial third reading of a major bill to change the country's 2013 Constitution.

This comes after two of its minor partners, whose support was key to his forming a government in December 2022, have instructed their members of parliament to vote against the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2026 later this week.

Rabuka needs a two-thirds majority - at least 36 votes - to pass the bill through a 53-seat parliament following the passing of two MPs form the original 55-member parliament.

Rabuka has promised to press on with tabling the bill when parliament resumes on Monday for a vote from lawmakers to get it over the line for a proposed national referendum on 9 December.

Last month, Rabuka had downplayed coalition tensions after prematurely announcing Fiji's first-ever referendum date.

However, things have moved quickly over the weekend after the National Federation Party (NFP) withdrew from the special parliamentary committee led by Rabuka, and declared that the party would not be voting in favour of the bill.

It comes just days after the Social Democratic Liberal Party (Sodelpa) told its three MPs in the coalition - all of whom are Cabinet ministers - to vote against the bill.

"The National Federation Party's exit from the review process leaves the administration facing a high-stakes political showdown ahead of this week's decisive reading of the draft legislation," according to The Fiji Times.

The NFP believes the process is being rushed, while Sodelpa wants a total replacement of the 2013 Constitution - not just amendments to it - as well as the removal of immunity clauses protecting previous coup leaders.

During a consultation on the bill with Lau Province leaders on Friday, Rabuka said it was important to have the numbers for the third reading of the bill.

"Because that determines whether we keep going or [the constitution reform process] ends there."

The prime minister has faced criticism from the opposition, rights groups and community advocates and leaders for rushing the process as Fiji is scheduled to hold an election on or before 6 February 2027 at the latest.

Last week, Mahendra Chaudhry, Fiji's first and only prime minister of Indian descent, warned that the island nation was "worse off today than we were at independence" and that its political leadership had its priorities wrong.

But Rabuka has continuously defended the process, stating that he has a responsibility to review and amend the 2013 Constitution and "that's what we're going for".

World.title: Fuel rises become top-three concern, as Labour extends lead - IPSOS poll
World.content:
The latest IPSOS poll adds pressure on National in the final week before election day, even as the party clashes with its coalition partners over vote-splitting.

Fuel costs have shot up from fifth to third in the October survey of voters' biggest concerns, behind inflation and cost of living, and Labour has extended its lead over National on all the top five concerns.

Labour also made gains on law and order, and crime - the only top-20 issue National remains most trusted on - narrowing the gap to one percentage point, after the disputes over politicians meeting with gang members led one candidate to resign.

Top five issues

Cost of living/inflation remains the top concern by a significant margin, with 64 percent of New Zealanders putting it in their top three.

It edged up 1 percentage point from the previous month, reaching a new high, and while National's perceived ability to manage inflation rose three points to 24 percent, Labour's rating climbed seven points to 38 percent.

Labour leads all the top five election issues. Ipsos Issues Monitor, October 2026

In second place, healthcare also rose one point overall to 45 percent and Labour made gains there too - rising four points to 42, while National remained steady at 21 percent.

Concern about fuel prices shot up the rankings from seventh place to third, with a staggering 14-point rise to 31 percent.

Labour gained there too - up six points to 35 - while National continued its decline by two points to 20 percent.

Listen to Caucus: Top political commentators unpick and make sense of New Zealand's election campaigns with frank and forthright discussion.

Meanwhile, concerns about the economy fell four points to 30 percent, with Labour further gaining four points to 34, while National gained one point to 29 percent.

Rounding out the top five, unemployment fell two points to 19 percent.

Labour recovered lost ground there, compared to the previous poll - up four points to 38 - with National steady at 21 percent.

Labour dominates the top 20 election issues. Ipsos Issues Monitor, October 2026

'Clear message' over law and order

IPSOS New Zealand manager Carin Hercock said the survey was collected during prominent media coverage of politicians engaging with gangs, but the results showed New Zealanders were "sending a clear message about what matters most to them".

"Inflation and cost of living remain the country's leading concern, and continue to dominate the public agenda," she said.

The issue fell one percentage point to 14 percent, continuing a long-term decline and putting it eighth in the rankings.

National's perceived ability to handle law and order remained steady at 29 percent, making it the only issue in the top 20 it was rated highest, but Labour's three-point gain to 28 put the left-leaning party just one point away.

National still lead on law and order, and crime - but only just. Ipsos Issues Monitor, October 2026

Housing was the sixth-highest concern for New Zealanders, falling one point to 18 percent. Labour gained four points to 35 percent, while National fell one point to 22.

The other top 10 were rounded out with poverty/inequality (16 percent, down one) at seventh, climate change (12 percent, down one) at ninth and education (8 percent, down one) at 10th.

Ratings of the current government's performance remained static at 4.1 for the third survey in a row.

World.title: Backroads to the Beehive: Fuel, food and the future at top of the south
World.content:
Across the South Island, voters have singled out fuel, food and the future as the big issues on their mind at the ballot box and people at the top of the south are no different. Politicians are calling it a cost of living election. With five days until Election Day, RNZ South Island correspondent Tim Brown and camera operator Louis Dunham head to Tasman for the fifth journey from the 'Backroads to the Beehive'.

The character of the top of the south is hard to pin down, with sprawling vineyards, hop gardens and orchards, golden beaches, a military base and some of the country's most well-known alternative lifestylers.

Tasman has long been a Labour stronghold and Marlborough an equally staunch National heartland, but there has been little enthusiasm for either Chris Hipkins or Christopher Luxon during a campaign many have dubbed a cost-of-living election.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407640505112

Toni Marshall, who runs Mrs Smith's Cafe in Riwaka, says families are struggling and financial survival seems harder than ever.

"What they say is you get paid in sunshine around here," she says. "Basically, there are not huge amounts of money to be forking out to make people's life easier, that's for sure.

"Pricing in the supermarkets is just getting more and more horrific. I go in there and think, 'Wow, how do some families do this?', especially families who are on a single wage.

"I just can't even comprehend how they can afford to get week to week."

Business is also tough, affecting workers and the families they support, Marshall says.

Listen to Caucus: Top political commentators unpick and make sense of New Zealand's election campaigns with frank and forthright discussion.

"So many businesses have shut down over the last couple of years. It's been quite the talk of the town.

"People can't afford all the increases. There are the fuel costs, the overheads, the wages and staff wanting more wages.

"They should be able to rely on a bit of a bonus every year or at least their wages increasing slightly, but it's just not doable, because the money's not there."

Riwaka's Georgina Fry has also seen businesses struggling.

Families in Riwaka are struggling with the cost of living. RNZ / Louis Dunham

"I worked on the High Street for 21 years and I've never known it to be so quiet," she says. "Even at peak times, like a Thursday or a Friday afternoon, it's just so quiet."

'The longer we've been here, the harder and harder it gets'

Leigh Knowles, from Murchison's Hampden Hotel, says winter was horrible and truck drivers are no longer a reliable source of income.

"I've got 22 rooms upstairs, so I do rely on them a lot, but the way the economy is going at the moment, a lot of truck drivers are sleeping in their trucks," she says. "The owners are putting beds in their trucks, so they can stay in there."

Murchison's Tutaki Bakery owner Lee Morgan says margins are tight.

"There are so many businesses now that are looking tired, because people haven't got the money to re-invest in the businesses, like a lick of paint or just making it presentable," he said. "Before, you'd have a little bit of money to be able to put back into the business.

"Now, they can't, because it's just surviving."

Small towns around the south have struggled with the economic pain. RNZ / Louis Dunham

The cost of living crunch has exacerbated economic pain that has been decades in the making.

Morgan says today's New Zealand does not compare to the country he arrived in 20 years ago.

"When I first came to New Zealand, there was so much opportunity there for people, but the longer we've been here, the harder and harder it gets," he says.

"I don't see anything getting any easier, at all. I think, as the years go by, it's going to get harder and harder.

"There are so many businesses closing and it's not because there are not people there, people just haven't got the money to spend."

{h] 'It is quite scary'

From Murchison to Motueka, a dollar is hard to come by and even harder to hold onto.

Fears about the future are a common theme, especially for young people.

Motueka student Mareikura Ikin wonders if her future will even be in Aotearoa.

"I have worries of securing a job, after I get my degree," she says. "A lot of my friends and family have gone over to the likes of Australia.

"What are our government doing to ensure that our students and just people have job security here in Aotearoa, as opposed to going overseas?"

The cost of living is hurting young and the old, Ikin says.

"It's tough out there, you know, whānau are doing it really hard," she says. "No matter who you are, where you come from, everyone's doing it tough."

Jacinda Piggott grew up on Tākaka Hill and returned to New Zealand four years ago, after a decade living in Australia.

She is pregnant, and says the contrast between being a mother in New Zealand and Australia is stark.

"My husband owns his own business, so we're trying so hard to get ahead, but I can't be a stay-at-home mum.

"In six months, I'm going to have to be working again and childcare is expensive. It is quite scary, all of that.

"I don't really want to think about it. I'm trying to ignore it, but I know that, in Australia, I didn't have to work.

"I could be a stay-at-home mum for my kids and here I know, in July next year, I'll have to be back at work and my baby will be at daycare, costing me probably half my wage, so it's crazy.

World.title: 'Disingenous': Questions arise over timing of Government train loan
World.content:
Audio player for " Ria Bond questions timing of commuter rail announcement " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics/2292356%2Fdisingenous-questions-arise-over-timing-of-government-train-loan

Ria Bond questions timing of commuter rail announcement Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Invercargill's mayor says ratepayers should not be asked to pay for a new train service, at a time when the government is asking councils to cut down on spending.

Winston Peters and Shane Jones announced yesterday that the government would be loaning some of the money to councils for a 12-month trial Mainlander train between Christchurch, Dunedin and Invercargill as a regular service.

The Regional Infrastructure Fund will provide a loan of $3.4 million to support the project, introducing regular services between Christchurch, Ashburton, Timaru, Oamaru, Dunedin, Gore and Invercargill starting in mid-2027.

Councils are yet to sign off on the project, but are expected to fund a $1.7 million gap in the budget.

Invercargill mayor Tom Campbell told RNZ it was not fair for ratepayers to be asked to fund a train service.

"We've got a government that tells us that we must not increase our rates behind a certain point.

Listen to Caucus: Top political commentators unpick and make sense of New Zealand's election campaigns with frank and forthright discussion.

"I'm afraid an invitation to support a train is not going to be well received here."

It was not clear how many councils would be expected to help fund the service, while the Government's announcement said letters of support had been received from Christchurch, Selwyn and Waimakariri so far.

Campbell said the loan announcement came as a surprise.

"You'd almost think there's a general election coming up."

A similar train line previously known as The Southerner operated from 1970 to 2002, before stopping due to low passenger numbers.

Campbell said the service had a better chance of succeeding today, as populations across the cities had increased.

However, he said the train service needed to stand up commercially, or not at all.

Campbell said a 12-month trial period - while better than nothing - was too short for ratepayers to invest in.

Invercargill councillor Ria Bond, who had been advocating for the service to return, said the timing of the loan was "disingenuous".

"It's great that they're hanging this carrot in front of us.

"At the same time, we're being penalised because government is blaming local councils for wastage of ratepayer money."

Bond - who was formerly a NZ First MP - said a trial period was unnecessary as it was already clear that there was a market for more public transport.

"I almost feel like we're being set up to fail."

World.title: Husband of woman killed by bus calls for tougher driving tests for older drivers
World.content:
Audio player for " Pregnant woman’s death prompts call for driver checks " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/emergencies_local/2292095%2Fhusband-of-woman-killed-by-bus-calls-for-tougher-driving-tests-for-older-drivers

Pregnant woman’s death prompts call for driver checks Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The husband of a pregnant woman killed by a bus is calling for more thorough testing of older bus drivers, saying he breaks down crying at work every day thinking about her.

Olawande Braimoh, who was 36, was hit and killed by a 72-year-old bus driver in Napier on 17 April this year on a pedestrian crossing on her way to work.

The bus driver, Alma George Randell, 72, later admitted a charge of careless driving causing death, and was sentenced to a mixed sentence of community work and community detention.

The intersection where Olawande was hit is notoriously dangerous, and the council had received a number of complaints about the pedestrian crossings over the years.

Judge Earwaker said Randell drove onto the intersection under a green light and Olawande was crossing on a green signal.

However, Randell did not heed a sign requiring turning traffic to give way to pedestrians and, when he struck Olawande, he momentarily hit the accelerator in a "panic response", before applying the brake.

In an exclusive interview with RNZ, Olawande's husband Segun Braimoh, expressed his frustration over how the driver wrote to him as part of the court process, saying he didn't see her "until it was too late".

He feels that older drivers should undergo more rigourous and regular driver licence testing.

"If this driver was a younger driver I believe my wife would have been alive today.

"I try not to think about her yet, there is no single day at my workplace I don't break down and cry," he said.

NZ Transport Agency told RNZ that bus drivers who carry passengers must have a passenger 'P' endorsement, as well as appropriate driver licence class for the size of vehicle. As part of the renewal process, drivers may be required to provide a current medical certificate and must meet eyesight requirements.

"There are no additional age-based driver licence testing requirements that start at age 65. For all drivers, the senior driver licensing requirements begin at age 75.

"Drivers must renew their licence at age 75, again at 80, and every two years after that. Each time they renew from age 75 they must provide a medical certificate assessing their fitness to drive," NZTA head of driving regulation Chris Rodley said.

He said a medical assessment considered factors that may affect someone's ability to drive safely, including their physical abilities, health, eyesight, memory and thinking.

"A health practitioner can require further assessment where necessary, including an on-road safety test, specialist assessment or occupational therapy driving assessment."

But he said research from the Royal NZ College of GPs has found routine cognitive screening is not recommended.

"Health practitioners are best placed to determine what is most appropriate when assessing medical fitness to drive due to their medical training, ongoing relationship with their patients, and understanding of any underlying health concerns," Rodley said.

Napier City Council received a number of complaints about a deadly intersection before a woman was killed there earlier this year. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The police investigation shows the bus accelerated after hitting Olawande, and witnesses described hearing bus passengers scream as it happened, and seeing the bus keep moving.

Braimoh is speaking out about Olawande's death in the hope that it might result in more scrutiny of older commercial drivers.

"Not that it's going to change what has happened, but... no other family should go through this. And I hope that policies will be looked more into properly and so that someone is not going to end up that way too.

"People from 65 are retirees in New Zealand. And there's a reason why they are considered retired. But no one is talking about that," Braimoh said.

A sign says "give way to pedestrians". RNZ / Alexa Cook

The family moved to Hawke's Bay from Nigeria in 2023 and when Olawande died, she was four months pregnant. The couple have an eight year old son and Braimoh told RNZ Olawande was looking forward to expanding their family.

"She was really excited about it. My son was really looking forward to having another baby.

"She cannot be the mother of her child anymore. She cannot be the wife to her husband anymore. She cannot have a baby."

Go Bus 'deeply sorry'

Go Bus declined RNZ's request for a interview and said in a statement that their thoughts are with Olawande Braimoh's family.

"Wande's death was a tragedy, and we are deeply sorry for the loss they continue to carry.

"The driver pleaded guilty in court, and we respect the court's findings. We cooperated fully with all external investigations. Hazard awareness is a core part of training for all our drivers. After Wande's death, we carried out our own investigation into the crash and reinforced our training on busy intersections," chief operating officer Ben Barlow said.

The company said all Go Bus drivers must hold the appropriate class of licence for the vehicle they operate and a passenger endorsement.

"To keep the endorsement current, drivers must pass an NZTA fit and proper person check and regular medical and eyesight assessments. Medical checks are required at least every five years, and more often from age 75.

"Before starting with Go Bus, every driver completes a driving assessment with one of our qualified driver trainers. Drivers have ongoing and random driving assessments throughout their time with us, and receive further training where needed."

The company said its driver trainers carry out unannounced driving assessments on an ongoing basis, rather than on a fixed schedule, so drivers can be assessed at any time. It said there is a dedicated, qualified driver trainer in Hawke's Bay who supports assessment and training locally, and drivers receive further training where needed.

GoBus said it met with Olawande's family in May, and remains open to further contact with them.

Worksafe and police confirmed to RNZ they are not investigating further, but the death has been referred to the coroner.

The bus driver resigned from Go Bus after Olawande's death.

Older drivers increase risk on roads

The head of Transporting New Zealand, Dom Kalasih, told RNZ that older drivers were often talked about in the industry.

"New Zealand has an ageing workforce in terms of commercial drivers... and it is important that industry recognises that and we know the risk increases so we do need to be reviewing the risk control is currently still appropriate.

"As drivers get older risk for fitness to drive does increase - best demonstrated that under our regulations NZTA require more stringent and regular checks as people get older," Kalasih said.

He said some good transport operators go above and beyond what's required for older drivers.

World.title: How Saintly, the 'horse from heaven', won the Melbourne Cup 30 years ago
World.content:
Legendary racing trainer and "Cups King" Bart Cummings rarely showed emotion after big wins or defeats, and he always told people not to get too attached to racehorses.

But even Cummings had exceptions to the rule, and one was the "horse from heaven", Saintly.

The big-striding chestnut gelding with an army of fans gave Cummings a landmark triumph 30 years ago this week in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington.

Going into the big race, Cummings had already won a record nine Cups (his nearest rival at the time was French trainer Etienne de Mestre back in the 1800s), and his campaign to win a 10th proved to be an absolute masterclass.

In his biography, My Life, Cummings told readers there was no particular secret to winning Melbourne Cups.

"There's no magic," he wrote. "There's relentless work, discipline, adherence to your methods and plans, taking a genuine interest in the horse's welfare and above all else, plain commonsense."

Do all this, Cummings believed, and "you make your own luck".

Bart Cummings's normal plan for the Melbourne Cup included the Mackinnon Stakes on Derby Day, like Rogan Josh (right) in 1999. (Getty Images: ALLSPORT/Robert Cianflone)

There may not have been any magic, but there was a plan. A 10,000-metre prep plan, to be precise.

Cummings believed horses that ran in the cup should have completed a series of lead-up runs, and have a total of 10,000m or race distance in their legs before Melbourne Cup day.

A run on Derby Day in the Mackinnon Stakes (2,000m) or the Archer Stakes (2,500m) was usually the cherry on top, training-wise, before the Melbourne Cup three days later.

One person who saw this plan in action up close was Joe Agresta, who was trackwork rider for Cummings for 34 years. When he first saw Saintly for the first time, he wasn't overly impressed.

Joe Agresta rode trackwork for Bart Cummings for 34 years, working five of his Melbourne Cup winners including Rogan Josh (pictured). (Getty Images: ALLSPORT/Julian Herbert)

"He was a nice horse but he was a gangly type of three-year-old," Agresta says.

"Then he came out and he just blitzed them in the Carbine Club Stakes [at Flemington].

"He went back [to Sydney], and [Bart] built him up, then he came back and won the Australian Cup."

Cummings had a beautiful property near the Nepean River in Western Sydney called Princes Farm. The great trainer unofficially referred to it as "horse heaven".

Saintly was bred at Princes Farm and was born there in 1992, the year after Cummings's ninth Cup win with Let's Elope.

When Cummings nearly went bankrupt with the collapse of the Cups King syndicate in the late 1980s, Malaysian businessman Dato Tan Chin Nam was among those who helped support him to keep him afloat.

Chin Nam had owned Think Big, which had won back-to-back Melbourne Cups for Cummings in 1974 and 1975.

When Saintly was born, Cummings gave the businessman a half-share in gratitude for his help.

Saintly's three-year-old season included the Carbine Club Stakes win, and then the Australian Cup win in March 1996 marked another win at Flemington, where his long stride had plenty of room to move.

A few more runs in Sydney followed before Cummings gave Saintly a decent spell. He wouldn't return to the track for nearly five months.

Cummings's lesson learned

For his most important campaign, Saintly was running every couple of weeks in Sydney. After three runs, it was clear Cummings had expectations, but what would come next?

By this time, the permanent jockey had long been Darren Beadman, a top operator who had ridden Cummings's eighth Melbourne Cup winner on Kingston Rule in 1990.

It was early October when Saintly had his fourth and fifth runs, over the space of a weekend at Randwick in Sydney.

The chestnut ran second in the Craven Plate on the Saturday and third in the Metropolitan on Monday, although in the latter race Saintly hit the front but was flat at the end, out-finished by Hula Flight and Nothin Leica Dane.

"Bart rang me and said, 'I'm sending Saintly down [to Melbourne]. I want you to freshen up the horse, I've learned something about him,'" Agresta says.

Saintly was quickly jumping out of his skin, but Cummings didn't want to run him in the Caulfield Cup in mid-October. Instead he aimed him at the Cox Plate.

The two most famous races in Australia are the Cox Plate and the Melbourne Cup.

The Cox Plate (run over 2,040m) is known as the weight-for-age championship of Australasia, where the race does what it says on the box. Horses are given a certain weight depending on their age, with female horses (fillies and mares) given a discount because they are racing against males (colts, horses and geldings).

Then there is the Melbourne Cup, which is a handicap run over 3,200m. This kind of race sees horses given a weight (or handicap), decided by a range of factors including age and past performances. Generally it sees more weight for better horses and less weight for less experienced runners.

At least until earlier this century, the point of the exercise was to produce a hypothetical result where every runner finished together.

The reality is usually far different, but that's the aim of the game.

Up to 1996, only three horses (Nightmarch in 1929, Phar Lap in 1930 and Rising Fast in 1954) had won both the Cox Plate and the Melbourne Cup in the same year.

That year, before it was commonplace, Cummings opted for the Cox Plate as the lead-up for the Melbourne Cup, not the grand final.

The Cox Plate

Moonee Valley's narrow circuit and short finishing straight were not expected to suit Saintly in the 1996 Cox Plate. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

Some thought the Moonee Valley circuit would be too tight for Saintly. Cummings wanted a solid run in the legs of his star horse of the spring.

When the race began, Beadman kept Saintly quiet back in about sixth place near the fence.

How the Diva did the impossible, 20 years on From quiet beginnings, an unknown English filly came Down Under and changed Australia's racing history by achieving the impossible. This is how Makybe Diva won a historic third Melbourne Cup 20 years ago.

The field began to stretch out. At halfway, he was 10 lengths behind the leaders. Saintly was still sixth 700m out when Beadman began to urge his mount forward.

By the 500, Saintly was making ground going five-wide. Rounding the corner, Filante was leading on the fence narrowly from Juggler then All Our Mob. Saintly went four, five then six-wide as he briefly was on the wrong lead leg.

Watching from the stands, Agresta thought that might be the end of his chances, but once Beadman balanced Saintly up, he moved in. As the crowd roared, the gaps narrowed further, and all four horses were in it. It was Filante leading and Saintly closing.

Saintly rattled down the outside, and they called for a photo as the crowd buzzed about the frantic finish. "From where I was I thought he just got beat, but they said he won," Agresta recalls.

The lesson Cummings had learned was that Saintly didn't back up, so instead of running on Derby Day, the trainer had Agresta gallop him at Flemington.

"The clocker was a guy called Des Spain, and he said to Bart afterwards, 'You know that horse ran a quicker time than [the sprinters] go down the straight [for 1,200],'" Agresta says.

"Bart said something silly like his watch must be broken, but that's when he knew Saintly had a great chance in the Cup."

The Bart Cummings-trained Saintly carried joint-owner Dato Tan Chin Nam's famous chessboard colours with gold sleeves. (Supplied: State Library of Victoria/VRC)

Chin Nam was fascinated with the game of chess, and so his horses ran in eye-catching colours. The black and white checks were like a chessboard, while the sleeves were gold or yellow to represent the sun.

Would the sun rise on another Cummings Cup win?

The Cup itself

Only three years on from Vintage Crop's famous Flemington win, another Irish-trained horse was favourite for the Cup.

Oscar Schindler had won the Irish St Leger, and come third in the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe, so he was seen as the class horse in the race. But would he handle Australian conditions?

Saintly was not a frontrunner, but he drew barrier three for the Cup. This was a simple set-up for Cummings's horse.

"Bart never gave any instructions, but Darren knew he had to bury him [Saintly] away," Agresta says, meaning a spot on the inside.

Cummings didn't want his horse too close to the lead.

Beadman quickly had Saintly out of the ruck and into position on the fence, and by the time the field thundered past the post the first time, the gelding was neatly placed in sixth, right on the fence.

Grey Shot led from Few Are Chosen, Court of Honour and Centico. Not much changed for much of the race.

At halfway Saintly was perfectly placed, still sixth on the fence. The big chestnut had not spent a penny, until about the 800m, when Beadman shifted him off the fence and in a few strides he was into the clear.

"We were up in the stands watching it, and when Darren Beadman pulled out at the 800, he pulled out three-deep, I said, 'This is home,' because there was no way he'd pull that horse out three-deep if he didn't think it was travelling well," Agresta says.

Grey Shot still led at the turn with Nothin Leica Dane coming, but Saintly was in clear air, and he loved the long Flemington straight.

He hit the front at the 300, and soon after moved clear, as nothing could go with him.

"When Beadman let him down, he just sprinted away. It was a great effort by [Beadman and] the horse, and it was probably Bart's greatest training feat. With this horse, everything he did seemed to work," Agresta says.

Flemington erupted, as Beadman rode Saintly past the post, clear of Count Chivas and Skybeau, to clinch Cummings's 10th Cup.

Late challenges from Count Chivas and Skybeau could not stop Saintly from winning an incredible 10th Melbourne Cup for Bart Cummings. (Supplied: VRC)

It was a sign of Cummings's experience, that even 31 years after his first Cup win, he was willing to go away from his tried-and-trusted plan because of his understanding of Saintly.

"When I first started working for him, we won a couple of Group 1s and we were in the mounting yard jumping around," Agresta says.

"[Bart] said, 'Don't be like those other idiots [celebrating wildly]. We celebrate in our own time.'"

Dato Tan Chin Nam and Bart Cummings were composed at Flemington after Saintly's win, but the celebrations that night included an unlikely duet. (Supplied: VRC)

But after another Melbourne Cup win, all bets were off.

"We went to Crown Casino [that night], there were about 30 of us," Agresta recalls.

"Bart and Dato Tan Chin Nam were drinking wine, and they started singing Danny Boy!

"It was a good night. Bart never worried too much about being beaten, but I could see it: the relief and the happiness on his face; it was something special [for him] to win the Cup with Saintly."

'He nearly died': Illness in Japan

The next challenge was overseas, with the Japan Cup in Tokyo, less than a month on from the Melbourne Cup. But Saintly would not get to test himself against the best.

Saintly fell ill the night before the race. Vets would not treat the horse without the trainer's permission, because it would mean Saintly could not run in the Japan Cup. Cummings gave the OK.

"The next morning I was crying," Agresta says. "Bart said, 'What's the matter with you?'

"I said, 'I'm devastated.' He said, 'Don’t worry son, it wasn't meant to be.'"

Asked how serious the illness was in Japan, Agresta pauses and says: "He nearly died."

Bart Cummings's training base in Melbourne for four decades was eventually named Saintly Place, after the "horse from heaven". (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

Saintly came back to Australia, and began another campaign at Caulfield in early 1997 in the CF Orr Stakes. Once again he came from behind, still five lengths back at the 250m mark before storming home to win.

But within a week, he had bowed a tendon in training, and that race at Caulfield proved to be his last.

Agresta says Cummings denied that he had a particular love for Saintly, but his actions say otherwise.

"Living Legends wanted him [Saintly] to come there for them to look after him. He [Bart] said no," Agresta says.

"Graham Salisbury wanted him for the clerk of the course. [Bart] said no, 'He's going to live the rest of his life on my property.'"

And he did.

Saintly lived at Princes Farm, or horse heaven if you prefer, until he died in 2016 at the age of 24.

Cummings himself was already gone, dying at his home a year earlier. He had won two more Melbourne Cups, with Rogan Josh in 1999 and Viewed in 2008. Both horses ran on Derby Day.

A statue of Bart Cummings looks out at Flemington racecourse from an area named Saintly Place. (Getty Images: Vince Caligiuri)

His Flemington stables are also gone, turned into apartments. But there is still a Saintly Place, fittingly a section of the Flemington course Cummings made his own, complete with a life-sized statue of him.

And while no-one will ever forget the Cups King, neither will anyone who loves racing forget the "horse from heaven".

World.title: What time is the Melbourne Cup? How to watch and the weather forecast
World.content:
A strong field of Australian hopefuls and international raiders is preparing for the race that stops the nation on Tuesday.

Tuesday's Melbourne Cup will be the 166th running of the famous horse race, with rain forecast in the Victorian capital ahead of the meet.

From start time to weather forecast, below are some key things to know before the 2025 Melbourne Cup.

What time is the Melbourne Cup?

Melbourne Cup Day is held on the first Tuesday of November, which is November 3 this year.

The Melbourne Cup will be the seventh race of 10 at Flemington Racecourse.

Here are the start times for the Melbourne Cup in each state and territory, including New Zealand.

3pm AEDT: Victoria, NSW, Tasmania, ACT

2:30pm ACDT: South Australia

2pm AEST: Queensland

1:30pm ACST: Northern Territory

12pm AWST: Western Australia

5pm NZDT: New Zealand

How to watch and follow the Melbourne Cup

The Nine Network has the television rights to broadcast the 2026 Melbourne Cup.

All 10 races at Flemington will be broadcast on Channel Nine, and streamed on Nine Now.

ABC Sport will have live digital coverage of Melbourne Cup Day with a live blog. You can also listen to the live call of the Melbourne Cup on the radio, online, or via the ABC Listen app.

What is the weather forecast for the Melbourne Cup?

There is forecast to be some rain around Melbourne for Cup Day on Tuesday.

The Bureau of Meteorology has forecast between 3-15 millimetres to fall in Melbourne on Monday, with a possible morning shower on Tuesday.

There was plenty of rain in the lead-up to last year's race, won by Half Yours, with the track rated a Soft 6 for the Cup.

Who is the favourite to win the Melbourne Cup?

There will be a field of 24 for the Melbourne Cup.

The favourite to win is number 20, Point of Law.

Point Of Law showed sustained speed for an impressive win at Geelong. (Racing Photos via Getty Images: Pat Scala)

Point of Law is a UK thoroughbred, sired by the great Frankle, trained by Ciaron Maher.

The three-year-old colt has just five race starts for three wins, including the Geelong Cup last month.

World.title: Tonga and Samoa can be State of Origin for the new century
World.content:
It's not often you can feel when history is happening right around you but that is what happens when Samoa meets Tonga.

The two island nations met in the most eagerly anticipated clash of the Rugby League World Cup and in the end it was Tonga who claimed the honours with a 20-18 victory.

It sets up two classic semi-finals, where Samoa will play Australia and Tonga take on New Zealand, but that feels secondary to what happened at Parramatta on Sunday.

It took everything Tonga had and then it took a little more, with the result in the balance until the final minute of a contest that was fuelled by the power of the past and teased a golden vision of tomorrow.

As State of Origin once changed the sport by creating matches that feel as big as rugby league ever can, games like this prove Samoa and Tonga can do the same.

It can be the Origin of the new century, a rivalry without end that makes itself anew every year as a date every fan — Samoan, Tongan and otherwise, rusted-on and casual — can circle on the calendar as one of rugby league's biggest nights.

It can fill stadiums as easily as it does hearts. The crowd for this one was the highest for any sporting event at the new Parramatta Stadium and would have eclipsed last year's Lang Park total of 45,000 if only the place was bigger.

It was a mighty occasion between Tonga and Samoa in Parramatta. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

It draws in eyeballs, demands attention and adds zeroes to television deals — which means it can turn a profit, In a world where games are reduced to content on a balance sheet, that alone makes the case for more.

This was a match that delivered on its promises of blood and fire and speed and craft, and it was right that it felt timeless because rugby league is just the newest framework for something that has been happening for centuries.

What happens on the field and in the stands is the expression of a relationship that has existed between Tonga and Samoa since before either had written word.

It was already old when the colonisers came, and there are moments you can feel its power so fully and clearly you may as well be able to reach out and touch it.

It was in the steel eyes of Tim Lafai, the retired Samoan legend who grew up in a house with walls, as he led the team out dressed in traditional garb.

It was in the sound of the anthems, the notes that rose and the tears that flowed and the flags that flew, and the carnivore roaring of the cultural challenges.

It was in the ferocious tackling, as both teams dished out hits that would scare a starving dog off a meat truck. Just watching was enough to wake up with bruises in the morning.

Jarome Luai's effort to fight well out of his weight class and pop Demitric Vaimauga was the pick of a brutal bunch but Vaimauga's own effort on Spencer Leniu in the second half was near as thunderous.

Most of all, it was in the way this game felt like it was on the edge of a knife as time ran down.

Both teams were bound to play again next week, but for brief moments it seemed like tomorrow wouldn't exist for whoever end up on the wrong end of things — because they would not lose a game, but a part of themselves.

Samoa's speed put them ahead, and they seemed to be riding home the stronger, only for Tonga's power to show one last time as Addin Fonua-Blake snake-hipped past Leniu for the winning try.

A rematch in the World Cup final is possible, even as both teams are likely outsiders, but regardless this has to happen again soon. People want this and supply must meet demand.

Finding room for international football is difficult given the bloated club season but the possibilities of regular Tonga-Samoa matches feel endless, not just regarding what can happen but where it can happen.

This is a show that can play on the road — it electrifies not just in the old strongholds of Sydney, Brisbane and Auckland or new enclaves like Melbourne, but far beyond.

This game can go to so many places because it can go anywhere the Pasifika diaspora has found itself and, if rugby league wants a way into America that's more than Aussies heading over for the punt and the piss, this is it.

Samoa and Tonga's rivalry turns fans into heroes Ahead of the latest instalment of their timeless rivalry, a new generation of Samoan and Tongan stars have transformed from fans into the new heroes of their nation.

There were pre-game parades as far afield as Houston, Salt Lake City and San Francisco as the Tongan and Samoa communities bolted speakers and flags to their cars and let the Yanks know what was going down on the far side of the world.

They will do it every time because the depth of love for their people is endless and while both teams have evolved to the point where any game they play is a fair event, when they are together a special kind of alchemy occurs.

For some of the players it is bigger than a grand final, and any time you have that kind of emotional investment in this kind of spectacle at this scale it's a sin if you don't do it all the time.

An annual game would be a start. A three-match series in regular intervals would be better. They are ready to come, so get to building it.

What Samoa and Tonga have together goes beyond this sport. These games are just the newest spin on an old story.

But what a story it is, and rugby league must find a way to tell it as many times as possible.

World.title: Lebanon's team of tradies win in all-time great finish at World Cup
World.content:
Rugby league fans had been salivating over what might transpire at Western Sydney Stadium on November 1 for months.

It was the first fixture of the World Cup to sell out weeks ago.

Everyone was hyping it up as the moment we would see this tournament catch fire and the international men's game ascend to higher levels than ever seen before.

And that all transpired, except it came a game early.

There was a triple header here, the Jillaroos against Wales, followed by Lebanon and France, to whet the appetite before the main event of Tonga and Samoa.

What no-one anticipated was that Lebanon and France, two minnows who were already well out of contention for the semifinals, would dish up what is roundly being called one of the greatest finishes in the international game.

One that has proven that just because this sport does a World Cup a little differently from the rest, it doesn't diminish its meaning.

Tradies' time to shine

The vast majority of players spread through the teams in this tournament were born in Australia or New Zealand, choosing to represent the country of their heritage.

The French are a rare exception, and after humbling defeats in their first two pool games, they were the underdogs against a Lebanese squad almost entirely consisting of Australian-born players.

But this was no mismatch.

Trailing by two late, France was denied a match-winning try when Lebanon just grounded the ball in the in-goal.

France's Arthur Mourgue then kicked a two-point field goal to send it to golden point shortly after, and in the first period of extra time, Cesar Rouge slotted a one-pointer.

The scenes were beautiful, joyous, crushing, devastating, a chaotic melting pot of emotions savoured by the growing crowd of largely Tongan and Samoan fans.

But it was disallowed for an escort. And so it went on.

The Cedars' Alex Conti missed a long-range penalty goal, which was collected by Mourgue.

He should've held onto it. A more experienced player under this sort of pressure would've taken the tackle, and the quick breather.

But he went for glory, a chip and chase that could've been his crowning glory.

Instead it became his never-ending nightmare.

Abbas Miski gleefully grabbed the goodies, and strolled the short distance to unleash mayhem unlike anything else we've seen at this tournament so far.

Abbas Miski is chaired by teammates after scoring the winning try. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Most of the 30,000 tickets for this game were snapped up by Tongan and Samoan fans.

But a healthy contingent of Sydney's huge Lebanese diaspora turned up, and they were in a heady delirium, as the players danced dazed but delighted, alongside Lebanese drummers on the sidelines.

"It was the saddest I've been this whole tournament and then the happiest I've been this whole tournament. I don't even know what to feel," Lebanon captain Alex Twal told Channel 7.

"We've got plumbers, electricians, foreman, builders … these blokes came here just to have a crack and they're playing against some of the best in the world.

"Abbas, he's a winger, he's never played back row. For him to come up with a play like that, it's true Lebanese spirit.

"I've got goosebumps. I love being Lebanese."

Loading Instagram content

Twal was born a stone's throw from this stadium at Westmead. He played his junior footy for the Parramatta City Titans and his entire NRL career has been with Wests Tigers.

Born and raised in Australia, he has a Jordanian father and Lebanese mother.

It is a story similar for so many children of migrants in Australia. An identity that is multidimensional, not having to remain in one neat box, but able to feel connection to many places, roots spread near and far.

Lebanese drummers accompanied hundreds of fans marching to the stadium before the game. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

Lebanese flags flew proudly outside the stadium ahead of the game. (ABC Sport: Amanda Shalala)

And so often sport is the powerful vehicle that helps drive that message home.

That is why even though this game was a dead rubber, a result that ostensibly wouldn't change the world, it still meant something more than footy.

Because for people who have sometimes felt like they're between worlds, between cultures, there is somewhere they belong.

The hundreds of Lebanese fans who sang and marched to the beat of their traditional drums to the stadium today felt it, and no doubt many more in Australia's sizeable Lebanese community.

This may be the end of the line for the Cedars, in the short term at least.

They are ineligible for future tournaments having been downgraded to an affiliate member by the International Rugby League.

Meaning, for now, their greatest World Cup moment may very well be their last.

And the French must take heart from showing fight till the very end.

They were a team always up against it when facing players who have had league in their blood from birth.

And there will be hope they can try to inspire some sort of renaissance in the sport in the Northern Hemisphere, where it is currently on life support.

But rising from the ashes is what rugby league does best.

World.title: Australia's latest World Cup smash-up helps nobody
World.content:
Gallows humour was the order of the day for Australia's World Cup match against Wales, which was only fitting given it trudged towards its inevitable conclusion like the condemned to the executioner's block.

The Jillaroos ran out 124-6 winners in a game where the only element of contest was whether the reigning world champions could bring up the century.

They did it easily in the end, smashing their own record for biggest World Cup win, with Jaime Chapman's sixth try in the shadows of the full-time siren eclipsing France's 116-0 victory over Serbia in 2023 in the most lopsided result in women's international rugby league history.

Wales was helpless in the face of the Australian onslaught. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

In the first half, as they ran up a 60-0 lead, Australia scored 10 tries and Wales played the ball just 15 times. Five-eighth Jesse Southwell finished with 44 points on her own.

The Jillaroos did not make a tackle from the fifth minute until after the half-time siren and Australian halfback Tarryn Aiken did not make a tackle until 10 minutes before full-time.

After Australia scored its 15th try of the match it started getting booed by the sparse Parramatta Stadium crowd, who reserved their biggest cheer of the day for Welsh second rower Paige Travis's score that narrowed the gap to 100-6.

It was the sole bright spot of the match but the punters soon returned to an idle stupor as Australia added four more tries in the final seven minutes.

All World Cups are going to have their blowouts and rugby league's more than most. But they must serve a wider purpose and this one did not.

It benefited nobody and served to damage the tournament's credibility and its only legacy can be like Australia's 110-4 win over Russia in the men's 2000 World Cup, which is to say as a historical oddity for the trainspotters.

The night a rag-tag group of rugby league Russians took on the world champions Russia might only make one trip to the Rugby League World Cup but the memories forged in the 2000 tournament, especially in their record loss to Australia, are wild enough to last a lifetime.

As the women's World Cup reckons with what has been an uneven tournament at best, marred by the same enormous scorelines of the men's edition but with few of the strong crowds, questions must be asked as to why a game like this could happen at all.

The uninterested and meagre turn-out for this match was proof it did not maximise the product, which very much felt like a curtain-raiser to the two men's matches that followed. Nor does it aid development.

It stuffed some stat sheets and gave ammunition to the bad-faith actors who are always on the hunt for an opportunity to take a shot at women's sport.

The Jillaroos are the best team in the world by an order of magnitude and have been for years. They gain nothing by putting the cleaners through Wales, who exist in a different universe.

That's why the Welsh should be spared any blame for how this went down. When the criticism comes it should not fall on them.

They qualified fair and square but they did not ask for this and there's no way to say it without sounding patronising but they did their best in the face of impossible odds.

While they have Canterbury halfback Tayla Preston and North Queensland winger Sian Williams as well as a smattering of Super League talent in Bethan Daiton, Carys Marsh and Agnes Wood, most of their players ply their trade in the women's second division in England.

It's a competition that can still have the draw disrupted by forfeits and a far cry from the semi-professional existence most of the Australians lead.

Cardiff plays the same sport as the Sydney Roosters, but the two teams live in different worlds.

Some of the Welsh players had only played a handful of rugby league games before this tour and their entire coaching staff is filled by volunteers.

As Australia moves on to the semi-finals, Wales heads home with a few bumps and bruises and perhaps a few stories to tell.

It is part of the developing arm of a developing sport and while it has its place on the international scene it is not across from an Australia side who are so dominant it's starting to become a problem.

They are overwhelming against everyone they play, let alone a team from the sport's frontiers packed with players who have never taken on athletes like Chapman, Tamika Upton or Jess Sergis in their lives.

Even so, lopsided results are not an issue on their own, so long as they serve a wider purpose.

Australia's dominance looms over World Cup Ahead of the women's Rugby League World Cup, the dominance of the Jillaroos looms like a spectre.

The progress of Samoa, Fiji and Papua New Guinea through this World Cup would not have happened if they were not exposed to teams like Australia and New Zealand, even if there were growing pains.

Hours later, in the same stadium, Tonga and Samoa played out the most eagerly anticipated clash of the men's World Cup, one which could have sold out the ground twice over.

None of that happens without some blow-outs along the way.

But there are limits to what can be found amid the wreckage when a team who shouldn't be there are thrown into the fast lane.

Total obliteration leaves nothing behind. This was not a building block; this was a massacre that left no survivors.

World.title: Suns miss top four by a whisker despite win over Giants
World.content:
Gold Coast won its final game of the home and away season, but left the field shattered after letting slip the double chance in the finals.

The Suns needed a solid win to boost their percentage sufficiently to replace Carlton in fourth spot after the Blues' win over Brisbane on Saturday.

But instead their 9.8 (62) to 7.11 (53) victory at Henson Park left them just 0.2 percentage points behind Carlton.

GWS could be proud of its efforts, having fought hard before a home crowd to send off the retiring Alicia Eva and Isabel Huntington at their final game.

Eva was an inaugural AFLW player 10 years ago with Collingwood and served as the Giants' captain for five years.

Huntington was a number one draft pick and All-Australian, though three separate ACL injuries plagued her six-year career.

It seemed it was going to be a walk in the park for the Suns, who dominated the first half around the stoppage and in midfield and led the clearances 16-10 thanks to Charlie Rowbottom and Lucy Single, who had five each.

But the Giants came out with a bang in the third quarter.

They led disposals 68–46 and converted from eight of their 10 entries inside-50, kept the Suns scoreless and took an 11-point lead before the final term.

Rowbottom did everything she could in the fourth quarter to claw back the lead and kicked a goal in the dying minutes to put the Suns back in front.

She ended with 33 disposals, two goals and 12 clearances, but didn't have much to celebrate after the Suns' ninth win of the season.

"Obviously we're happy to get away with the four points, but I wanted to finish fourth," Rowbottom said post-game.

"We'll take the long way home."

Meanwhile, Essendon's 4.14 (38) to 4.7 (31) win over Collingwood handed outgoing Bombers coach Natalie Wood one last win and Pies boss Sam Wright one final loss.

In Adelaide, Melbourne franked its premiership credentials with a 6.11 (47) to 3.11 (29) victory over the Crows. The win confirmed a third-place finish for the Demons and a qualifying final date with Geelong.

In the final game of the season, Sydney held on for a thrilling one-point away win over Fremantle.

Though the Swans were already guaranteed of an elimination final against the Western Bulldogs, the 5.7 (37) to 5.6 (36) win over the Dockers will provide a timely boost on the eve of the post-season.

The Dockers even attempted to implement "Wharfie Time" during the game's final minutes, but it proved as successful as it did in the men's grand final as Chloe Molloy took a critical intercept mark to ice the game for the Swans.

Molloy kicked four of Sydney's five goals, in the process winning the league's goalkicking award.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Agony and ecstasy for Australian duo in WNBA Finals game seven
World.content:
Opal Miela Sowah has etched her name in Australian women's basketball history books as her Golden State Valkyries overcame Izzy Borlase's Atlanta Dream 68-63 to win the WNBA championship.

The 26-year-old entered the league's first-ever game seven at San Francisco's Chase Centre on Saturday (Sunday AEDT) looking to join the 11 previous Australian winners of the top women's basketball competition in the world.

That list includes some of the country's biggest basketball names such as Lauren Jackson and Penny Taylor, while Sowah was also aiming to become the first Australian winner since Cayla George in 2023.

The Opal didn't take the court as she is on a player development contract, making her ineligible to feature in the playoffs.

But Sowah was an avid supporter from the sidelines, as she helped spur on Gabby Williams to a masterclass as the forward posted 30 points and four blocks.

Of those, 28 were in the second half — a WNBA finals record for most points by a player in a half.

Izzy Borlase had some big moments as her Dream went down in game seven. (Getty Images: Matthew Huang)

Ex-Bendigo Spirit star Veronica Burton was also busy, registering 10 points, 11 rebounds and five assists to help Golden State claim a maiden championship in the franchise's second season.

While Sowah will bask in title glory, her Opals teammate Borlase will not after her team missed a golden opportunity to claim a historic first championship.

The 22-year-old played another important role off the bench as she recorded eight points and two rebounds in 14 minutes of game time.

Her best moment came in the third quarter when she coolly sank a three to end the Valkyries' 6-0 run before she later drove to the basket and earned a three-point play in the fourth period.

A title would have capped off a remarkable year for Borlase, who became the WNBL's youngest MVP in 15 years, made her Women's World Cup debut with the Opals and played her first minutes in the American league.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

Tech.title: Apple’s HomeView could add security camera features
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Reddit user pdfu found hints hidden in the HomeView 27.2 code that Apple could be adding security camera features to its smart home hub. The strings describe a security camera mode with motion detection, live streaming, and recording options, as well as privacy functions. According to pdfu, there is a setup page that even explicitly reads: “Your HomeView can be used as a security camera with HomeKit Secure Video.”

Supposedly, the video feeds will only be visible to members of the home, and will both show an indicator light and play a sound when either someone is watching the camera feed or when it starts to record. Home members will also get a notification anytime settings are changed for the Secure Video mode. It will also include customizable options for what to detect, stream, or record, based on whether you’re home, away, or asleep.

Some wondered why Apple did not allow HomeView to double as a security camera at launch, and the company hasn’t said anything to suggest the features are coming. But, considering how central privacy is to Apple’s marketing, the company may be waiting to fine-tune those features before launch.

Tech.title: A fully playable version of Portal prequel F-Stop leaked
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Leakers have pieced together a playable version of the canceled Portal prequel F-Stop. Most of the assets came from the massive 12-terabyte leak that dropped this August. That didn’t include the game’s source code or map data, but those final pieces apparently hit the Valve Cut Content Discord this week, allowing a nearly complete version to be pieced together.

Some dialog and elements of F-Stop eventually found their way into Portal 2. But it differs dramatically from the mainline Portal games in that it’s built around a camera mechanic that lets you capture an item by taking its picture and place it elsewhere using the resulting Polaroid-like photos. It’s not unlike Viewfinder in that way.

The game is short, with videos showing off its full campaign all clocking in at under an hour. That’s not terribly surprising, though. F-Stop was developed as part of the “Directed Design Experiments,” a three-month period in 2007 when Valve broke into five teams to build new video game experiments.

Tech.title: North Korea linked to massive Binance crypto heist
Tech.content:
North Korea Responsible for $6 Billion+ Binance Attack

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026. The FBI refers to this specific North Korean malicious cyber activity as “TraderTraitor.”

The FBI, together with partners at the USSS and IRS-CI, has observed TraderTraitor actors converting stolen assets primarily into Ethereum (ETH). It is expected these assets will then be further laundered by converting them using DeFi and instant swap services as they prepare them for further laundering stages.

Tech.title: HomePod Mini 2 first look: Three things I love and one disappointment
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When I first heard about the new $149 HomePod Mini 2 at Apple’s Welcome Home event last month, I was disappointed. It’s been six years since Apple launched its entry-level smart speaker, and all it got in the second gen was a chip bump, some color glowy stuff, and better AirPlay? For $50 more than the original, which launched at $99, Apple didn’t even upgrade the sound system. It felt like the company phoned this one in.

Now that I’ve got my hands on a couple and set them up in my home office, I’m more enthused. The Mini 2 is so much faster than the first-gen Mini, playing music in a few seconds and responding to smart home commands just as quickly. If you’re fed up with standing over your HomePod waiting for it to finally do what you asked, then that alone is worth the upgrade.

Here are my three favorite features of the new Mini 2 after spending a couple days with it, and my one big disappointment.

Siri is much snappier and much less chatty

The biggest upgrade for the Mini 2 is Siri AI, but that isn’t available yet. Apple says it’s coming “later” in a software update. However, the basic smart voice assistant has definitely improved. Siri on the Mini 2 is much snappier than on the first-gen Mini, regularly responding in under three seconds. This is thanks to a newer, faster processor (the S10, up from the S5) and Wi-Fi 6E support (up from Wi-Fi 4).

When I asked Siri to play Taylor Swift, a song started in a couple of seconds. It correctly told me who won this year’s World Series in under two seconds, and turned off the light or opened the shades in under three seconds.

That’s a huge improvement over the up to 10 seconds I often have to wait for Siri to get things done on the first-gen Mini. However, asking something harder, like who will win the US midterm elections, still brings up the familiar offer to look at some web results on my iPhone. As I said, Siri AI isn’t here yet.

The other new behavior I am really enjoying is that when I ask Siri to perform a smart home action, such as open the shades or turn on the lights, instead of “OK, Jen,” or “One sec,” followed by a wordy confirmation of the action that I often get on the first-gen Mini, the Mini 2 just does it and doesn’t talk back. It’s not silent for every action, but it’s quiet enough to be a noticeable improvement.

This Mini is gorgeous in green and sounds great

The green color is divine. This is the prettiest small smart speaker I’ve seen — and I’ve tried them all.

Yes, Amazon’s Echo Dot Max’s purple is fun, the Google Home Speaker’s pale green is elegant, but Apple’s deep green is seriously sophisticated. It’s a color that fits in really well in various places around my home, and I’m so glad the company finally released a green option. It’s a big improvement over the slightly garish yellow and orange of the prior-gen Minis and the best of the new colors.

The Mini in green. Other than the color, it looks identical to the first-gen speaker. It comes with a power brick and a color-matched fabric cord. The cord is very pale green, practically white. The base now has an embossed logo instead of a painted one.

I saw all the colors in person at Apple’s Welcome Home event, and while the pink is pretty, it’s very pale, and the blue is functionally identical to the first-gen blue, maybe a shade lighter. While a lot of folks will be happy with black (don’t get white unless you plan to dust it regularly), the green is my new go-to.

Two green HomePod Mini 2s look so good on the walnut Nanoleaf monitor stand I’m testing; it’s like my office got an instant upgrade. And while Apple didn’t update the speakers in the Mini 2, it’s still a very good speaker for its size, doing a fine job with Bad Bunny’s bass and delivering clear mids and vocals. While $300 is steep for computer speakers, two as a stereo pair in my office definitely delivered on room-filling sound.

You can finally disable touch

A few weeks ago I fumbled for my phone on my nightstand and accidentally hit the top of my HomePod Mini, blaring music in the bedroom at 3AM. My husband was not happy.

Sound Glow illuminates the top of the Mini in colors that match the album art. It only works with Apple Music and Apple Podcasts.

A new setting in the Home app now lets you lock the Mini’s top controls. This goes for all HomePods, old and new, and it’s a major quality-of-life upgrade. How often do you intentionally touch the top of your HomePod? I bet far less often than accidentally!

The other new trick for the top of the HomePod is Sound Glow. This makes the LEDs display colors that match the album art of the song you’re playing (it’s also backward compatible with the first-gen Mini and the second-gen HomePod). It’s neat, but only works with Apple Music and Podcasts and is so subtle that I don’t feel it adds much to my music-listening experience.

A stereo pair of Minis sounds very good. Here they’re pictured on Nanoleaf’s new monitor stand, which has built-in LED lighting.

Signature feature fail

Beyond the speed improvement, the other new feature I was excited about is the HomePod Mini 2’s ability to be the default speaker for your Mac using what Apple calls “a responsive and persistent AirPlay connection.” This creates a wireless point-to-point connection between the computer and the HomePod.

You can pair a single speaker or a stereo pair to your Mac, and the feature also works with the second-gen HomePod. (Two or four HomePod Mini 2s can also now be part of a surround sound setup using the new Apple TV 4K.)

Disappointingly, I couldn’t get the Mac speaker set up to work. I have the required hardware: a Mac that supports Wi-Fi 6E, running the public release of macOS 27.2 (a Mac Mini M4), and HomePods on HomePod Software 27.2. But the Sound pane in my Mac’s settings didn’t offer an option to set a HomePod via AirPlay as the default sound output.

The Mini showed up and connected like any other AirPlay speaker, with the same flaws as regular AirPlay — occasional artifacting, drop-offs, and some lag with notification sounds — along with the Mac defaulting to its built-in speakers when the computer restarts, or anytime I activate Siri on the HomePod. I also tried with a stereo pair of Minis, but they also played over regular AirPlay.

The chip bump and speed improvements make this a bigger upgrade than it initially seemed

According to a 9to5Mac’s hands-on, when the persistent AirPlay is enabled, the HomePod Mini should show up as a default system output device in the System Information, and there should be an option to enable it under “Play sound effects through” in the Sound pane in System Settings, but neither was there for me. I have seen other reports of the same issue.

I tried resetting both HomePods completely after they updated to 27.2 out of the box (I was on the HomePod Software betas, but 27.2 is now in general release), and the feature still isn’t working. I reached out to Apple, but the company hasn’t responded to my requests yet; I’ll update this article if I hear back or find a solution.

There’s more to come

I’ve only been testing the Mini 2 for two days, and while the real test will come when it gets its Siri AI upgrade, the chip bump and speed improvements make this a bigger upgrade than it initially seemed. Apple does need to work on the Mac pairing feature; it has a lot of potential, but based on my struggles here, it feels unfinished.

I plan to do a full review once Siri AI launches, and of course compare it to Apple’s big new smart home release: the upcoming $299 Apple HomeView smart display. It is also a Home hub, but the screen gives it more functionality. At $149, though, the Mini 2 is now the cheapest way to get an Apple Home hub with Thread and Matter support.

Tech.title: New Zelda and GTA represent a games industry that no longer exists
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the biggest game releases of the year, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepbackhere.

How it started

The two biggest games of 2026 are set to launch just a few weeks apart in November.

On the one side you have the behemoth that is Grand Theft Auto VI, an experience 13 years in the making, and the sequel to one of the best-selling games in history. Its predecessor, GTA V, has sold a staggering 230 million copies since it launched in 2013, and was re-released across three generations of consoles. Developer Rockstar is a pioneer in the realm of open-world games, dating back to GTA III, and the scale and ambitions of those worlds have steadily grown since then. With GTA V and later Red Dead Redemption 2, the studio’s ideas reached a new level of realism. And the sixth GTA looks poised to eclipse them both, which has created an unprecedented level of demand.

Analyst firm Circana estimates that 29 percent of gamers in the US intend to buy the game, with demand so large it could boost flagging console sales. “Many consumers who have yet to upgrade to a current-generation console may choose to purchase a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series specifically to play the title,” analyst Mat Piscatella says in a statement. GTA VI’s reach is so vast that almost every other major game launched early to avoid it.

The one exception is Nintendo. The company’s tentpole release for the holidays, and its next major exclusive for the Switch 2, is a lavish remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

The release is notable for a few reasons. For one thing, it’s an attempt from Nintendo to modernize one of the most influential and beloved games in its long history. The original Ocarina of Time was the world’s first introduction to a 3D iteration of Hyrule, which, in turn, made it an early glimpse at what was possible in three-dimensional spaces, laying a blueprint for countless games that came afterward. Nintendo has since expanded on that, turning Switch-era adventures Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom into wide-open adventures designed for player creativity. They went on to become some of the best-selling games for Nintendo’s most successful console.

These aren’t just two blockbuster games – they’re two series with the pull to make this a real cultural moment, akin to “Barbenheimer” but for video games. They’re the kind of launches that make it onto Saturday Night Live and have NBA players worried.

It’s just too bad about the rest of the industry.

How it’s going

These major November releases are something of a mirage, two outliers that stand out amid the wreckage that is the rest of the video game industry. While there have been plenty of major releases and great games this year, the main theme of 2026 has been just how dire things have become. Layoffs, studio closures, unpopular business models, the ever-looming threat of AI, and massive increases in hardware costs have combined to create an ominous cloud over the medium.

What happens next

It’s not all doom and gloom. There have been rare success stories, where studios like FromSoftware and Remedy have managed to carve out a sustainable existence in a turbulent field. But for the most part, the established norms that have been part of the blockbuster games industry for years are going away. Big games are too expensive to make, hardware is too expensive to buy (and the cost is only going up), and somewhere, something has to give.

It’s tempting to look at Zelda and GTA as answers to these problems. After all, if Nintendo and Rockstar are doing so well, there must be a solution out there. But they’re also two very specific cases that are essentially impossible to replicate. Nintendo maintains ownership over all aspects of its platform, from the hardware to the games, and it has taken a careful and largely risk-averse approach that has allowed it to weather the current storm and create a growing entertainment empire. Rockstar, meanwhile, is the rare example of being too big to fail. GTA V was so massive for so long — Circana says it was among the top 20 best-selling games in the US for 13 straight years — that it allowed the studio to build up both an unprecedented amount of anticipation and, it seems, a game big enough to match it.

In that way, Zelda and GTA are throwbacks to a time when major games were sure bets. Their duelling releases are fascinating both because these games are so impactful, but also because, with all of the impending upheaval, the industry might never see a moment like this again.
